content.topicNotes: 3D Printers What is a 3D printer A 3D printer is an output device that creates physical objects from digital models. 3D printing is an example of additive manufacturing. Additive manufacturing builds objects layer by layer. Subtractive manufacturing removes material to shape an object. A digital model is required before printing begins. How 3D printers work The digital model is sliced into thin layers by software. The printer deposits material layer by layer. Direct printing extrudes material through a nozzle. Direct printing pushes melted material out to form layers. Binder printing joins powdered material using a liquid binder. Binder printing sprays a binding agent onto powder. Uses of 3D printers Engineers use 3D printers to create prototypes quickly. Schools use 3D printers in design and technology lessons. Doctors produce medical models and prosthetics. Manufacturers create custom parts and tools. Hobbyists design and print personalised objects. Advantages and disadvantages Advantages of 3D printing Complex shapes can be produced easily. Additive manufacturing reduces material waste. Rapid prototyping speeds up product development. Disadvantages of 3D printing Printing can be slow for large objects. 3D printers can be expensive to purchase and maintain. Available materials may be limited compared to traditional manufacturing.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Input & Output Devices > Output Devices

content.topicNotes: Automated Teller Machines (ATMs) What is an ATM An automated teller machine (ATM) is a computer-based banking system. ATMs allow customers to access bank accounts without staff assistance. A computer controls all ATM operations. Users authenticate using a bank card and a personal identification number (PIN). ATMs are available in banks and public locations. Services provided by ATMs ATMs allow users to withdraw cash. Account balances can be checked using an ATM. Some ATMs allow deposits of cash or cheques. Funds can be transferred between accounts. Mini statements can be printed. How ATMs work A card reader reads data stored on the bank card. The user enters a PIN using a keypad. The ATM communicates with the bank’s computer system. The system checks account details and authorises transactions. Cash is dispensed automatically if approved. Advantages and disadvantages Advantages Banking services are available 24 hours a day. Queues inside banks are reduced. Disadvantages ATMs can be targeted by criminals. Technical faults can prevent transactions.

content.topicNotes: Actuators What is an actuator An actuator is an output device that causes a physical action. It converts electrical signals from a computer into movement. Actuators control mechanical systems. They are used in automated and control systems. Actuators do not produce visual or audio output. Types of actuators Electric motors are actuators that produce rotational movement. A motor converts electrical energy into mechanical energy. Solenoids are actuators that create linear movement. Linear movement is movement in a straight line. Relays act as switches controlled by electrical signals. Uses of actuators Actuators are used in automatic doors to open and close. Washing machines use actuators to rotate the drum. Heating systems use actuators to control valves. Robots use actuators to move arms and wheels. Traffic lights use actuators to control signals. Advantages and disadvantages An advantage is that actuators enable automatic control of systems. An advantage is reduced need for human intervention. A disadvantage is that actuators require power to operate. A disadvantage is that mechanical parts can wear out. Faulty actuators may cause system failure.

content.topicNotes: Adjusting Brightness and Contrast Understanding Brightness Users adjust brightness to control the overall lightness or darkness of an image. Brightness: the relative intensity of light emitted or reflected by an image. Reducing brightness helps correct an overexposed photo to make it look more natural. Overexposed: a term for an image that is too bright because it was exposed to too much light. Increasing brightness makes a dark or underexposed image much easier to see. Adjusting Contrast Users modify contrast to change the difference between the darkest and lightest parts of a graphic. Contrast: the scale of difference between the blackest shadows and the whitest highlights in an image. High contrast makes shadows darker and highlights brighter, creating a more dramatic and vivid look. Low contrast reduces the difference between tones, making the image appear flatter or more grey. Practical ICT Applications Designers balance brightness and contrast to ensure that image details remain visible during the printing process. Poorly adjusted images may hide important features in very dark shadows or very bright highlights. Technicians often use these tools to enhance scanned documents or low-quality photographs for school publications. Accurate adjustments help maintain the professional standard required for ICT project portfolios.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Images > Images

content.topicNotes: Advanced Tables Rowspan The rowspan attribute allows a cell to span multiple rows. A cell with rowspan extends vertically across rows. Web developers use rowspan to avoid repeating information. This feature improves table organisation. Colspan The colspan attribute allows a cell to span multiple columns. A cell with colspan extends horizontally across columns. Web developers use colspan to create grouped headings. This feature improves readability. Table and Cell Sizes Web developers can set table sizes using pixels or percentages. Pixels create fixed sizes such as 500px. Percentage values create flexible sizes such as 80%. Percentage sizes adapt more easily to different screen sizes. Applying Styles Styles change the appearance of a table. Web developers can apply colours, borders and text formatting. Consistent styles improve readability. Styles help tables match the design of a website. Instead of using HTML attributes like <table width="80%">, sizes should be set using CSS properties. Meeting User Needs Web developers choose table features based on the audience. Large cells and clear layouts improve accessibility. Complex tables should remain easy to understand. Appropriate formatting helps users read data quickly.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Website Authoring > Creating a Web Page

content.topicNotes: Microprocessor-Controlled Devices in Transport What are microprocessor-controlled transport systems Microprocessor-controlled transport systems use computers to manage vehicle functions. A microprocessor processes data from sensors and controls outputs. Systems operate automatically according to programmed instructions. Transport systems include cars, trains and aircraft. Sensors provide real-time data such as speed and distance. Rail and airline network control Rail networks use central control systems to monitor train positions. Track sensors send data to control centres. Signals are controlled automatically to prevent collisions. Airlines use computer systems to manage flight routes and schedules. Air traffic control systems track aircraft and maintain safe distances. Advantages in transport Microprocessors improve safety through systems such as anti-lock braking. Automated signalling reduces human error on railways. Air traffic control systems improve flight safety. Navigation systems optimise routes and reduce travel time. Traffic flow is improved using computer-controlled signals. Disadvantages in transport Advanced systems increase the cost of vehicles and infrastructure. Software faults can disrupt rail or airline networks. Cyberattacks may target transport control systems. Over-reliance on automation may reduce human vigilance. Power or system failures can cause widespread disruption.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > The Effects of Using IT > Microprocessor-controlled Devices in Transport

content.topicNotes: Booking Systems What is a booking system A booking system is computer software used to reserve services or resources. Booking systems manage availability and reservations automatically. Common uses include travel, events, and accommodation. Data is stored in a central database. Real-time processing is essential to guarantee immediate database updates. Users can make bookings online or through terminals. Advantages of booking systems Booking systems operate 24 hours a day. Availability is updated instantly after each booking. Human errors such as double-booking are reduced. Customers can book services remotely. Businesses save time and administrative effort. Disadvantages of booking systems System failures can prevent bookings. Technical problems may cause data loss. Users require internet access. Setup and maintenance costs can be high. Some users may prefer human assistance. Examples of booking systems Airlines use booking systems to reserve seats. Hotels use booking systems to manage room availability. Cinemas use booking systems to sell tickets. Hospitals use booking systems for appointments. Transport services use booking systems for schedules. Examples of Booking Systems Booking a flight Booking a hotel room Booking a concert Booking a sport event
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > ICT Applications > Booking Systems

content.topicNotes: Advantages and Disadvantages of Conference Types Audio conferencing Audio conferencing allows communication using sound only. Advantages Audio conferencing uses low bandwidth. Audio conferencing works well on slow internet connections. Disadvantages Visual information cannot be shared. Audio-only communication can reduce engagement. Video conferencing Video conferencing allows participants to see and hear each other. Advantages Visual cues improve communication and understanding. Meetings feel more personal than audio-only calls. Disadvantages Video conferencing requires higher bandwidth. Poor connections can cause lag or frozen video. Web conferencing Web conferencing combines audio, video and screen sharing. Advantages Documents and presentations can be shared live. Collaboration is improved during meetings. Disadvantages Web conferencing software can be complex to use. High system and network requirements are needed.

content.topicNotes: Advantages and Disadvantages of User Interfaces Command Line Interface (CLI) A command line interface uses text commands typed by the user. Advantages It uses very little memory and processing power. Experienced users can work very quickly. Disadvantages Users must remember exact commands and correct syntax. It is difficult for beginners to learn. Graphical User Interface (GUI) A graphical user interface uses icons, windows and menus. Advantages It is easy to learn and user-friendly. Users do not need to memorise commands. Disadvantages It uses more memory and processing power. It can be slower for expert users. Voice Activated Assistants Advantages Hands-free operation, quick access to information, and can help users with accessibility needs. Can control smart home devices using voice commands. Disadvantages May misunderstand accents, speech or background noise. Requires an internet connection for many features. Privacy concerns, as voice data may be recorded or processed. Gesture-Based Interface A gesture-based interface uses physical movements detected by sensors. Advantages Interaction feels natural and intuitive. No keyboard or mouse is required. Disadvantages Gestures may be misinterpreted by the system. Specialist hardware is often required.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Types & Components of Computer Systems > User Interfaces

content.topicNotes: Advantages and Disadvantages of Computer Types Desktop computers Desktop computers are designed for use at a fixed location. Advantages Desktop computers offer high performance for demanding tasks. Internal components can be easily upgraded or replaced. Disadvantages Desktop computers are not portable. A fixed workspace and mains power supply are required. Laptop computers Laptop computers are portable computers with built-in components. Advantages A laptop computer can be used in different locations. A rechargeable battery allows use without mains power. Disadvantages Hardware upgrades are limited. Battery life restricts usage time. Smartphones Smartphones are handheld computers with mobile network connectivity. Advantages Smartphones combine communication and computing features. A wide range of apps is available for different tasks. Disadvantages Small screens limit productivity. Smartphones are less powerful than laptops or desktop computers. Tablets and phablets Tablets and phablets are portable touch-screen computers. Advantages Touch screens provide intuitive interaction. Battery life is usually longer than laptops. Disadvantages Typing long documents is difficult using on-screen keyboards. Professional software support is limited.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Types & Components of Computer Systems > Types of Computer

content.topicNotes: Advantages of Cloud Computing Lower costs Cloud computing reduces the need to buy expensive hardware. Users pay only for the services they use through subscriptions. Organisations save money on maintenance and upgrades. Easy access Users access files and software from any device with Internet access. This supports working and learning from different locations. Data remains available even if a local device fails. The systems often have high availability, meaning that the users can access the systems even if one component fails, due to built-in redundancy. Automatic updates The service provider updates software automatically. Users always work with the latest version of applications. This reduces security risks and saves time for users. Scalable resources Cloud services adjust storage and processing power when needed. Scalability means the system increases or decreases resources easily. This helps organisations handle changes in demand efficiently.

content.topicNotes: Align Headers, Footers, and Tab Stops Default Tab Stops Word processors insert predefined tab stops automatically inside headers and footers. Tab stops are preset horizontal positions where the text cursor moves when you press the Tab key. The system sets a center tab stop in the middle of the margin boundaries. The system configures a right tab stop precisely at the right margin line. Modifying page margins requires updating header and footer tab stops to ensure right-aligned items remain aligned. Header and footer content must stay within the set page limits and avoid colliding with the body text. Three-Part Alignment Users achieve three separate alignments on a single line using default tab stops. Alignment refers to the positioning of text relative to the page margins. Left-aligned text starts immediately at the left margin without pressing Tab. Centered text requires the user to press the Tab key once. Right-aligned text requires the user to press the Tab key a second time. Custom Tab Alignment Students clear or alter default alignment positions using the Ruler bar. Ruler bar is a visual measuring scale displayed at the top of the workspace. Left-clicking on the ruler inserts custom alignment markers at precise coordinates. Dragging these custom markers left or right repositions the corresponding text dynamically. Decimal Tab Stops Word processors offer decimal tab stops to organize numbers neatly. This special marker aligns tabbed text so that numeric data sits around a fixed position. The software anchors figures automatically so that the decimal points match up vertically. Decimal tab stops are markers that align columns of numbers by their decimal points.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Layout > Headers & Footers

content.topicNotes: Analogue & Digital Data Analogue Data Analogue data changes smoothly and continuously over time. It can take any value within a range rather than fixed discrete steps. For example, there is an infinite amount of possible numbers between 5 and 7 or there is an infinite amount of different colours in a rainbow. There are no fixed steps in its colour spectrum. Sensors collect analogue data from the real world. Examples include sound waves, temperature, and light intensity. Digital Data Digital data uses discrete values instead of continuous changes. For example, traffic lights usually only can light up in 3 different colours. Red, yellow and green are the only discrete values, that are possible. There are no colours between. Computers store digital data using binary numbers. Binary means base two and uses only 0 and 1. A bit is a Binary Digit and stores one 0 or 1. Comparing Analogue and Digital Analogue data is continuous and often represents real-world values more naturally. Digital data is discrete with fixed steps and is more accurate when storing and copying information. Digital data resists noise, which is unwanted interference. Computers prefer digital data for reliability. Analogue to Digital Conversion Computers cannot process analogue data directly. An Analogue Digital Converter (ADC) converts analogue data into digital data. The ADC samples the signal at regular intervals. Sampling means measuring the signal value at a moment in time. Digital to Analogue Conversion Some output devices need analogue signals to work. A Digital Analogue Converter (DAC) changes digital data into analogue signals. Speakers use a DAC to produce sound waves. The output becomes continuous again.

content.topicNotes: Anti-Malware Software What is malware Malware is software designed to harm computer systems or data. Malware includes viruses, worms, spyware and ransomware. A virus is a program that can copy itself and damage files. Malware can spread through networks and the internet. Malware is a major network security threat. What is anti-malware software Anti-malware software is used to detect and remove malicious software. Anti-malware software scans files, programs and network activity. The software compares files against known malware signatures. A signature is a unique pattern used to identify malware. Anti-malware helps protect systems and networks. How anti-malware software works The software scans files in real time or on demand. Heuristic analysis detects suspicious behaviour, which can trigger alerts and help early identification of malware. Infected files may be quarantined. Quarantine means isolating files so they cannot cause harm. Frequent updates improve detection of new threats. Advantages and limitations Advantages Anti-malware software reduces the risk of infection. Automatic scanning provides continuous protection. Disadvantages New malware may not be detected immediately. Scans can slow down system performance.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Networks and the Effects of Using Them > Network Issues: Security

content.topicNotes: Arithmetic in Spreadsheets Entering Formulas Spreadsheet cells can contain formulae, which always start with an equals "=" sign. A formula is a mathematical expression that calculates new values from existing cell data. The equals sign instructs the spreadsheet to calculate the result instead of displaying raw text. Users typically use cell referencing when entering formulae. Using Cell References Formulae use cell references to link data dynamically across a spreadsheet model. A cell reference is the unique address of a cell formed by its column letter and row number. Typing "=A1+B1" adds the values inside those two specific boxes together automatically. The formula updates the calculated total instantly whenever a user modifies the underlying cell data. Arithmetic Operators Spreadsheets use specific arithmetic operators to perform basic calculations. Addition: the "+" sign. Subtraction: the "-" sign. Multiplication: the "*" symbol. Division: the "/" symbol. Indices (powers): the "^" symbol. Order of Operations Spreadsheets strictly follow the rules of BIDMAS to evaluate mathematical expressions. BIDMAS is an acronym that defines the correct sequence of operations: Brackets, Indices, Division, Multiplication, Addition, and Subtraction. Users must place brackets carefully to control which numbers add or multiply first.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Spreadsheets > Data Models

content.topicNotes: Artificial Blood Vessels What they are Artificial blood vessels replace damaged or blocked natural vessels. Surgeons use them to restore normal blood flow. Computers help design vessels to match patient needs. Computer design Specialists design vessels using Computer Aided Design (CAD). CAD means software creates precise digital models. Computers calculate correct size, shape, and thickness. This improves safety and accuracy. Simulation and testing Computers simulate blood flow through artificial vessels. A simulation tests how something works without real surgery. This helps identify problems before implantation. Benefits for patients Artificial vessels reduce the risk of heart attacks and strokes. Computer use lowers surgical risks and errors. Patients recover faster with well-designed implants.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > ICT Applications > Computers in Medicine

content.topicNotes: Artificial Intelligence (AI) What is artificial intelligence Artificial intelligence (AI) is technology that allows computers to perform tasks that normally require human intelligence. Human intelligence includes learning, decision-making and problem-solving. AI systems analyse data to identify patterns and make decisions. AI can improve its performance over time using experience. AI is used in many everyday digital systems. Impact of AI in everyday life AI is used in voice assistants to recognise and respond to speech. Recommendation systems suggest videos, music or products based on user behaviour. Navigation apps use AI to predict traffic and suggest faster routes. Smart home devices use AI to automate heating and lighting. These systems improve convenience and efficiency. Impact of AI in work and industry AI is used in manufacturing to control robots and monitor quality. Businesses use AI to analyse large amounts of data quickly. Customer service chatbots answer common questions automatically. A chatbot is a program that simulates human conversation. AI can increase productivity and reduce costs. Advantages of artificial intelligence AI can process data faster and more accurately than humans. AI systems can work continuously without fatigue. Automation of repetitive tasks saves time. AI can improve safety by handling dangerous jobs. Decision-making can be more consistent. Disadvantages of artificial intelligence AI may replace some jobs previously done by humans. Development and maintenance of AI systems can be expensive. AI decisions depend on the quality of data used. Bias in data can lead to unfair outcomes. Over-reliance on AI may reduce human skills.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Types & Components of Computer Systems > Impact of Emerging Technologies

content.topicNotes: Audience & Presenter Notes Audience Notes (Handouts) Audience notes are documents printed from a presentation software to distribute to the attendees. Handouts are structured layouts containing scaled-down versions of slides alongside blank lines for participants to write their own notes on. They help listeners follow along during a dense or highly detailed slideshow. Providing physical sheets allows the audience to review the technical data after the briefing has finished. Presenter Notes (Speaker Notes) Presenter notes are hidden reminders added to individual slides that only the person giving the talk can see. Speaker notes reference a dedicated text panel beneath the main slide workspace used to input key talking points. They assist the speaker by prompting them on complex figures and cues without cluttering the digital layout. Utilizing Presenter View displays these prompts on a private monitor while the audience looks at the clean slides on a secondary screen. Benefits of Notes Separating visible information from underlying data keeps the visual presentation highly professional. Presenters maintain better eye contact and pacing because they do not have to read text directly off the main projection screen. Handouts reduce the pressure on attendees to copy down every word during the live event. Both types of notes work together to ensure the content of presentations is communicated effectively.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Presentations > Edit Presentations

content.topicNotes: Analysing Audiences What is Audience Analysis? Audience analysis means identifying the characteristics of the people who will use or view a product. Audience analysis helps designers create content that is suitable and effective. Designers consider factors such as age, gender, interests, and technical ability. Understanding the audience ensures the product meets their needs and expectations. Purpose of the Product The purpose of a product influences the design choices a creator makes. An educational website for children uses different fonts and images than a business report. Designers match the tone, layout, and content to the intended purpose. Mismatching purpose and design can confuse or alienate the audience. Gathering Audience Information Designers collect information about their audience before creating a product. Questionnaires and surveys allow designers to gather opinions directly from users. A questionnaire is a set of written questions used to collect data from respondents. Interviews and focus groups provide more detailed feedback from potential users. Analysing existing products helps designers understand what the audience already expects.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Audience > Audience Appreciation

content.topicNotes: Analysing the Needs of an Audience Age and Technical Ability Designers adapt content based on the age group of the target audience. The target audience is the specific group of people a product is designed for. Younger audiences benefit from larger text, bright colours, and simple language. Adult audiences use smaller text, softer colours, and structured information like tables or charts. Technical ability describes how confident a user is with technology. A novice user needs simpler interfaces than an expert user. Accessibility Needs Accessibility means designing products so that all users can access and use them effectively. Designers consider users with visual impairments by using high-contrast colours and alt text. Alt text is a written description of an image used by screen readers. Audio content should include subtitles or transcripts for users with hearing difficulties. Considering accessibility ensures the product reaches the widest possible audience. Cultural and Language Considerations Designers consider the cultural background and language of their target audience. Using appropriate language ensures the content is clear and respectful. Symbols, colours, and images can carry different meanings in different cultures. Providing multiple language options increases a product's reach and usability.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Audience > Audience Appreciation

content.topicNotes: Audio and Video Editing Audio Editing Software Audio editing software allows users to record, cut, and join sound clips. Users can add effects such as fade in, fade out, and noise reduction. Audio editing is used for podcasts, music production, and voiceovers. Video Editing Software Video editing software allows users to trim clips and arrange them on a timeline. Users can add transitions, titles, and background music. Video editing is used for films, school projects, and social media content. Key Editing Tasks Users can crop and resize media to focus on important parts. Users can adjust brightness, contrast, and colour balance for video. Users can export the final work into a suitable file format for sharing.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Types & Components of Computer Systems > Applications Software

content.topicNotes: Audio and Video Adding media You can add audio or video files to a web page using HTML tags. Use the <audio> tag to insert sound files. Use the <video> tag to insert video files. Media can make a website more interactive and engaging. Text placed inside the <video> container displays only if a user's browser cannot play the file format. Media controls Controls allow users to play, pause and adjust media. Add the controls attribute to display media buttons. Remove the controls attribute if users should not see playback options. Users can control media only when controls are available. Autoplay Autoplay starts media automatically when a web page loads. Add the autoplay attribute to enable automatic playback. Autoplay can annoy users or increase data usage. Designers should use autoplay carefully. Choosing media settings Web designers choose settings based on the audience's needs. Educational websites may display controls so users can replay content. Background music may hide controls if user interaction is unnecessary. Media settings affect the user experience.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Website Authoring > Creating a Web Page

content.topicNotes: Autonomous Vehicles What are autonomous vehicles An autonomous vehicle operates without direct human control. Microprocessors process data from sensors and cameras. Satellite signals (GPS) combine with mapping software (GIS) to navigate routes automatically. Artificial intelligence software makes driving decisions. Real-time data is analysed continuously. Autonomous systems aim to reduce human error. How autonomous systems work Cameras detect road markings and traffic signs. Radar measures speed and distance of nearby objects. LiDAR stands for Light Detection and Ranging. LiDAR uses laser pulses to measure distances precisely. A central computer controls steering, braking and acceleration. Autonomous trains and planes Autonomous trains use automated signalling and track sensors. Train control systems adjust speed and braking automatically. Some metro systems operate without drivers. Aircraft use autopilot systems for navigation and stability. Advanced flight management systems support semi-autonomous planes. Advantages and concerns Advantages Human error is reduced, improving safety. Transport systems can operate more efficiently. Disadvantages Technology is expensive to develop and maintain. Software faults or cyberattacks could cause accidents. Legal responsibility in incidents can be unclear. Job losses for drivers and vehicle operators.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > The Effects of Using IT > Microprocessor-controlled Devices in Transport

content.topicNotes: Autonomous Vehicles What are autonomous vehicles An autonomous vehicle is a computer-controlled system that can drive without human input. The vehicle uses computers to make driving decisions. Sensors collect data from the surrounding environment. Software processes data to control movement. Autonomous vehicles are an example of computer controlled systems. How autonomous vehicles work Sensors detect obstacles, road markings and traffic signs. A Global Positioning System (GPS) module determines the vehicle's precise position and plots navigation paths. Cameras capture visual information. Radar and lidar measure distance and speed. A microprocessor processes data in real time. The system controls steering, braking and acceleration. Advantages of autonomous vehicles Human error is reduced, improving road safety. Traffic flow can become more efficient. Autonomous vehicles support elderly or disabled users. Fuel use may be reduced through precise control. Travel time can be used productively by passengers. Disadvantages and concerns Systems are expensive to develop and maintain. Software or sensor failures can cause accidents. Ethical decisions are difficult to program. Legal responsibility in accidents is unclear. Cybersecurity risks may affect safety.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > ICT Applications > Computer Controlled Systems

content.topicNotes: Background Properties Background Colour CSS uses the background-color property to change a page background. Background colours can improve appearance and readability. You can use colour names, RGB values or hexadecimal values. Example: background-color: lightblue;. Background Images CSS uses the background-image property to add an image behind content. Background images can improve the design of a web page. Example: background-image: url('image.jpg');. Images should not make text difficult to read. Repeating Backgrounds Background images repeat automatically by default. CSS uses the background-repeat property to control repetition. repeat repeats an image across the page. no-repeat displays the image only once. Positioning Backgrounds CSS uses the background-position property to place an image. You can position images at the top, centre, or bottom. Positioning changes where the background appears. Example: background-position: centre;. Background Size The background-size property sets the image dimensions. cover expands the image to fill the area, cropping if needed. contain fits the whole image inside without cropping. Values like 100% 100% stretch it to match exact boundaries.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Website Authoring > Stylesheets

content.topicNotes: Backing Storage What Is Backing Storage Backing storage stores data and programs permanently. It is also called secondary storage. Backing storage keeps data when the power is turned off. Computers use it to save files and software. Hard Disk Drives A hard disk drive (HDD) uses magnetic storage. Magnetic storage uses magnetism to store data. HDDs offer large storage capacity at low cost. They contain moving parts that can wear out. Solid State Drives A solid state drive (SSD) uses flash memory. Flash memory stores data electronically with no moving parts. SSDs are faster than HDDs. They are more durable but usually cost more. Optical Storage Optical storage uses lasers to read and write data. Examples include CDs, DVDs, and Blu-ray discs. They are portable and easy to distribute. Optical discs store less data than HDDs or SSDs. Uses of Backing Storage Backing storage saves documents, photos, and videos. It stores operating systems and application software. It allows data to be backed up for safety. Users can transfer data between computers.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Types & Components of Computer Systems > Main Components of Computer Systems

content.topicNotes: Backing Storage vs Internal Memory Internal Memory Internal memory is used by the CPU during processing. It includes RAM and ROM. RAM stores data and programs currently in use. ROM stores start-up instructions. Backing Storage Backing storage stores data permanently. It is also called secondary storage. Examples include hard disk drives and solid state drives. Backing storage keeps data when power is off. Speed Difference Internal memory provides very fast access for the CPU. RAM allows quick reading and writing of data. Backing storage is much slower than internal memory. Computers load data from backing storage into RAM. Volatility Volatile memory loses data when power is turned off. RAM is volatile memory. Non-volatile memory keeps data without power. ROM and backing storage are non-volatile. Capacity and Cost Backing storage usually has a much larger capacity. It costs less per gigabyte than internal memory. Internal memory has smaller capacity but higher speed. Computers use both types to work effectively.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Types & Components of Computer Systems > Main Components of Computer Systems

content.topicNotes: Barcode and QR Code Readers Barcode readers A barcode reader scans a barcode using a laser or LED light. A barcode is a series of vertical lines representing numeric data. Reflected light is converted into digital data by the reader. Supermarkets use barcode readers at checkouts. Barcodes allow fast and accurate product identification. QR code scanners A QR code scanner reads a square matrix code. QR stands for Quick Response. QR codes store more information than traditional barcodes. Smartphones scan QR codes using built-in cameras. QR codes link to websites, tickets or payment systems. Advantages and disadvantages of barcode readers Advantages of barcode readers Barcode readers provide very fast data entry at checkouts. Barcode readers reduce human typing errors. Disadvantages of barcode readers Damaged or dirty barcodes may not scan correctly. Specialised scanning equipment is required. Advantages and disadvantages of QR code scanners Advantages of QR code scanners QR codes store more data than barcodes. QR codes can be scanned using smartphones. Disadvantages of QR code scanners Poor lighting can affect scanning accuracy. Users may scan malicious QR codes that link to unsafe websites.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Input & Output Devices > Direct Data Entry & Associated Devices

content.topicNotes: Biometric Recognition What is Biometric Recognition? Biometric recognition identifies a person using unique physical or behavioural features. The system captures a sample and compares it to stored data. A match allows access to a system or building. Biometric data is usually stored securely in a database. Finger and Thumb Recognition Fingerprint recognition scans the unique patterns of ridges on a finger. Thumb recognition works in the same way using the thumb. The scanner converts the pattern into digital data. The system compares the data to a stored template. Face, Iris and Retina Facial recognition measures distances between key facial features. Iris recognition scans the coloured ring around the pupil. Retina recognition scans blood vessel patterns at the back of the eye. These patterns are unique to each individual. Hand and Voice Recognition Hand geometry recognition measures the shape and size of the hand. The system analyses finger length and joint positions. Voice recognition analyses tone and speech patterns. The system compares the sample to stored voice data. Advantages Biometric systems improve security because traits are difficult to copy. Users do not need to remember passwords or carry cards. The system provides quick access to authorised users. Each person has unique biological characteristics. Disadvantages Injuries, dirt or background noise can reduce accuracy. The system may produce false positives or false negatives. A false positive incorrectly accepts an unauthorised user. A false negative incorrectly rejects an authorised user. Storing biometric data raises privacy and security concerns.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > ICT Applications > Recognition Systems

content.topicNotes: Biometrics What are Biometrics? Biometrics use unique physical features to identify a person. A biometric is a measurable biological characteristic. Examples include fingerprints, facial recognition and iris scans. These features are difficult to copy or share. Types of Biometrics Fingerprint recognition scans patterns on a finger. Facial recognition analyses features of a face. Iris recognition scans the eye's unique pattern. Voice recognition identifies speech patterns. How Biometrics Protect Data Biometrics control access to systems and devices. Only authorised users can unlock the system. This reduces the risk of unauthorised access. It replaces or supports passwords. It may be used in smartphones or security systems. Data must be stored securely to prevent misuse. Encryption protects stored biometric information. Advantages Biometrics are convenient and quick to use. They cannot be forgotten or lost like traditional passwords. Unique biological traits make authentication very difficult to fake. Disadvantages Stolen biometric data cannot be changed or reset if compromised. Systems may fail to recognise users in certain conditions, such as injury or low light. Implementing and maintaining biometric equipment carries higher costs than standard password protection.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Safety & Security > Security of Data

content.topicNotes: Blog, Forum, Wiki & Social Networking Blogs A blog acts as a personal online journal where an author publishes entries in reverse chronological order. Blog: short for 'weblog', a website containing personal reflections or hyperlinks to other sites. Owners update blogs regularly to share opinions or news with a global audience. Readers usually provide feedback by leaving comments at the bottom of each post. Forums An online forum provides a platform for people to hold asynchronous discussions through posted messages. Forum: an online discussion site where people can hold conversations in the form of posted messages. Administrators organise conversations into specific threads to keep different topics separate. Thread: a running commentary of messages linked to a specific original post. Wikis A wiki allows multiple users to collaborate by creating and editing web pages directly from their browser. Wiki: a website that allows collaborative editing of its content and structure by its users. It maintains a history of all changes, which allows editors to revert to previous versions if errors occur. Most wikis focus on sharing collective knowledge on specific subjects or projects. Social Networking Social networking sites enable individuals to build digital profiles and connect with friends, family, or colleagues. Social Networking: the use of dedicated websites to communicate with other users or groups. Users share multimedia content, such as photos and videos, and send private or public messages. These platforms use algorithms to suggest new connections based on mutual interests or existing friends.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Communication > The Internet

content.topicNotes: Blu-ray Discs What is Blu-ray Blu-ray is an optical storage medium designed to store large amounts of data. Blu-ray uses a blue-violet laser to read and write data. A blue-violet laser has a shorter wavelength than a red laser. The shorter wavelength allows data to be stored more densely. Blu-ray discs are non-volatile storage devices. Storage capacity A single-layer Blu-ray disc typically stores 25 GB of data. A dual-layer Blu-ray disc can store about 50 GB of data. Blu-ray discs store much more data than CDs and DVDs. High-definition video requires large storage capacity. Blu-ray is suitable for high-quality media. Uses of Blu-ray Blu-ray discs are used to distribute high-definition films. Games consoles use Blu-ray discs for large games. Blu-ray discs store large software packages. Backup systems may use Blu-ray for archiving data. Blu-ray provides high-quality audio and video output. Advantages and disadvantages Advantages Blu-ray discs offer very high storage capacity. Blu-ray supports high-definition video and audio. Disadvantages Blu-ray discs are more expensive than DVDs. Special Blu-ray drives are required.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Storage Devices & Media > Optical Devices & Media

content.topicNotes: Bluetooth What Bluetooth Is Bluetooth is a wireless technology that connects devices over short distances. It uses radio waves instead of cables. Bluetooth uses 79 different frequencies that are referred to as channels. The frequencies are distributed close to 2.45 GHz. Devices must pair before they can communicate. Pairing creates a secure connection between two devices. Common Uses of Bluetooth People use Bluetooth for wireless headphones and speakers. It also connects keyboards and mice to computers. Some phones share files using Bluetooth. Bluetooth works well for simple device-to-device connections. Advantages of Bluetooth Bluetooth removes the need for cables. It uses low power, so it saves battery. It is easy to set up for small devices. It works well in short-range environments. Disadvantages of Bluetooth Bluetooth only works over short distances. Has relatively low data transfer rates, making the transmission of large files noticeably slower. Interference from other devices can reduce performance. Bluetooth is not suitable for large networks.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Networks and the Effects of Using Them > Bluetooth & Wi-Fi
ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Networks and the Effects of Using Them
ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > ICT Applications

content.topicNotes: Booking Trips and Events What are booking systems for Booking systems are used to reserve travel and event places electronically. Trips include flights, trains and holidays. Events include concerts, sports matches and theatre shows. Booking systems use databases to store availability. Users make bookings through websites or apps. Booking trips Airlines use booking systems to allocate seats on flights. Train companies use booking systems to reserve tickets. Travel websites combine transport and accommodation bookings. Payment is processed securely during booking. Selected seats or rooms are temporarily reserved in the database while transaction processing is completed. Confirmation details are sent electronically. Booking events Event organisers use booking systems to sell tickets. Seat numbers can be allocated automatically. Ticket availability is updated in real time. Electronic tickets can be sent by email. Entry can be verified using barcodes or QR codes. Advantages and disadvantages Advantages Bookings can be made at any time. Double-booking is prevented automatically. Disadvantages System outages can stop bookings. Internet access is required to make bookings.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > ICT Applications > Booking Systems

content.topicNotes: Bookmarks and Hyperlinks Hyperlinks and anchors A hyperlink connects a user to another location or resource. An anchor uses the <a> tag to create clickable links. Hyperlinks can connect text or images. Hyperlinks improve navigation around websites. Bookmarks using IDs A bookmark links to a specific place on the same web page. A bookmark uses an id attribute to mark a location. The link can use <a href="#section1">. Bookmarks help users move quickly through long pages. Types of hyperlinks Internal links move users to pages within the same website. External links connect users to different websites. You can create email links using mailto:name@example.com. Links can open in the same window or a new window. Relative file paths A relative file path uses the current folder location. images/photo.jpg is an example of a relative path. Relative paths work when files move together between devices. Relative paths make websites easier to transfer. Absolute file paths An absolute file path gives the full location of a file. C:/Users/Documents/image.jpg is an example. Absolute paths should not link to local files in websites. Absolute paths may fail because other users have different folders.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Website Authoring > Creating a Web Page

content.topicNotes: Breaks in Documents Page Breaks A page break forces content to start on a new page. Users insert page breaks instead of pressing Enter multiple times. Page breaks keep document layouts consistent. New chapters often begin after a page break. Section Breaks A section break divides a document into separate sections without pushing content to the next page. Users can apply different formatting to each section. Section breaks allow changes to margins, headers or orientation. A landscape table may require a section break. Column Breaks A column break moves content to the next column. Users insert column breaks in newsletters and brochures. Column breaks control where text starts in a column. They improve the organisation of multi-column documents. Choosing the Correct Break Users should choose the break that matches the required layout. Page breaks start a new page. Section breaks allow different formatting. Column breaks move content to the next column. Widows and Orphans A widow is a line of text left alone at the top of a page. An orphan is a line of text left alone at the bottom of a page. Users can adjust breaks to avoid widows and orphans. This improves the appearance and readability of a document.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Document Production > Organise Page Layout

content.topicNotes: Bridge and Building Design Modelling What is design modelling Design modelling uses Computer Aided Design (CAD) software to create and test structures virtually. A model represents a real bridge or building design. Engineers use models before construction begins. Computer modelling reduces the need for physical prototypes. Modelling helps identify design problems early. How modelling is used in construction Dimensions and materials are entered into the model. Forces such as weight and wind are simulated. Stress testing shows how structures respond to loads. A load is a force acting on a structure. Weak points can be identified and improved. Uses in bridge and building design Bridges are tested to ensure they can carry traffic safely. Buildings are modelled to withstand weather and earthquakes. Architects use models to visualise designs. Engineers test different materials and shapes. Safety standards can be checked before construction. Advantages and disadvantages Advantages Design changes can be made quickly and cheaply. Dangerous testing can be done safely on computers. Disadvantages Models depend on accurate data and assumptions. Real-world conditions may not be fully represented.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > ICT Applications > Modelling Applications

content.topicNotes: Bridges What a Bridge Is A bridge connects two parts of the same network. It helps manage traffic between network segments. A bridge works within a LAN. LAN means Local Area Network. How a Bridge Works A bridge examines data before sending it on. It uses MAC addresses to decide where data should go. A MAC address is a Media Access Control address that identifies a device. This reduces unnecessary data traffic. Benefits of Using Bridges A bridge reduces network congestion. It prevents data collisions between network segments. This improves network performance. Bridges make networks more efficient. Bridge vs Other Devices A bridge is more intelligent than a hub. It is less advanced than a switch. Switches perform the same role as bridges. Modern networks usually use switches instead of bridges.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Networks and the Effects of Using Them > Common Network Devices

content.topicNotes: CAD and Graphics Editing Computer-Aided Design (CAD) Computer-Aided Design (CAD) software helps users create detailed technical drawings. CAD allows designers to model objects in 2D or 3D. CAD is used in engineering, architecture, and product design. Graphics Editing Software Graphics editing software allows users to create and modify images. Users can crop, resize, and add effects such as filters and text. Graphics editing is used for posters, logos, and digital artwork. Differences and Uses CAD focuses on accurate measurements and technical details. Graphics editing focuses on visual design and creative image changes. Both tools help users present ideas clearly and professionally.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Types & Components of Computer Systems > Applications Software

content.topicNotes: CD and DVD What are optical storage devices Optical storage devices store data using laser light. Data is stored as pits and lands on the disc surface. Pits and lands are microscopic changes that represent binary data. A laser reads the reflected light to retrieve data. Optical storage is non-volatile. Compact Disc (CD) A compact disc (CD) is an optical storage medium. A standard CD can store about 700 MB of data. CDs are used to store music, software and documents. Digital Versatile Disc (DVD) A digital versatile disc (DVD) is an optical storage medium. A DVD can store much more data than a CD. DVDs are commonly used for films and large software packages. Dual-layer DVDs increase storage capacity. DVD drives use a laser with a shorter wavelength than CDs. CD-ROM / DVD-ROM ROM stands for Read-Only Memory Data is pre-recorded at the factory. Ideal for mass-producing music, movies, or video games. Data cannot be altered or accidentally deleted. CD-R / DVD-R The letter "R" stands for recordable Data can be burned onto the blank disc once. Once written, it cannot be erased or overwritten. Good for making a permanent backup copy of a photo album. CD-RW / DVD-RW RW stands for rewritable Data can be written, erased, and rewritten multiple times. Ideal for moving files between computers but slower than a USB drive. Advantages and disadvantages Advantages CDs and DVDs are cheap to produce and distribute. Optical discs are portable and easy to store. Disadvantages Storage capacity is low compared to modern devices. Discs can be easily scratched or damaged.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Storage Devices & Media > Optical Devices & Media

content.topicNotes: CSS and Colour Purpose of CSS CSS stands for Cascading Style Sheets. CSS controls how elements on a web page look. CSS changes features such as colours, fonts and spacing. CSS separates content from design to make web pages easier to edit. Applying styles CSS applies styles to web page elements. A style changes the appearance of content. For example, color:red; changes text colour. Using CSS keeps the appearance of pages consistent. Colour names CSS can use colour names directly. Examples include red, blue and green. Colour names are simple to remember. Colour names provide fewer colour choices than other methods. RGB colours RGB stands for Red, Green, and Blue. It adds these three colours together to form various other colours. RGB colours use three numbers between 0 and 255. These represent the intensity of Red, Green, and Blue. rgb(255,0,0) represents red. rgb(0,255,0) represents green. rgb(0,0,255) represents blue. rgb(255,255,255) represents white. rgb(0,0,0) represents black. Different values combine to create many colours. Hexadecimal colours Hexadecimal colour codes also represent RGB colours. Hex codes begin with a # symbol. Instead of using decimal digits ranging from 0 to 9, Hex codes use hexadecimal digits ranging from 0 to F. F stands for 15, and FF for 255 in decimal numbers. In Hex codes, every two digits represent the intensity of a red, green, or blue. #FF0000 represents red. #00FF00 represents green. #0000FF represents blue. Hexadecimal colour codes allow the same colour selection as RGB colours.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Website Authoring > Creating a Web Page

content.topicNotes:
CSS Classes Purpose of Classes A class is a named style that can be applied to HTML elements. Classes help organise and control formatting. CSS uses a full stop before the class name. Example: .title { color: blue; }. Reusable Formatting Classes allow the same formatting to be reused many times. Reusable formatting reduces repeated code. One class can style many elements. This keeps websites consistent and easier to edit. Multiple Classes An element can use more than one class. Multiple classes combine different styles. Example:

. This allows several formatting rules to work together. Applying Styles Classes apply styles only to selected elements. HTML uses the class attribute to apply a class. Example:

Heading

. Different elements can share the same class.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Website Authoring > Stylesheets

content.topicNotes: CSS Syntax Selectors A selector identifies the HTML element that a CSS rule affects. A selector tells the browser where to apply formatting. In p {color:red;} the selector is p. Properties and Values A property defines the feature that will change. A value defines the setting applied to the property. In p {color:red;} the property is color and the value is red. Curly Brackets Curly brackets contain CSS declarations. A declaration is a property and value pair. In p {color:red; font-size:16px;} everything inside { } belongs to the p selector. Semicolons Semicolons separate CSS declarations. A semicolon marks the end of one property and value pair. In p {color:red; font-size:16px;} the semicolon separates the two declarations.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Website Authoring > Stylesheets

content.topicNotes: CT & MRI Scans CT scans CT stands for Computed Tomography. A CT scan uses computers to create detailed images of the body. The scanner takes many X-ray images from different angles. Computers combine these images into cross-sectional views. MRI scans MRI stands for Magnetic Resonance Imaging. An MRI scan produces detailed images of soft tissues. The system uses strong magnets and radio waves, not X-rays. Computers process signals to create clear images. Role of computers Computers control the scanning equipment during CT and MRI scans. They process large amounts of data quickly. The system creates accurate images for doctors to analyse. Medical benefits Doctors use CT and MRI scans to diagnose illnesses and injuries. The images help locate tumours, fractures, or internal bleeding. This supports faster and more accurate treatment.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > ICT Applications > Computers in Medicine

content.topicNotes: Card Fraud Methods What is Card Fraud? Card fraud is the unauthorised use of a bank card. Attackers use stolen card details to make payments. Victims may lose money or have accounts compromised. Shoulder Surfing Shoulder surfing is watching someone enter sensitive data. Attackers observe PINs or passwords in public places. A Personal Identification Number (PIN) secures a card. Users should cover keypads when entering PINs. Card Cloning Card cloning copies data from a bank card. Devices called skimmers read card information.A skimmer is a covert hardware device fitted onto cash machines or payment terminals to capture information stored on the magnetic strip. Attackers create duplicate cards to make transactions. Users should check machines for unusual attachments. Key Logging Key logging records what a user types. A keylogger is software or hardware that captures keystrokes. It can collect passwords and card details. Antivirus software can detect keyloggers. Preventing Card Fraud Users should keep PINs and passwords secret. Public computers should be avoided for banking. Bank statements should be checked regularly. Suspicious activity should be reported immediately.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Safety & Security > Security of Data

content.topicNotes: Card Readers What is direct data entry Direct data entry is the automatic input of data into a computer system. Data is captured directly from a source without manual typing. Direct data entry improves speed and accuracy. Errors caused by retyping are reduced. Card readers are common examples of direct data entry devices. Magnetic stripe and chip and PIN readers A magnetic stripe reader reads data stored on a magnetic stripe on the back of a card. A chip and PIN reader reads data from a microchip embedded in the card. Users enter a personal identification number (PIN) to confirm identity. A PIN is a secret numeric password. Chip and PIN systems provide greater security than magnetic stripe systems. Contactless card readers A contactless card reader uses radio frequency identification (RFID) or near field communication (NFC). The card does not need to be inserted or swiped. The user taps the card near the reader. Data is transmitted wirelessly over a short distance. Contactless systems are commonly used for small payments and travel cards. Advantages and disadvantages Advantages of card readers Card readers provide fast and accurate data entry. Card readers reduce errors compared to manual entry. Contactless readers improve speed and convenience. Disadvantages of card readers Damaged cards may not be read correctly. Specialised hardware is required. Installation and maintenance costs can be high.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Input & Output Devices > Direct Data Entry & Associated Devices

content.topicNotes: Cascading Stylesheets Characteristics of CSS CSS stands for Cascading Style Sheets. CSS controls the appearance of web page elements. CSS can change colours, fonts, spacing and page layouts. CSS keeps content separate from presentation. Cascading Behaviour Cascading behaviour means styles can come from different places. CSS applies rules in an order to decide which style is used. More specific rules can replace more general rules. Style Precedence Style precedence means some styles have a higher priority than others. In-line styles usually override internal and external styles. Internal styles usually override external styles when the same property is changed. External Stylesheets An external stylesheet stores CSS rules in a separate file. External stylesheets can apply the same formatting to many web pages. This makes websites easier to update and maintain.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Website Authoring > Stylesheets

content.topicNotes: Cell Referencing Relative Referencing Relative cell referencing happens when a cell address alters when you copy a formula to another cell. You write a relative reference using standard column letters and row numbers like "A1". Excel updates the row or column references to maintain the same relative distance from the original data. Absolute Referencing Absolute cell referencing refers to a fixed cell address that stays the same, no matter where you copy the formula. You create an absolute reference by placing dollar signs before the column letter and row number, like "$B$2". Excel keeps this exact cell locked to prevent errors when multiplying by constant values. Replicating Formulae Replicating formulae refers to the process of copying a formula across multiple cells using the fill handle. The fill handle is used to extend patterns, sequences, and formulas to adjacent cells. The fill handle is accessed by dragging the bottom-right corner of the selected cells. Excel changes the relative parts of the formula but keeps the absolute parts perfectly locked. You achieve accurate spreadsheet models by balancing both reference types during replication.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Spreadsheets > Data Models

content.topicNotes: Central Processing Unit (CPU) What the CPU Does The CPU is the main processor of a computer. CPU stands for Central Processing Unit. It processes data and instructions from programs. The CPU controls how the computer operates. Main Parts of the CPU The CPU contains the Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU). The ALU performs calculations and logical comparisons. The CPU also contains the Control Unit (CU). The CU manages and coordinates CPU activities. The CPU is usually implemented on integrated circuit microprocessors, that often contain multiple CPUs Registers Registers are small, fast memory locations inside the CPU. They temporarily store data and instructions being used. Registers allow the CPU to work quickly. Examples include the accumulator and program counter. Clock Speed Clock speed measures how fast the CPU processes instructions. It is measured in hertz (Hz). A higher clock speed means more instructions per second. Faster clock speeds usually improve performance.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Types & Components of Computer Systems > Main Components of Computer Systems

content.topicNotes: Characteristics and Uses of Email Core Characteristics Email stands for electronic mail, which is a method of exchanging messages between people using electronic devices. Users send and receive messages almost instantly across the globe using an internet connection. Messages consist of a subject line, the main body text, and a digital signature. High-speed delivery allows for efficient communication compared to traditional paper-based mail. Common Uses Businesses use email for formal internal communication and sending newsletters to customers. Individuals use email for personal messaging and sharing photos with friends or family. Educational institutions distribute course materials and reminders to students via mailing lists. Automated systems send notifications such as password resets or booking confirmations. Legal Requirements Organisations must follow data protection laws when sending electronic communications to individuals. Senders often require an opt-in from the user before they can legally send marketing materials. Opt-in: a process where a user explicitly gives permission to receive communications. Companies must provide a clear way for users to unsubscribe from future messages.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Communication > Email Communication

content.topicNotes: Characteristics & Uses of the Internet Nature of the Internet The Internet acts as a worldwide 'network of networks' connecting billions of devices using standard protocols. It uses a decentralised structure, which means no single entity, government, or company owns or manages the entire system. Decentralised: a system where control is distributed among various nodes rather than being held by a single central authority. Data travels across this global infrastructure via physical connections like fibre-optic cables, copper wires, and wireless satellite links. Accessing Information Users primarily use the Internet to access the World Wide Web to find information and digital resources. World Wide Web: a service that runs on the Internet, consisting of hyperlinked documents accessed via a web browser. Cloud computing allows individuals to run software and store data on remote servers instead of their local computer's hard drive. Cloud Computing: the delivery of computing services over the Internet to provide faster innovation and flexible resources. Commercial and Media Uses Consumers use the Internet for E-commerce to browse and purchase products from retailers worldwide at any time of day. E-commerce: the process of buying and selling goods or services electronically over the Internet. Online banking provides a secure way for users to check balances and pay bills without visiting a physical bank branch. Streaming services deliver media content like video and music in real-time, removing the need for users to download entire files before playing them.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Communication > The Internet

content.topicNotes: Cloud Computing What is Cloud Computing? Cloud computing is the delivery of computing services over the internet. Users access storage, software and processing power online. Data is stored on remote servers instead of local computers. A server is a computer that provides services to other computers. How Data is Stored and Managed Data is stored in large data centres owned by providers. The provider manages security, backups and maintenance. Users upload and download files through an internet connection. The system allows authorised users to share files easily. Types of Cloud A public cloud provides services over the internet to many users. A private cloud is used by one organisation only. A hybrid cloud combines public and private cloud features. Organisations choose the type based on security and cost needs. Advantages Users can access data from any device with internet access. The system reduces the need for expensive hardware. Providers handle updates and security management. Businesses can increase or decrease storage as needed. Disadvantages Users rely on a stable internet connection. Data breaches may occur if security is weak. Service outages can prevent access to important files. Storing data on remote servers may raise privacy concerns.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Networks and the Effects of Using Them > Cloud Computing

content.topicNotes: Chart Types Selecting Data for Charts Users must select the correct data before creating a chart. Contiguous data is stored in adjacent cells. Non-contiguous data is stored in separate cell ranges. Users can also select specified data ranges to include only relevant data. Bar Charts Bar charts use horizontal rectangular bars to represent values. Bar charts use horizontal bars to compare values between different categories. The length of each bar shows the value. Bar charts make it easy to identify the largest and smallest values. Column Charts Column charts display values using vertical rectangular bars. They compare discrete categories by displaying column height as the value. Vertical columns help highlight highs, lows, and trends across categories. Line Charts A line chart uses points connected by lines. Line charts show trends and changes over time. The horizontal axis often shows dates or time periods. Users can quickly identify increases, decreases and patterns. Pie Charts A pie chart is a circle divided into slices. Each slice represents a proportion of the whole. Larger slices represent larger percentages or values. Pie charts help users compare how parts contribute to a total. Choosing the Correct Chart Users should choose a chart type that matches the data. Bar and Column charts compare categories. Line charts show trends over time. Pie charts show proportions of a whole. Chart title should be visible, meaningful, and located above the chart. Both X and Y axes should have clear labels with appropriate units of measurement.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Graphs & Charts > Graphs & Charts
ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Presentations > Edit Presentations

content.topicNotes: Cheques What is a cheque A cheque is a written instruction to a bank to pay money from an account. The cheque is issued by the account holder. The payee is the person or organisation receiving the money. Cheques are a traditional banking method. Cheques are processed using computer systems. Information on a cheque A cheque includes the payee’s name. The amount to be paid is written in words and numbers. The account holder signs the cheque. The cheque includes the account number and sort code. This information allows the bank to process the payment. How cheques are processed The cheque is deposited at a bank or scanned digitally. Magnetic Ink Character Recognition (MICR) reads special digits along the bottom. The bank’s computer system verifies account details. Funds are transferred electronically between banks. The payment is recorded in both accounts. Advantages and disadvantages Advantages Cheques provide a paper record of payment. Cheques do not require internet access. Disadvantages Cheques are slow to process. Cheques can be lost, forged or altered.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > ICT Applications > Banking Applications

content.topicNotes: Chip and PIN and RFID Readers Chip and PIN readers A chip and PIN reader is a direct data entry device used for secure payments. A smart card contains an embedded microchip. A microchip is a small integrated circuit that stores encrypted data. The user inserts the card and enters a personal identification number (PIN). The system verifies the PIN before authorising the transaction. RFID system components An RFID system has three main components. An RFID tag contains a microchip and an antenna. The microchip stores data such as an identification number. The antenna transmits and receives radio signals. An RFID reader sends radio waves and receives data from the tag. How RFID works The RFID reader emits radio waves. The antenna in the RFID tag receives the signal. The tag transmits stored data back to the reader. Data is sent to a computer system for processing. Contactless payments and access systems use RFID technology. Advantages and disadvantages of chip and PIN Advantages of chip and PIN Chip and PIN provides strong authentication using a PIN. Fraud is reduced compared to magnetic stripe systems. Disadvantages of chip and PIN Physical contact is required to insert the card. Damaged chips may prevent transactions. Advantages and disadvantages of RFID Advantages of RFID RFID allows fast and contactless data entry. Wear and tear are reduced because no insertion is needed. Multiple RFID tags can be scanned at the same time from a distance without requiring a direct line of sight Disadvantages of RFID Radio signals may be intercepted without proper security. Specialised readers and infrastructure are required.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Input & Output Devices > Direct Data Entry & Associated Devices

content.topicNotes: Classes & Divisions Purpose of <div> The <div> tag is used as a division element that groups content in a web page. A division element is a container used to organise related elements together. Developers use <div> to apply structure and layout to sections of a page. Classes for Styling A class is a reusable label used to apply the same style to multiple elements. A class allows consistent formatting across different parts of a web page. For example, a class called 'highlight' can style multiple paragraphs the same way. Reusable Formatting Reusable formatting means applying the same style rules to different elements using classes. This reduces repetition and keeps web pages consistent. Styles can be reused across headings, paragraphs, and divisions. Applying Styles to Divisions Styles can be applied to a <div> to control the appearance of grouped content. A styled division can change background colour, text size, or spacing. This helps make sections of a web page visually organised.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Website Authoring > Creating a Web Page
ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Networks and the Effects of Using Them

content.topicNotes: Colour and Text Formatting Text Colour CSS uses the color property to change text colour. You can use colour names such as red or blue. You can also use hexadecimal or RGB colour values. Text colour can improve readability and appearance. Text Alignment CSS uses the text-align property to position text. You can align text to the left, right or centre. Alignment changes where text appears on the page. Correct alignment can make content easier to read. Font Weight Font weight controls how thick or bold text appears. CSS uses the font-weight property. bold makes text stand out from normal text. Bold text can draw attention to important information. Multiple Properties CSS can apply several formatting properties at the same time. You can combine colour, alignment, and font weight. Example: color: blue; text-align: centre; font-weight: bold;. Multiple properties help create a consistent design.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Website Authoring > Stylesheets

content.topicNotes: Columns Purpose of Columns Columns divide a page into vertical sections. Columns organise large amounts of text. Narrow columns make text easier to read. Users often use columns in newspapers, magazines and newsletters. Newspaper-Style Layouts Newspaper-style layouts use multiple columns on a page. Text flows from the bottom of one column to the top of the next. This layout allows more information to fit on a page. Readers can follow articles more easily. Column Spacing Column spacing is the gap between columns. Adequate spacing separates text clearly. Narrow spacing can make columns appear crowded. Wider spacing can improve readability and presentation. Document software measures column gaps (gutters) using precise units such as centimetres. Multi-column layouts maintain identical column widths unless custom dimensions are applied. Column Separators A column separator is a vertical line between columns. Separators help readers distinguish between columns. Users can add separators to improve document organisation. Not all column layouts require separators. Using Columns Effectively Users should choose the number of columns carefully. Too many columns can make a document difficult to read. Appropriate spacing and separators improve clarity. Well-designed columns create a professional layout.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Document Production > Organise Page Layout

content.topicNotes: CLI and GUI Command Line Interface (CLI) A command line interface (CLI) allows users to interact with a computer by typing text commands. A command is a text instruction entered using a keyboard to tell the computer what to do. Users must remember exact commands and correct syntax. CLIs use very little memory and processing power. Experienced users can work very efficiently. CLIs are commonly used by System Administrators, Programmers or Technicians Graphical User Interface (GUI) A graphical user interface (GUI) allows interaction using icons, windows and menus. Users control the system using devices such as a mouse or touch screen. GUIs are easier to learn than CLIs. They provide visual feedback for user actions. Most modern operating systems use GUIs. WIMP interface WIMP stands for Windows, Icons, Menus and Pointer. It is a type of graphical user interface. Users interact by pointing and clicking. A pointer is an on-screen indicator controlled by a mouse or touchpad. Desktop operating systems commonly use WIMP interfaces. Post-WIMP interface A post-WIMP interface goes beyond windows, icons and menus. It uses touch, gestures, voice or motion as input. Gesture input involves actions such as swiping or pinching. Smartphones and tablets use post-WIMP interfaces. These interfaces support more natural interaction. Comparing interfaces CLIs are efficient but difficult for beginners. GUIs and WIMP interfaces are user-friendly and visual. Post-WIMP interfaces focus on touch and gesture control. Different interfaces suit different users and tasks. Modern systems often combine multiple interface types.
