content.topicNotes: Common Physical Risks Electrocution Hazards Spilling liquids near electrical equipment can cause electrocution, so drinks should not be allowed close by. Touching live cables with wet hands is dangerous. Damaged or frayed cables expose live wires, increasing risk, so the cables should be checked regularly by an electrician. Overloaded power strips can overheat and cause sparks. A residual current breaker (RCB) should be installed to prevent electrocution. Fire Hazards from Overloading Overloading sockets causes overheating and fires, so install sufficient wall outlets and limit extension leads. Faulty wiring or aging hardware can spark; perform routine safety checks. Keep flammable items like paper or curtains clear of heat sources. Ensure adequate room ventilation to prevent heat buildup. There should be a sufficient number of fire extinguishers. Never tackle electrical fires with water; use CO2 or dry powder units instead. Tripping Over Trailing Cables Loose cables across walkways are a major tripping hazard. Cable ducts should be used instead. Cluttered floors (e.g., bags, boxes) block safe movement and should be avoided. Poorly secured rugs or mats can slide. Falling Equipment Injuries Heavy equipment (e.g., monitors, servers) can fall if not secured. Unstable shelves or overloaded surfaces may collapse, so desks and shelves should be used that are strong and large enough. Protective barriers around high shelves decreases risk. Improperly stacked items can topple and should be avoided.

content.topicNotes: Common Malware Types Virus A virus is malware that copies itself and spreads. It attaches to files and activates when opened. It can corrupt or delete data. Users should scan downloads before opening files. Trojan A trojan is malware disguised as legitimate software. It tricks users into installing harmful programs. It may create a backdoor for attackers. A backdoor is a hidden way to access a system. Spyware Spyware secretly monitors user activity. It collects personal data without permission. It may record keystrokes or browsing habits. Users should only download from trusted sources. Ransomware Ransomware locks files or systems. Attackers demand payment to restore access. It can spread through infected downloads. Regular backups help recover data safely. Worm A worm self-replicates and travels independently across computer networks. Worms operate without needing a host file or program to attach to. Worms propagate autonomously by taking advantage of flaws in network software security. Preventing Infection Antivirus software scans and removes threats. Files should be downloaded from trusted websites only. Suspicious email attachments should not be opened. Software updates fix security weaknesses.

content.topicNotes: Compilers and Linkers Compiler A compiler translates high-level code into machine code so the CPU can run it. High-level code is a programming language designed to be readable by humans. Machine code is binary instructions that the computer understands. A compiler checks the whole program for errors before it creates an executable file. An executable file is a program file that the operating system can load and run. Linker A linker combines compiled code files into one complete program. Compiled code is code that a compiler has already translated into machine code. A linker adds library files so the program can use pre-written functions. A library is a collection of ready-made code that programmers can reuse. A linker creates a final executable file that the operating system can run. Why they are needed A compiler allows programmers to write in a language such as C and still run the program on a computer. A linker allows programmers to build large programs from smaller parts called modules. A module is a separate section of a program that performs one main task. A linker helps the program run by connecting references between different modules. Compilers and linkers reduce errors by creating a single working executable.

content.topicNotes: Computer Modelling What is computer modelling Computer modelling is the use of software to represent real-world systems. A model is a simplified version of reality. Models use data and rules to simulate behaviour. Computer models allow predictions to be made. Modelling helps users understand complex systems. How computer models work Data is entered into the computer model. Variables represent factors that can change. The computer processes the data using formulas. Models enable "what-if" scenarios by adjusting variables to observe the effects of a decision. Uses of computer modelling Scientists use models to predict weather patterns. Engineers test designs using computer simulations. Businesses use models to predict sales and costs. Governments use models to plan transport systems. Modelling avoids testing in real-life situations. Advantages and disadvantages Advantages Computer modelling saves time and money. Dangerous situations can be tested safely. Disadvantages Models depend on the accuracy of input data. Simplified models may not reflect real life exactly.

content.topicNotes: Computer-Aided Learning What is computer-aided learning Computer-aided learning (CAL) uses computers to support teaching and learning. Educational content is made accessible through Virtual Learning Environment (VLE) platforms. VLEs facilitate online homework submission, direct messaging between teachers and students, self-marking quizzes, and round-the-clock resource access. CAL allows learners to work at their own pace. Content can include text, video, audio, and interactive activities. CAL is commonly used in schools and colleges. How CAL is used in schools Students use CAL software to practise skills and revise topics. Teachers assign online tasks and quizzes. Feedback is often given automatically by the system. Progress can be tracked over time. CAL supports both classroom and home learning. Advantages of computer-aided learning Learning can be personalised to individual needs. Immediate feedback helps learners correct mistakes. Interactive content increases engagement. Learning resources are available at any time. Teachers can monitor learner progress easily. Disadvantages of computer-aided learning Access to computers and the internet is required. Reduced face-to-face interaction may affect some learners. Technical problems can disrupt learning. Self-discipline is required for independent study. Overuse of screens may cause health issues.

content.topicNotes: Control, Measurement, Apps and Applets Control and Measurement Software Control software operates a system by responding to input from sensors. It sends instructions to actuators to perform actions. Sensors collect data from the environment. Actuators carry out actions. Measurement software collects, records and analyses data from sensors. Unlike control software, it does not operate or control the system. Uses of Control and Measurement Control software is used in: washing machines to control the drum and water pump traffic lights to change the lights at the correct time heating systems to switch the heating on or off based on temperature Measurement software is used to: record temperatures in weather stations monitor scientific experiments collect data in industrial processes Measurement software provides data, while control software uses data to make decisions and control a system. Apps and Applets An app is a small application designed for a specific task on a device. Apps commonly run on smartphones, tablets, and computers. An applet is a small program that runs within another application or a web page.

content.topicNotes: Copyright Legislation Purpose of Copyright Copyright law protects the original work of creators from unauthorised use. Copyright: a legal right that grants the creator of an original work exclusive rights to its use and distribution. Legislation ensures that authors, musicians, and software developers receive credit and payment for their efforts. Modern laws prevent the illegal copying and distribution of digital media. Software Piracy Users must avoid software piracy to remain compliant with the law. Software Piracy: the illegal copying, distribution, or use of software without a valid licence. Companies use unique product keys to ensure that only legitimate buyers can activate the software. Breaking copyright law can result in heavy fines or even imprisonment for individuals and businesses. Legal Use and Licencing Individuals must obtain a licence before using copyrighted material in their own ICT projects. Licence: a legal agreement that outlines how a piece of software or content can be used. Single-user licence: grants permission to install and run the program on a single workstation. Site licence: allows an organisation, such as a school or business, to deploy the software across all devices located at one physical address.

content.topicNotes: Corporate House Style What is a Corporate House Style? A corporate house style is a set of design rules and brand guidelines defined by an organization. It ensures a consistent corporate image across documents, websites, and publications. It may include logos, colour schemes, font families and margins that make an organization immediately recognizable to the public. Purpose of a House Style A house style helps customers recognise the organisation. Consistent presentation improves brand identity.Brand identity is the visual image of a company. Features of a House Style A house style may define font styles and colours. It may include rules for logos and layouts.Layout is the arrangement of content on a page. These rules ensure all documents match. Uses of a House Style Organisations use house styles in letters and reports. They also use them in websites and presentations. Marketing materials often follow the same style. This creates consistency across all media. Advantages of Consistency Consistent documents are easier to recognise. Staff can create documents more quickly. A professional image builds customer trust. Consistency improves communication and presentation.

content.topicNotes: Create and Label Charts Chart Labels A chart title explains what the chart shows. A legend identifies the data series using colours or patterns. Axis titles describe the data on each axis. Axis labels show the categories and values displayed on the chart. Data and Pie Chart Labels Data value labels display the exact values on a chart. Sector labels identify slices in a pie chart. Sector values show the numerical value of each slice. Percentages show each slice as a proportion of the whole. Formatting Values Users can format values to a specified number of decimal places. Decimal places are digits shown after the decimal point. Users can add currency symbols such as £ or €. Consistent formatting makes charts easier to understand. Adjusting Axis Scales Users can set the maximum and minimum values on an axis. An axis scale determines how values are displayed. Incremental values control the spacing between scale markings. Appropriate scales improve the readability of charts. Enhancing Appearance Users can extract a pie chart sector to emphasise important data. Extracting a sector separates it from the rest of the pie chart. Users can change colour schemes and fill patterns. Effective formatting makes charts more attractive and easier to interpret.

content.topicNotes: Image Cropping and Resizing Cropping Images Users crop an image to remove unwanted outer areas from the graphic. Cropping: the process of cutting away the edges of an image to improve framing or accentuate a subject. This process changes the dimensions of the image but does not scale the remaining content. Designers use cropping to remove background distractions and focus the viewer's attention on the most important part of the visual. Resizing and Proportions Users resize images by adjusting the number of pixels or the physical dimensions. Locking aspect ratio ensures height and width change proportionally so the image does not distort. Aspect Ratio: the proportional relationship between width and height. Changing only the height or width without locking the ratio results in a distorted image. Practical tasks often specify adjusting a single dimension without distortion (e.g., "resize the height to 3 cm while preserving aspect ratio"). Resampling Images Resampling changes the amount of image data when the physical dimensions are adjusted. Resampling: the process of increasing or decreasing the number of pixels in a digital image. Downsampling removes pixels to reduce file size, which is useful for web use or email. Downsampling: the process of reducing the pixel count of an image. Upsampling adds new pixels to increase the size, though this often causes the image to look blurry.

content.topicNotes: Customised Medicines What customised medicines are Customised medicines are tailored to a patient’s specific needs. Doctors use patient data such as age, weight, and genetics. Computers help create precise doses for better treatment. Use of patient data Computers analyse patient data to suggest the best medicine. Data includes medical history, allergies, and test results. This reduces the risk of side effects and incorrect doses. 3D printing medicines Some medicines use 3D printing to create exact doses. 3D printing builds objects layer by layer using a computer design. This allows personalised shapes and strengths for each patient. 3D printing enables the production of poly-pills, merging multiple distinct drugs into one pill. Benefits for patients Customised medicines improve the effectiveness of treatment. Patients experience fewer side effects and faster recovery. Computers make the process faster and more accurate.

content.topicNotes: Data Entry Forms Purpose of Data Entry Forms Data entry forms provide a user-friendly interface that allows users to input data into a database table. Interface refers to a layout with visual elements designed for human interaction. Users type information into interactive input fields rather than editing database tables directly. Forms isolate the raw database tables from the end-user to keep data structure safe. Importance and Benefits Forms improve data integrity by reducing human input errors through validation checks. Data integrity means the accuracy, completeness, and consistency of data. Validation checks refer to automated rules that check if data is sensible. Interactive forms speed up data collection processes for businesses. Forms accommodate non-technical staff members who do not know how to interact with database tables. How and When Forms Are Used Database administrators deploy data entry forms when adding new client records or product details. Customers use online forms to input personal details during digital registration processes. Forms link directly to tables to update information in real time. Staff members utilise search parameters inside forms to find and update existing database records. Features of Well-Designed Forms Designers include clear labels next to every input text box to assist the user. Well-designed forms use drop-down menus and checkboxes to limit invalid user entries. Developers add navigation buttons to let users scroll through multiple records easily. Forms maintain a logical layout with appropriate spacing and visible text instructions.

content.topicNotes: Why Data Protection Legislation Exists Personal Data Protection Data protection laws ensure that personal information, such as names, addresses, and bank details, is kept secure. They prevent unauthorised access to sensitive data. Organisations must follow strict rules when handling personal information. Key Principles of Data Protection Data must be processed fairly, lawfully, and for specified reasons. Records must be accurate, relevant, adequate, and deleted when no longer needed. Firms must ensure robust security and respect data subject rights. Data cannot be transferred overseas without equivalent legal protection. Preventing Identity Theft Identity theft occurs when someone uses another person’s personal data without permission. Data protection laws help reduce the risk of identity theft by requiring organisations to protect user data. They also allow individuals to request corrections if their data is incorrect. Trust in Digital Services Users are more likely to trust a service if they know their data is protected. Data protection laws ensure organisations are transparent about how they use personal data. They also give users the right to know what data is being collected about them. Ethical Responsibility Organisations have an ethical duty to protect the data they collect from users. Data protection laws set standards for how data should be handled. They encourage organisations to be responsible with user information.

content.topicNotes: Data Packets What Data Packets Are A data packet is a small unit of data sent across a network. Networks split large files into packets before sending them. This method makes data transfer faster and more reliable. Each packet travels independently across the network. What Packets Contain The header contains control information such as the sender and receiver IP addresses, packet number in the sequence, and instructions for routing. The payload is the actual data being sent, such as part of an email or a webpage. The trailer or footer usually contains an error-checking code (like a checksum) to help detect if the packet has been damaged during transmission. How Packets Travel Routers send packets along the best available path. Different packets from the same file may take different routes. Routers make decisions using IP addresses. This process helps avoid congestion on networks. Reassembling Packets The receiving device collects all packets and reassembles packets in the correct order using the sequence numbers that were sent with each packet. Missing packets are requested again. This ensures the data arrives complete and accurate.

content.topicNotes: Performing Searches Understanding Database Queries Database users perform searches by running a query. A query is a formal request to extract specific records from a database table based on criteria. Users define search conditions rather than looking through entire tables manually. Queries isolate the exact information required while hiding irrelevant records. How Queries Are Used Businesses use queries to extract targeted lists like outstanding customer invoices or low stock items. Search criteria act as filters to display records matching specific parameters. Criteria refer to the rules or conditions that data must meet to be selected. Users combine logical operators like AND, OR, and NOT to perform complex searches. Advantages of Using Queries Database queries save significant time compared to scrolling through large data sheets. Automated searches improve accuracy by eliminating human overview errors during inspection. Developers save query structures so users can run the exact same search instantly in the future. Databases dynamic links update query results automatically when underlying table data changes. Features of a Good Query Efficient queries target precise field attributes to minimise processing time. Well-designed criteria use clear comparisons like greater than or equal to operators. Good search queries output only relevant fields to make reports easy to read. Designers use wildcard characters to fetch records with incomplete search terms safely. A wildcard is a special character that represents one or more unknown text symbols.

content.topicNotes: Hardware Overview Definition of Hardware Hardware refers to the physical components of a computer system that you can touch. Hardware includes electronic and mechanical parts such as circuits and devices. Hardware works together with software, which is the programs and data that control the computer. Internal Hardware Components Internal hardware is located inside the computer case. The Central Processing Unit (CPU) processes instructions and controls the computer. The CPU acts as the brain of the computer. Random Access Memory (RAM) stores data temporarily while programs run. External Hardware Devices External hardware connects to the computer from outside the case. Input devices allow users to enter data into the computer. A keyboard is an input device used to type text. A camera is an input device that captures video or images. Output devices present results, such as a monitor displaying images.

content.topicNotes: Applications Software What is Software? Software are programs for controlling the operation of a computer or processing of electronic data It tells the computer what tasks to perform. It processes electronic data into useful information. Without software, computer hardware cannot carry out instructions. What is Applications Software? Applications software refers to programs designed to help users perform specific tasks. Applications software runs on top of system software. Users interact directly with applications software to complete work or leisure activities. Purpose of Applications Software Applications software helps users complete tasks efficiently. Tasks include writing documents, editing images, or browsing the internet. Each application is designed for a particular purpose. Common Examples A word processor allows users to create and edit text documents. A spreadsheet helps users organise data and perform calculations. A web browser enables users to access and view websites.

content.topicNotes: Design File & Data Structures What Is a Design File A design file documents how a new information system will store and manage data. It describes required files, their purpose and where they are used in the system. The design file guides programmers and testers during system development. It helps ensure the new system meets user needs and legal requirements. A good design file reduces errors during implementation. Key Contents of a Design File A design file usually includes file names, field lists and record formats. It specifies data types, field lengths and any default values. It lists validation rules and security requirements for each file. It documents relationships between files and required reports. The design file may include sample records to show expected data. Common Data Structures Records and fields are basic structures used to store related data. A record is a collection of fields that describe one item or person. A field is a single piece of data such as a name or date. Tables or arrays hold many records of the same type. A primary key uniquely identifies each record in a file. A foreign key links a field in one table to the primary key in another table. Daily Examples, Validation and Pros/Cons Daily-life example: a school database has a student record with fields for name, DOB and class. Validation rules check that dates are real and mandatory fields are not empty. Advantage: structured data makes searching and reporting fast and reliable. Disadvantage: poor design causes duplicate data and costly fixes later. Good data design improves security, accuracy and maintainability.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > The Systems Life Cycle > Designing the New System

content.topicNotes: Design Input Formats What Are Input Formats An input format is the way a user provides data to a system, for example a text field or checkbox. Input formats limit and structure user input to reduce errors. Designers choose formats to match the type of data required, such as dates or numbers. Good input formats speed up data entry and improve accuracy. Common Input Controls Text field: for free-form text such as names or addresses. Drop-down menu: for selecting one item from a list. Radio buttons: for exclusive choices where only one option is allowed. Checkboxes: for multiple independent selections. Date picker and file upload are specialised input controls. Design Principles Use clear control buttons to help users navigate and manage entries, such as Next, Previous, Save, or Exit. Display explicit guidance so users know how to fill out the form. Label each input clearly and place labels close to controls. Use placeholder text and default values to guide users. Apply validation and format checks to catch errors early. Keep input sequences logical and minimise the number of required fields. Use consistent formats for similar data across the system. Accessibility and Usability Ensure keyboard access for all controls so users can tab through forms. Provide descriptive labels for screen readers to aid visually impaired users. Use sufficient contrast and large clickable areas for touch users. Offer sensible error messages that explain how to fix input mistakes. Allow users to review and edit input before final submission. Daily Examples, Advantages & Disadvantages Example: an online school form uses text fields for names and a drop-down for class. Advantages Structured inputs reduce typing and speed up processing. Validation prevents invalid data such as wrong dates. Disadvantages Poorly chosen controls frustrate users and increase errors.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > The Systems Life Cycle > Designing the New System

content.topicNotes: Design Output Formats What are output formats An output format is the way a system presents processed data to users or other systems. Output formats include printed reports, on-screen displays, files and multimedia. Designers choose formats to match user needs, context and accessibility requirements. Consistent output formats improve clarity and reduce user errors. Printed reports and letters Printed reports provide a permanent physical record for audits or meetings. A report usually contains a clear title, date and organised sections. An invoice must include invoice number, totals and payment terms. School report letters present pupil grades, teacher comments and next steps. On-screen reports and dashboards Dashboards display key performance indicators using charts and gauges. Interactive on-screen reports allow users to filter and sort data immediately. Colour, labels and clear scales help users interpret charts correctly. Real-time dashboards update automatically to show current system status. Multimedia outputs Multimedia outputs include slide presentations, video and audio summaries. A presentation should use legible fonts and concise bullet points for audiences. Short video clips can demonstrate procedures clearly and efficiently. Accessibility features such as captions improve usability for all users. File formats and data export PDF files preserve layout and print reliably across devices. CSV files store tabular data for easy import into spreadsheets and databases. XML or JSON formats support structured data exchange between systems. Export options must include appropriate metadata and character encoding. Design trade-offs Advantages of clear output formats include faster decision-making and fewer follow-up queries. Designers should balance visual detail with simplicity to avoid information overload. A disadvantage is that rich multimedia outputs may increase file size and require more bandwidth. A disadvantage is that poorly chosen formats can hinder accessibility and automated processing.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > The Systems Life Cycle > Designing the New System

content.topicNotes: Design Validation Routines What is validation Validation routines check input data to ensure it is reasonable and correct. A validation routine enforces rules before data enters the system. A rule is a specific test such as 'must be numeric' or 'cannot be empty'. Validation prevents incorrect or harmful data from being stored. Validation improves data quality and system reliability. Common validation types Presence check ensures required fields are not empty. Format check ensures data matches a pattern, for example an email address. Range check ensures numeric values fall between set limits. Type check ensures data is the correct data type, such as integer. Length check ensures a specific amount of characters is entered. Check digit verifies identifiers using an algorithm such as for ISBNs. Practical examples (school form) Student number: presence check and type check for numeric only. Date of birth: format check and range check to ensure realistic age. Email address: format check to verify contains '@' and domain. Class code: lookup check against a list of valid class identifiers. Mark entry: range check to ensure value is between 0 and 100. Implementation & feedback Validation can run client-side in the browser or server-side on submission. Immediate feedback helps users correct errors before submission. Error messages should explain what is wrong and how to fix it. Examples of messages: 'Enter a number between 0 and 100.' or 'Invalid email format.' Logging invalid attempts helps detect repeated input problems. Advantages and limitations An advantage is higher data accuracy and fewer processing errors. An advantage is improved security by rejecting malformed input. A limitation is that overly strict rules may reject valid exceptions. A limitation is false positives where valid input fails a check. Designers must balance strictness with user convenience.

content.topicNotes: Desktop Computer What is a desktop computer A desktop computer is a non-portable computer designed to be used at a fixed location. A desktop computer usually consists of separate components such as a monitor, keyboard, mouse and system unit. The system unit contains the main internal hardware components. Desktop computers require a constant mains power supply. Desktop computers are commonly used in homes, schools and offices. Uses of desktop computers Desktop computers are used for office and business tasks such as word processing and spreadsheets. Schools use desktop computers for teaching and learning activities. Gaming and entertainment often use desktop computers due to high performance. Designers use desktop computers for graphics and video editing. Businesses use desktop computers for data processing and management. Desktop computers are typically connected to a network to share files, printers, and internet access. Advantages of desktop computers Desktop computers usually offer higher performance than portable computers. Internal components such as memory and storage can be easily upgraded. Larger cases provide better cooling for hardware. Desktop computers are often cheaper than laptops with similar specifications. Desktop computers are suitable for long periods of continuous use. Disadvantages of desktop computers Desktop computers are not portable and must remain in one place. A desktop computer requires more space than a laptop or tablet. Multiple cables are needed to connect external devices. A desktop computer cannot be used without a mains power supply. Desktop computers are unsuitable for users who need to work while travelling.

content.topicNotes: Drivers and Utilities Device Driver A device driver is system software that allows the operating system to communicate with hardware. The driver translates OS commands into instructions the hardware can understand. Examples include drivers for printers, graphics cards, and network adapters. System Utilities Utilities are system software tools that help maintain and optimise a computer. Examples include antivirus software, disk defragmenters, and backup tools. Utilities help keep the system secure, fast, and organised. How They Work Together The operating system uses drivers to control hardware devices. Utilities run alongside the operating system to improve performance and safety. Both drivers and utilities are essential for reliable computer use.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Types & Components of Computer Systems > System Software

content.topicNotes: Digital Certificates What is a Digital Certificate? A digital certificate verifies the identity of a website or user. It is issued by a trusted organisation. It helps users know a site is genuine. This reduces the risk of fraud. Purpose of Certificates Digital certificates enable secure communication. They support encryption to protect data. Encryption converts data into a coded form. This prevents unauthorised access during transmission. Certificate Authority A Certificate Authority (CA) is a trusted organisation that issues digital certificates. It verifies the identity of the certificate owner. Examples include companies that manage internet security. Contents of a Certificate A certificate contains the owner's public key. The public key can be accessed by anyone and is used to verify the sender or owner of a website. The sender or owner has a private key that only they can access. This private key is used to sign the content, so it can be validated with the public key by others. It also includes the owner's identity details. The certificate has an expiry date and digital signature. Secure Websites Websites with certificates use HTTPS. Often a padlock symbol shows a secure connection. Users should check certificates before entering sensitive data. This helps ensure the website is trustworthy. Certificates include a digital signature applied by the Certificate Authority to confirm the data remains unaltered and authentic.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Safety & Security > Security of Data

content.topicNotes: Disadvantages of Cloud Computing Internet dependency Users need a reliable Internet connection to access cloud services. Slow or lost connections prevent access to files and software. This can interrupt work and learning. Security and legal concerns Security means protecting data from unauthorised access. Data is stored on remote servers owned by another company. Hackers may target cloud systems. Users have less direct control over data protection. Cloud data centers may reside in overseas jurisdictions, potentially causing conflicts with local data privacy regulations. Storing sensitive information on servers located abroad can lead to legal non-compliance for businesses. Downtime risk Cloud services may become unavailable due to technical problems. Downtime means a service is not available for use. Users cannot access data or applications during downtime. Ongoing costs Cloud services often charge monthly or yearly fees. This payment model is called a subscription.This business model is called Software as a Service (SaaS) Costs increase as users need more storage or features. Long-term use may become expensive compared to buying software or hardware once.

content.topicNotes: Display and Print: Values and Formulae Values vs Formulae View Spreadsheets present calculated values by default within the cell workspace. Values view displays the final numerical or text result generated by a formula. Formulae view displays the actual functions and cells referenced instead of the results. This mode allows examiners and creators to verify the logical structure of the model. Spreadsheet Editing Tools Users can employ other editing utilities like copy, cut, and paste to replicate formulae efficiently. Copy duplicates selected data to the clipboard while leaving the original cell unaltered. Shortcuts like Ctrl + C for copy, Ctrl + X for cut, and Ctrl + V for paste expedite spreadsheet construction. Data Accuracy and Integrity Authors must maintain absolute accuracy during manual data entry and formula creation. Data accuracy refers to the process of ensuring that data is free from errors and correctly reflects real-world figures. A singular erroneous character can corrupt cascading cell dependencies and invalidate the whole data model. Cell dependency describes a relationship where a formula relies on the value of another cell to calculate properly.

content.topicNotes: EFTPOS What is EFTPOS? EFTPOS stands for Electronic Funds Transfer at Point of Sale. EFTPOS allows customers to pay electronically using a debit or credit card. The system transfers money directly from the customer’s bank account to the retailer’s account. The transaction takes place at the checkout terminal. How a transaction works The customer inserts, taps or swipes their card on the card reader. The terminal sends the payment details securely to the bank for authorisation. The system verifies whether the card has been flagged as missing or stolen. The user's PIN entry or biometric data is validated for security. Authorisation checks if sufficient funds are available. The bank approves or declines the transaction and sends a response back to the terminal. Advantages of EFTPOS EFTPOS reduces the need to handle cash in shops. The system speeds up transactions at busy times. The system automatically records each payment in the retailer’s database. The retailer reduces the risk of theft compared to storing large amounts of cash.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > ICT Applications > Computers in the Retail Industry

content.topicNotes: Electronic Funds Transfers (EFTs) What is an EFT An electronic funds transfer (EFT) is the movement of money between bank accounts using computer systems. EFTs are processed electronically without using cash or cheques. Banks and financial institutions manage EFT systems. Transactions are carried out over secure networks. EFTs are widely used in modern banking. How EFTs work Payment details are entered into a banking system. The bank verifies the sender’s account and available funds. Data is transmitted securely to the receiving bank. The receiving account is credited automatically. The transaction is recorded in both accounts. Uses of EFTs Salaries are paid directly into bank accounts using EFTs. Online shopping payments use EFT systems. Utility bills are paid automatically by electronic transfer. Businesses transfer money between accounts electronically. EFTs support international money transfers. Advantages and disadvantages Advantages Transactions are fast and convenient. Cash handling and paperwork are reduced. Disadvantages Internet or network access is required. Errors can occur if incorrect details are entered.

content.topicNotes: Email Groups, CC, and BCC Email Groups Users create email groups to send a single message to multiple people simultaneously using one specific name or address. Email Group: a collection of email addresses stored under a single name, also known as a distribution list. Using groups saves time because the sender does not have to type out every individual address manually. Groups ensure that no team member is accidentally missed when important information is shared. Carbon Copy (CC) Senders use Carbon Copy (CC) to send a copy of an email to people who need to be kept informed but are not the primary recipients. Carbon Copy: a feature that sends a copy of the message to additional recipients while showing their addresses to everyone else. All recipients in the 'To' and 'CC' fields can see the email addresses of everyone else included in these fields. This method promotes transparency within a team or project. Blind Carbon Copy (BCC) Senders use Blind Carbon Copy (BCC) to send a copy of an email to recipients without revealing their email addresses to others. Blind Carbon Copy: a feature that hides the recipient's identity from all other people receiving the email. This feature protects the privacy of recipients by preventing the distribution of a contact list. It also prevents 'Reply All' loops from cluttering the inboxes of people in the BCC field.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Communication > Email Communication

content.topicNotes: Email Security Encryption and Privacy Users should use encryption to protect sensitive data sent via email from unauthorised access. Encryption: the process of converting information or data into a code to prevent unauthorised access. Digital signatures verify the identity of the sender and ensure the message has not been tampered with. Strong passwords prevent unauthorised users from gaining access to an email account. Malware and Attachments Email attachments can contain malware that harms the computer system or steals data. Malware: software that is specifically designed to disrupt, damage, or gain unauthorised access to a computer system. Users should never open attachments or click links from unknown or suspicious senders. Antivirus software scans incoming emails and attachments to detect and remove potential threats. Phishing and Spam Phishing emails attempt to trick users into revealing personal information like passwords or bank details. Phishing: the fraudulent practice of sending emails purporting to be from reputable companies to induce individuals to reveal personal information. Spam filters identify and move unsolicited bulk emails to a separate folder to reduce risk. Spam: irrelevant or unsolicited messages sent over the internet, typically to a large number of users.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Communication > Email Communication

content.topicNotes: Encryption What is Encryption? Encryption converts data into unreadable data called ciphertext. Unencrypted data begins as readable text called plaintext. An encryption algorithm scrambles plaintext into unreadable ciphertext. Only authorised users can read encrypted data. Decryption changes unreadable ciphertext back into readable form. Purpose of Encryption Encryption protects data from being accessed by attackers. It ensures privacy and confidentiality. It is used when storing and sending data. It builds trust in digital systems. It is essential for secure online services. Encryption on Hard Discs Hard disc encryption protects data that is stored locally on a computer. If the device is stolen, data remains secure, because only users with the correct key can access it. Encryption in Communication Emails can be encrypted to protect messages. Cloud storage uses encryption to secure files that are stored on servers. HTTPS websites use encryption for safe data transfer.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Safety & Security > Security of Data

content.topicNotes: Evaluating Efficiency, Ease and Appropriateness Evaluating efficiency Efficiency measures how well the system uses time and resources. Response time shows how quickly the system processes requests. Processing speed and storage usage are monitored. Efficient systems reduce operational costs. Daily example: a faster checkout system reduces customer waiting time. Evaluating ease of use Ease of use refers to how simple the system is for users. Clear menus and instructions improve usability. Training time indicates how easy the system is to learn. User feedback helps identify usability problems. Example: teachers quickly learn to record attendance without extra training. Evaluating appropriateness The final outputs of the system are evaluated against the initial requirements specification. The system should solve the intended problem. Outputs must match user needs. Security and legal requirements must be satisfied. Example: a banking system must handle transactions securely. Methods of evaluation Questionnaires gather user opinions. Interviews provide detailed feedback. Performance logs measure system speed and reliability. Error reports identify recurring problems. Outputs of the new system are compared to outputs of the old system. Evaluation results guide future improvements.

content.topicNotes: Expert Systems – Examples Medical diagnosis system A medical expert system helps doctors diagnose illnesses. The system asks questions about symptoms. A knowledge base stores medical facts and rules. A knowledge base is a collection of stored expert knowledge. An inference engine applies rules to the answers. An inference engine uses logical rules to reach conclusions. The system suggests possible diagnoses. Car fault diagnosis system A car fault expert system identifies mechanical problems. The user enters details about warning lights or noises. The system compares symptoms with stored rules. The system suggests likely faults. Mechanics use the advice to guide repairs. Loan approval system A loan approval expert system helps banks assess applications. The system analyses income, credit history and debts. Rules determine whether the applicant qualifies. The system provides a recommendation. Final decisions may still require human review. Crop management system A crop management expert system advises farmers. The system considers soil type, weather and crop disease. Expert knowledge is stored in the knowledge base. The system suggests fertiliser or treatment options. Farmers use recommendations to improve yields.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > ICT Applications > Expert Systems

content.topicNotes: Expert Systems – Examples (Cont.) Mineral exploration system A mineral exploration expert system helps locate valuable resources. Geological data is entered into the system. The knowledge base contains expert geological rules. The inference engine analyses patterns in the data. The system suggests areas likely to contain minerals. Tax advisory system A tax advisory expert system provides guidance on tax rules. Users enter financial details and income information. The system applies stored tax regulations. The system suggests tax liabilities or allowances. Advice is based on programmed expert knowledge. Network fault diagnosis system A network fault expert system identifies technical issues. The user enters symptoms such as slow connections. The knowledge base stores troubleshooting rules. The inference engine suggests possible causes. Technicians use recommendations to solve problems. Legal advisory system A legal expert system provides advice on legal matters. The system asks questions about the case. The knowledge base stores legal rules and precedents. The inference engine applies rules to the answers. The system suggests possible legal actions.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > ICT Applications > Expert Systems

content.topicNotes: Expert Systems What is an Expert System? An expert system is a computer system that mimics human expert decision-making. It uses knowledge and rules to solve problems. A rule is a logical statement used to make decisions. It provides advice or solutions based on input data. Characteristics Expert systems use a knowledge base to store information. A knowledge base is a collection of facts. They use inference to make decisions. Inference is the process of drawing conclusions from data. They can explain their reasoning to users. Advantages Expert systems provide consistent decisions. They are available at any time. They reduce the need for human experts. They can process large amounts of data quickly. Disadvantages Expert systems can be expensive to develop. They require regular updates to remain accurate. They lack human intuition and judgement. Errors in the knowledge base can lead to wrong decisions. Uses and Purpose Expert systems are used in medical diagnosis and financial planning. They help with car engine fault diagnosis and route scheduling. They are used in mineral prospecting and species identification. Their purpose is to support decision-making in complex tasks.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > ICT Applications > Expert Systems

content.topicNotes: Expert Systems – Explanation System What is an explanation system An explanation system is a component of an expert system. The explanation system shows how a decision was reached, increases user trust in the system, works with the inference engine. Users can query why specific questions are being asked during the consultation. Clear explanations improve understanding of advice. How the explanation system works The explanation system records the rules used during reasoning. The system tracks the sequence of IF…THEN rules applied. The explanation system displays the logical steps. The user can review the reasoning process. Transparency improves confidence in the system. Why explanations are important Explanations allow users to check the accuracy of decisions. Explanations help identify incorrect input data. Users can understand why advice was given. Professionals can justify decisions using the explanation. Explanation systems support accountability. Advantages and limitations Advantages Users gain confidence in system decisions. Errors can be identified more easily. Limitations Complex reasoning may be difficult to explain clearly. Explanations depend on accurate rule recording.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > ICT Applications > Expert Systems

content.topicNotes: Exporting Data from Databases Why Export Reports? Users export database reports to change or manipulate the data in other software packages. Exporting means transferring data from a database into a different file format for another application. Exporting allows analysts to create advanced graphs or charts in spreadsheet software. This process allows people to share critical database information without giving others direct database access. Hiding Data in Reports Database designers hide sensitive fields from reports to maintain data privacy and security. Data privacy means protecting personal information from unauthorised viewing or distribution. For example, a school clerk hides student home addresses on a class merits report shared with teachers. Hiding unnecessary data keeps the final report clean, relevant, and easy for the reader to understand. What are Labels? Labels display descriptive information used for identifying items or addressing mail. Users generate address labels to automate the distribution of letters to large groups of customers. Marketing teams print promotional labels directly from inventory data to advertise specific product details on packaging. Practical Tips for Exporting Data Export File Formats RTF (.rtf) exports formatted text for editing in word processors. CSV (.csv) exports raw comma-separated data for spreadsheet analysis. PDF (.pdf) exports a read-only layout view for shared reading. Text (.txt) exports basic plain text for broad software access. Hiding Search Criteria Fields Databases let you filter records using a field without showing it in results. Uncheck the Show box in design view to hide the field. Useful when a report title already explains the filter choice. Mail Merge and Address Labels Databases produce structured labels using filtered records. Labels are arranged in multi-column grids across pages. Each label contains embedded field tags (e.g., {First_Name} {Last_Name}) that populate automatically for every record. Labels often require student details printed in a specific position on every item.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Databases > Presenting Data

content.topicNotes: Exporting Files: Application Package Defining Exporting Users export files to save data in a format that other applications can recognise. Export: the process of converting a file from its native format into a different format for use in other software. This process allows for greater portability between different computer systems. Portability: the ability of software or data to be moved easily from one system environment to another. Spreadsheets and Databases Users often export data from Microsoft Excel or Access into plain text formats to transfer information. Microsoft Access: a database management system used to store, manipulate, and report on large sets of related data. CSV (Comma Separated Values): a file format where a comma separates each piece of data. Exporting an Access table as a CSV file allows an Excel user to open the data without needing the original database software. Word Processing Documents Microsoft Word users export documents to universal formats to ensure consistency across different platforms. RTF (Rich Text Format): a universal document format that retains basic formatting like bold and italic text. PDF (Portable Document Format): a file type that captures a document's layout so it looks the same on every device. These formats enable sharing with people who do not have Microsoft Office.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > File Management > Managing Files

content.topicNotes: Exporting Files: Generic File Format Need for Generic Formats Users require generic formats to ensure data can be opened across different platforms and software brands. Generic File Format: a standard file type that is not restricted to one specific application. These formats solve the problem of software incompatibility. Incompatibility: a situation where one software package cannot open or read a file created in another. Text File Formats Text-based generic formats allow for the transfer of data and documents between word processors and databases. .csv (Comma Separated Values): a plain text format that organises data into tables using commas. .txt (Plain Text): a format containing only characters with no styling or fonts. .rtf (Rich Text Format): a format that preserves basic styling like bold and italics. Generic Image Formats Standard image formats allow graphics to be viewed regardless of the operating system. .jpg: a compressed format ideal for digital photographs. .png: a format that supports transparency and high-quality detail. .gif: a format used for simple animations and low-colour images. .pdf: a fixed-layout format used to present documents and images exactly as designed. Audio and Video Formats Standardised media formats allow high-quality sound and moving images to be shared easily. .mp3: a generic audio format that uses compression to reduce file size while maintaining sound quality. .mp4: a generic video format used to store digital video and audio streams. These formats are compatible with almost all media players and mobile devices. Web File Formats Web browsers use specific generic formats to display content and apply visual styles uniformly. .html (HyperText Markup Language): the code used to define the structure and content of a web page. .css (Cascading Style Sheets): the code used to define the visual layout, colours, and fonts of a web page. These formats ensure websites look consistent on different devices. Compressed File Formats Compressed formats allow users to bundle multiple files into one smaller package for easier storage or emailing. .zip and .rar: common formats used to reduce total file size without losing any data. Compression: the process of reducing the size of a file to save disk space or speed up transmission.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > File Management > Managing Files

content.topicNotes: Augmented Reality (AR) What is augmented reality Augmented reality (AR) overlays digital information onto the real world. The real world remains visible while digital objects are added. AR is commonly viewed through smartphones, tablets or smart glasses. Digital objects may include images, text or animations. AR enhances real-world experiences rather than replacing them. How augmented reality works AR uses a camera to capture the real-world environment. Software processes the image and adds digital content in real time. Sensors track position and movement to align virtual objects correctly. Real-time means the system updates instantly as the user moves. Accurate tracking improves realism and usability. Uses of augmented reality AR is used in education to display interactive 3D models. Retail apps allow users to preview products in their home. Navigation apps overlay directions onto live camera views. AR games combine virtual characters with real surroundings. Engineers use AR to visualise designs on real objects. Advantages of augmented reality AR improves learning through interactive visual content. Users remain aware of their real surroundings. Information is presented at the point of need. AR can increase engagement and motivation. Existing devices such as smartphones can support AR. Disadvantages of augmented reality AR applications require powerful hardware and cameras. Prolonged use may cause distraction or eye strain. Development of accurate AR content can be costly. Privacy concerns arise when cameras are always active. Performance depends on lighting and environment.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Types & Components of Computer Systems > Impact of Emerging Technologies

content.topicNotes: Virtual Reality (VR) What is virtual reality Virtual reality (VR) immerses the user in a fully computer-generated environment. The real world is completely replaced by a simulated digital world. VR is usually experienced using a headset. A headset is a wearable device that displays images close to the eyes. VR aims to make users feel present inside the virtual environment. How virtual reality works VR systems display 3D images on screens inside a headset. Sensors track head and body movement. The system updates the view in real time as the user moves. Real time means changes happen instantly with no noticeable delay. Controllers are often used to interact with virtual objects. Uses of virtual reality VR is used in gaming to create immersive experiences. Training simulations use VR to practise dangerous tasks safely. VR is used in education to explore places that are difficult to visit. Medical training uses VR to practise procedures. Architects use VR to explore building designs. Advantages of virtual reality VR provides immersive and engaging experiences. Users can practise skills in a safe environment. VR can improve understanding through realistic simulations. Training costs can be reduced over time. It allows experiences that are impossible in real life. Disadvantages of virtual reality VR equipment can be expensive. Some users experience motion sickness or discomfort. Extended use may cause eye strain. Users are isolated from the real world while using VR. High-performance hardware is required.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Types & Components of Computer Systems > Impact of Emerging Technologies

content.topicNotes: External Stylesheets CSS Files A .css file stores CSS rules separately from HTML content. A CSS file contains formatting instructions for web page elements. Developers use .css files to keep design separate from content. Attaching Stylesheets A web page can connect to a stylesheet using the <link> tag. The <link> tag is placed inside the <head> section. This allows one stylesheet to control the appearance of many pages. Relative and Absolute Paths A relative path gives the location of a file from the current folder. An absolute path gives the full location of a file. Relative paths are shorter and do not depend on a specific computer location. Relative paths continue to work when a website is moved to another server. Absolute paths for local files can stop working on other computers. Relative paths make websites easier to transfer and maintain.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Website Authoring > Stylesheets

content.topicNotes: Eye Problems and Headaches Eye problems Eye problems occur from prolonged use of computer screens. Staring at screens reduces blinking, which dries the eyes. Symptoms include sore, dry or irritated eyes. Blurred vision can occur after long periods of screen use. Eye strain is common when focusing on screens for too long. Causes of eye problems Poor screen brightness or contrast strains the eyes. Glare from windows or lights increases eye discomfort. Sitting too close to the screen increases eye strain. Long periods without breaks prevent eye muscles from relaxing. Small text forces the eyes to work harder. Headaches Headaches can be caused by prolonged screen use. Eye strain often leads to tension headaches. Poor posture can contribute to headaches. Stress from extended computer work increases headache risk. Dehydration during long sessions can worsen headaches. Prevention methods Regular breaks reduce eye strain and fatigue. The 20-20-20 rule helps relax the eyes. The rule involves looking 20 feet away for 20 seconds every 20 minutes. Screen brightness and contrast should be adjusted. Anti-glare filters or screens can be fitted to minimise light reflections. Proper lighting and correct screen position reduce headaches.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > The Effects of Using IT > Health Problems Related to IT Equipment

content.topicNotes: Methods of File Compression Compressing Files Users can create a compressed folder to bundle multiple files into one smaller package. Zip Folder: a common compressed file format that uses lossless compression to save space. Modern software allows users to export documents to generic formats that reduce size while preserving layout. Exporting: the process of saving a file in a different format than the one it was created in. Converting a Word document to a .pdf often reduces the file size for easier sharing. Lossy vs Lossless Compression Lossy compression reduces file size by permanently removing unnoticeable data. Lossy: a method where original data is lost, used for example in .mp3 or .jpg files. Lossless compression shrinks files by reorganising data without losing any information. Lossless: a method that allows the original file to be perfectly reconstructed, used for example in .zip or .png files. Users choose between these based on whether they value high quality or maximum storage savings. Compression Ratios Different algorithms provide varying levels of efficiency in shrinking data. Algorithm: a specific set of instructions or rules followed by a computer to complete a task. Lossy algorithms generally achieve much higher compression ratios than lossless ones. A high compression ratio means the final file size is a very small fraction of the original size. Technicians choose the algorithm based on whether they prioritise quality or storage savings.

content.topicNotes: Firewall What is a Firewall? A firewall is a security system that monitors network traffic. It checks data entering and leaving a network. It can be hardware or software. It helps protect systems from unauthorised access. Purpose of a Firewall A firewall blocks unwanted or harmful connections. It allows only trusted data to pass through. This reduces the risk of cyberattacks. It protects sensitive data on a network. How Firewalls Work Firewalls use rules to decide which traffic to allow. A rule is a condition that controls access. They inspect data packets before allowing entry. A packet is a small unit of data sent over a network. Types of Firewall Hardware firewalls are usually used to protect entire networks. Software firewalls are used to protect individual devices most of the time. Both types work together for better security. Users should enable firewalls on their devices.

content.topicNotes: Fixed and Portable Magnetic Hard Drives What is magnetic storage Magnetic storage stores data using magnetised areas on a disk. Data is stored as binary values. Binary values are represented using 0s and 1s. A read/write head accesses the data. Magnetic storage is non-volatile. Non-volatile means data is not lost when power is switched off. Fixed hard disk drive (HDD) A fixed hard disk drive is installed inside a computer. A fixed HDD is used as the main backing storage device. Data is stored on rotating metal platters coated with magnetic material. The disk spins at high speed during operation. A fixed HDD stores the operating system, software and user files. A fixed HDD offers large storage capacity at low cost per gigabyte. Portable hard disk drive A portable hard disk drive is an external storage device. A portable HDD connects to a computer using a USB cable. A portable HDD is used for backups and file transfer. A portable HDD can be moved between different computers. A portable HDD is also non-volatile storage. Advantages and disadvantages Advantages of magnetic hard drives Magnetic hard drives provide large storage capacity at low cost. Magnetic hard drives are suitable for backing up large amounts of data. Disadvantages of magnetic hard drives Moving parts make hard drives vulnerable to physical damage. Access speed is slower than solid-state drives (SSDs). Portable hard drives can be lost or stolen more easily.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Storage Devices & Media > Magnetic Devices & Media

content.topicNotes: Flood Water Management Modelling What is flood water management modelling Flood water management modelling uses computers to simulate water flow. Models represent rivers, rainfall and land surfaces. Computer models predict how floods may develop. Modelling helps authorities plan flood prevention. Real-world testing is replaced by safe simulations. How flood models work Data such as rainfall, river levels and terrain is entered. Terrain describes the shape and height of land. The computer simulates water movement over time. Different scenarios can be tested. Results show areas at risk of flooding. Uses of flood water modelling Governments use models to design flood defences. Emergency services plan evacuation routes. Town planners decide where buildings should be located. Flood warnings can be issued earlier. Damage to property and life can be reduced. Advantages and disadvantages Advantages Dangerous flood situations can be tested safely. Planning and decision-making are improved. Simulations can be sped up to quickly visualize years of coastal changes. Disadvantages Models depend on accurate input data. Unexpected weather patterns may reduce accuracy.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > ICT Applications > Modelling Applications

content.topicNotes: Font Properties Font Families A font family is a group of fonts with a similar design. CSS uses the font-family property to select text styles. You can write font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;. If a font name contains spaces, it must be enclosed in quotes (e.g., 'Times New Roman'). The browser tries the fonts from left to right. Serif and Sans-serif Serif fonts include small decorative lines at the ends of letters. Sans-serif fonts do not include these decorative lines. Serif fonts often appear in printed text. Sans-serif fonts often improve readability on screens. Fallback Fonts A fallback font is a backup font used if the first font is unavailable. Browsers move to the next listed font automatically. Fallback fonts help web pages display correctly on different devices. Generic options include serif and sans-serif. Font Sizes CSS uses the font-size property to control text size. Pixels (px) set an exact size. Percentages (%) set a size relative to another value. Different measurement units can make pages flexible on different screens.

content.topicNotes: Fonts Font Face A font face is the design style of text. Examples include Arial and Times New Roman. Different font faces create different appearances. Users choose font faces to suit the document purpose. Serif and Sans-Serif Serif fonts have small decorative lines on letters and are commonly used in printed documents. Examples are Times New Roman or Georgia Sans-serif fonts do not have decorative lines and are often easier to read on screens. Examples are Arial, Helvetica or Calibri Point Size Point size controls the height of text. A point is a unit used to measure font size. Larger point sizes make text easier to read. Headings often use larger point sizes than body text. Font Colour Font colour changes the appearance of text and can highlight important information. Users should choose colours with good contrast for improved readability for users. Using Fonts Effectively Consistent fonts improve document presentation. Too many font styles can confuse readers. Fonts should match the purpose of the document. Clear fonts make information easier to understand.

content.topicNotes: Formulae and Functions in Spreadsheets Formulae vs Functions Formulae are user-defined mathematical equations used to perform calculations in a spreadsheet. A formula always begins with an equals sign and uses cell references, such as "=B1+B2+B3+B4". Functions are built-in, ready-made formulae that simplify complex calculations. A function uses a specific keyword followed by a range, such as =SUM(B1:B4). Cell ranges define a block of cells using a colon, which instructs the software to include all cells between the two references. Mathematical Operators Mathematical operators instruct the spreadsheet to perform basic arithmetic operations. The plus sign (+) executes addition, whilst the minus sign (-) performs subtraction. The asterisk (*) carries out multiplication, and the forward slash (/) handles division. The caret symbol (^) calculates exponents, which raises a number to a specific power. Numeric Functions "SUM" adds all the values in a specified range together. "AVERAGE" calculates the arithmetic mean by dividing the total sum by the number of values. "MAX" identifies the largest value, whilst "MIN" finds the smallest value in a dataset. "INT" rounds a number down to the nearest whole integer (=INT(8.9) returns 8). "ROUND" changes a value to a specified number of decimal places based on standard rounding rules (=ROUND(3.14159, 2) returns 3.14). Counting Functions "COUNT" registers cells containing numeric data, so =COUNT(A1:A5) returns 5 if all cells contain numbers. "COUNTA" evaluates all occupied cells, meaning that =COUNTA(A1:A5) counts text entries alongside numeric entries. An occupied cell is a cell that contains any form of data, including letters, symbols, or numbers. "COUNTIF" verifies entries against a rule, meaning that =COUNTIF(A1:A5, ">3") returns 2 if only two cells exceed the value of 3. Logical and Conditional Functions "IF" conducts a logical test and returns one value if the condition is true, and another if it is false (=IF(A1>5, "Pass", "Fail") outputs "Pass" if cell A1 contains at least 6). "SUMIF" accumulates data selectively based on a condition (=SUMIF(A1:A5, ">3") only adds values that are greater than 3). Nested functions embed one function inside another to allow the spreadsheet to evaluate multiple complex conditions.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Spreadsheets > Data Models

content.topicNotes: Forwards and Attachments Forwarding Emails Users forward an email to send a copy of a received message to a new recipient. Forward: a function that redirects an existing email including its history and original attachments to a different address. Senders should check the previous message thread to ensure they do not share sensitive or private information accidentally. The user should add a brief note explaining why they are redirecting the message to the new recipient. Managing Attachments Senders attach files to emails to share documents, images, or spreadsheets with other users. Attachment: a separate computer file sent along with an email message. Users must consider the file size because large attachments can exceed the recipient's inbox limit or slow down the transmission. Compressing files into a zipped folder reduces the overall size and makes sending more efficient. Risky File Types Users should exercise extreme caution when receiving executable files as attachments. Executable File: a type of file, often ending in .exe, that contains a program or a set of instructions for the computer to run. Malicious content often hides within these files to install harmful software once the recipient opens them. Many professional email systems automatically strip or block .exe attachments to protect the network from potential security breaches.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Communication > Email Communication

content.topicNotes: Functionality of the Internet Internet Service Providers (ISPs) An Internet Service Provider provides the necessary infrastructure for users to access the Internet. ISP: a company that provides customers with access to the Internet and other related services. They assign IP addresses to users and provide routers to connect local devices to the global network. Most ISPs charge a monthly subscription fee for data usage and connection maintenance. Web Addresses and URLs A Uniform Resource Locator serves as the unique address used to locate a specific resource on the web. URL: a reference or address to a resource on the Internet that specifies its location. It contains the protocol used, the domain name, and the specific path to a file or page. Users type URLs into a browser to visit specific websites without needing to know numerical IP addresses. Hyperlinks Hyperlinks allow users to navigate between different web pages or sections of a document instantly. Hyperlink: a digital link in a document that opens a new page or resource when clicked. They usually appear as underlined text or clickable images within the browser window. These links use URLs to tell the browser exactly which server and file to request next. Web Browsers A web browser acts as the software application used to access and view websites. Web Browser: software that retrieves and renders HTML files from web servers for user display. It interprets the code of a web page to display text, images, and multimedia correctly. Common features of browsers include an address bar, navigation buttons, and the ability to manage bookmarks.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Communication > The Internet

content.topicNotes: Geographic Information Systems (GIS) What is GIS GIS is an abbreviation for Geographic Information System. It refers to a computer-based network built to collect and evaluate geographical data. Information is organized into distinct layers for storage and display. Every layer displays a unique category of data mapped over identical geographic locations. How GIS works Data is collected from satellites, surveys or GPS devices. The data is stored in a database. Layers such as roads, rivers and buildings are added. Users can turn layers on or off. The system analyses relationships between layers. Uses of GIS Town planners use GIS to design new developments. Emergency services use GIS to plan response routes. Environmental agencies use GIS to monitor deforestation. Businesses use GIS to choose store locations. Farmers use GIS to analyse soil and crop patterns. Advantages and disadvantages Advantages GIS helps visualise complex data on maps. GIS supports better planning and decision-making. Disadvantages GIS systems can be expensive to set up. GIS requires accurate and up-to-date data.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > ICT Applications > Satellite Systems

content.topicNotes: Global Positioning System (GPS) What is GPS The Global Positioning System (GPS) is a satellite-based navigation system. GPS uses a network of satellites orbiting the Earth. A GPS receiver calculates its position using satellite signals. GPS provides location, speed and time information. GPS is widely used in smartphones and vehicles. How GPS works Satellites transmit signals containing time and position data. A GPS receiver picks up signals from multiple satellites. The receiver calculates distance based on signal travel time. At least four satellites are needed for accurate positioning. The process is called trilateration. Uses of GPS Drivers use GPS for route navigation. Delivery companies track vehicle locations. Smartphones use GPS for maps and location services. Aircraft and ships use GPS for navigation. Fitness trackers use GPS to record distance travelled. Advantages and disadvantages Advantages GPS provides accurate global positioning. GPS improves navigation and route planning. GPS operates worldwide, 24/7, in all weather conditions. Disadvantages GPS signals require a direct line-of-sight and can be blocked by tall buildings or tunnels. GPS accuracy can be reduced by poor signal reception.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > ICT Applications > Satellite Systems

content.topicNotes: Graph Plotters What is a graph plotter A graph plotter is an output device used to produce large, precise drawings. It uses pens to draw lines on paper. Plotters are controlled by a computer. They are designed for high accuracy. Graph plotters are used for technical drawings. How graph plotters work A graph plotter is an output device that prints vector graphics. The computer sends instructions for the direction and length of each line. The plotter moves one or more pens over the paper. Pens draw continuous lines rather than dots. This produces very accurate output, making plotters suitable for technical drawings. Uses of graph plotters Engineers use graph plotters for technical diagrams. Architects use them for building plans. Designers produce large maps and charts. Graph plotters are used for computer-aided design (CAD). They are suitable for large-format printing. Advantages and disadvantages An advantage is extremely accurate line drawing. An advantage is high-quality output for large designs. A disadvantage is that graph plotters are slow. A disadvantage is that they are expensive. They are not suitable for general office printing.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Input & Output Devices > Output Devices

content.topicNotes: Graphics and Sound Cards Graphics Card A graphics card processes visual data and outputs images to a display. The Graphics Processing Unit (GPU) performs calculations needed for images and video. The GPU handles tasks such as drawing shapes, colours, and animations. Some computers have integrated graphics built into the motherboard. Sound Card A sound card processes audio input and output in a computer. The sound card converts digital data into sound played through speakers or headphones. The sound card also converts sound from a microphone into digital data. Purpose and Use Graphics cards improve performance in games, videos, and graphic design. Sound cards improve audio quality for music, videos, and communication. Both cards can be built-in or added as expansion cards.
