content.topicNotes: Groups and Layers of Images Working with Layers Users place different parts of a graphic on separate layers to edit them independently. Layers: transparent sheets stacked on top of each other that hold individual parts of an image. Designers arrange the layers stack so the bottom layer acts as the background and the top layer appears at the front of the image. Use .png files for background transparency, as .jpg files do not support it. Grouping Objects Users group multiple elements together so they can move or resize them as a single unit. Grouping: the process of combining two or more objects so they behave as one item. This process preserves the relative position of objects within the group during layout changes. Users can ungroup the items at any time to modify an individual component again. Layer Visibility and Locking Editors allow users to hide specific layers to focus on a particular area of the document without distractions. Locking a layer prevents accidental changes to the content while working on other parts of the graphic. Locking: a function that restricts editing or movement of a specific layer or object. These tools help manage complex ICT projects that contain many overlapping shapes and text boxes.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Images > Images

content.topicNotes: HTML Structure What HTML Is HTML stands for HyperText Markup Language. HTML is used to create the structure and content of a web page. Web browsers read HTML to display web pages. HTML forms the content layer of a website. HTML Tags A tag is a code element that defines part of a web page. Tags are written inside angle brackets like . Tags identify elements such as headings, paragraphs, and images. Tags help organise content into a clear structure. Opening and Closing Tags Most HTML elements use an opening tag and a closing tag. An opening tag marks the start of an element: A closing tag contains a forward slash and marks the end of an element: The content appears between the opening and closing tags. Some HTML tags do not contain text and do not have a separate closing tag e.g. and DOCTYPE Declaration The DOCTYPE declaration appears at the top of an HTML document. It tells the browser which version of HTML the page uses. Browsers use the declaration to display pages correctly. The declaration helps ensure consistent behaviour. The HTML Element The element contains all the content of an HTML document. It is the root element of a web page. Most other HTML elements are placed inside the element like this: other elements The element defines the start and end of the web page structure.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Website Authoring > Creating a Web Page

content.topicNotes: Hacking and Data Protection What is Hacking? Hacking is unauthorised access to a computer system. A hacker is a person who gains access without permission. Hackers may steal, change or delete data. Sensitive data is important or private information that must be protected. Strong Passwords A strong password is difficult for others to guess. Users should include letters, numbers and symbols. Password length should be at least 8 characters. Avoid using personal information such as names or birthdays. Encryption Encryption converts data into a coded format. Only authorised users can decrypt the data. Decryption changes coded data back into readable form. This protects data if it is intercepted. Firewalls A firewall monitors incoming and outgoing network traffic. It blocks unauthorised access to a system by inspecting incoming and outgoing data against predetermined security rules. Firewalls can be hardware or software. They act as a barrier between a trusted network and the internet. User Access Levels Access levels control what users can see or do. An administrator is a user with full control of a system. Standard users have limited permissions. This reduces the risk of accidental or malicious changes.

content.topicNotes: Hardware and Software Selecting Hardware The analyst identifies the hardware needed for the new system. Hardware means the physical components of a computer system. They consider input, processing, storage and output devices. They check performance factors such as processor speed, RAM capacity and storage capacity. Selecting Software The analyst chooses suitable software for the system. Software means the programs that control the hardware. They decide between off-the-shelf and custom-made software. Off-the-shelf software is ready-made and available to buy. Custom-made software is specially developed for one organisation. Compatibility and Integration The analyst checks that hardware and software are compatible. Compatible means devices and programs work together correctly. They ensure the new system integrates with existing systems. Cost and Future Needs The organisation considers the cost of hardware and software. This includes purchase, installation and maintenance including updating or repairing the system. The analyst plans for future expansion so the system can be upgraded.

content.topicNotes: Head and Body Sections The Head Section The <head> section contains information about the web page. Information in the <head> section is usually not displayed on the page itself. The <head> section can contain page titles and links to stylesheets. Browsers use this information when loading the page. The Body Section The <body> section contains the content displayed in the browser window. Text, images, tables, and hyperlinks are placed in the <body> section. Users view and interact with the content in the <body> section. The <body> section forms the visible part of a web page. Page Titles Page titles are set using the <title> tag. A page title identifies a web page. The page title is stored in the head section. Browsers display the page title in the tab or title bar. Clear page titles help users identify and navigate websites. Head and Body Together The <head> section stores information about the page. The <body> section stores the content shown to users. Both sections are contained within the HTML document. Separating these sections improves organisation and maintenance. Website Structure Web developers use the <head> and <body> sections to structure web pages. A well-structured page is easier to create and maintain. Proper organisation improves consistency across a website. Good structure helps browsers display pages correctly.

content.topicNotes: Hubs What a Hub Is A hub connects multiple devices in a network. It sends data it receives from one device to all other connected devices. This is called Broadcast. Therefore, a hub does not identify destination devices. This makes hubs simple but inefficient, because only the intended device uses the data. Disadvantages of Hubs There is a lot of unnecessary traffic in the network, because in most cases only one device uses the broadcasted data. This reduces the possible bandwidth of the network, so it is relatively slow. This is not very secure, because all devices receive data that was intended for other devices. Hub vs Switch A hub sends data to all devices. A switch sends data only to the correct device. Switches use MAC addresses to make decisions. Most networks now use switches instead of hubs.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Networks and the Effects of Using Them > Common Network Devices

content.topicNotes: Hyperlinks and Navigation Purpose of Hyperlinks A hyperlink is a clickable link that takes a user to another location. Hyperlinks help users navigate quickly through information. Users can access related content with a single click. Hyperlinks improve document usability. External Hyperlinks An external hyperlink connects to a different document, file or website. Users can link to online resources and reference materials. External links provide access to information outside the current document. Users should check that external links work correctly. Hyperlink Properties Display text is the clickable word or phrase shown in the document. It replaces full web addresses with user-friendly words or phrases. ScreenTips appear as pop-up boxes offering extra detail when hovering over a link. Practical exams often require modifying display text so that raw URLs are hidden. Internal Hyperlinks An internal hyperlink connects to another location within the same document. Internal links help users move quickly between sections. Large documents often use internal hyperlinks. Internal navigation improves efficiency. Bookmarks A bookmark is a named location within a document. Users create bookmarks to mark important sections. Hyperlinks can link directly to bookmarks. Bookmarks make navigation easier in long documents. Document Navigation Navigation allows users to move efficiently through a document. Hyperlinks and bookmarks support effective navigation. Good navigation helps users find information quickly. Well-designed navigation improves the user experience.

content.topicNotes: IP Address What an IP Address Is An IP address identifies a device on a network. IP stands for Internet Protocol. Networks use IP addresses to send data to the correct device. Each device on a network needs an IP address. How IP Addresses Work A device uses its IP address to send and receive data. Routers read IP addresses to forward data between networks. A router is a device that directs data between networks. This process allows access to the internet. Types of IP Address IPv4 uses four numbers separated by dots like this: 203.0.113.195 IPv6 uses longer addresses to provide more unique values like this:2001:0db8:85a3:0000:0000:8a2e:0370:7344 IPv4 means Internet Protocol version 4. IPv6 means Internet Protocol version 6.

content.topicNotes: Identifying & Preventing Spam Recognising Spam Users identify spam by looking for unsolicited bulk messages often sent for advertising or malicious purposes. Spam: irrelevant or unsolicited messages sent over the internet, typically to a large number of users. Recipients check for common signs such as generic greetings, poor grammar, and suspicious links. Senders often use sensationalist subject lines to trick the user into opening the message. Using Spam Filters Email providers use spam filters to automatically detect and move suspicious messages to a separate junk folder. Spam Filter: a program used to detect unsolicited and unwanted email and prevent those messages from reaching a user's inbox. These filters analyse the sender's reputation and the content of the message for known spam patterns. Users should regularly check their junk folder to ensure the filter has not blocked legitimate emails. Prevention Techniques Individuals prevent spam by keeping their email addresses private and avoiding public online directories. Users should never reply to a spam message or click the 'unsubscribe' link in a suspicious email. Unsubscribe Link: a link in an email that allows a recipient to opt out of future mailings. Replying confirms that the email address is active, which often leads to an increase in future spam messages.

content.topicNotes: Images in Web Pages Inserting Images The tag inserts an image into a web page. Images improve the appearance and understanding of content. The image source identifies the image file location. Web developers should use relevant images. Alternative Text Alternative text is stored in the alt attribute like Alt text describes an image if it cannot load. Screen readers use alt text to help visually impaired users. Alt text improves accessibility. Image Paths A relative path uses a file location within the website folder like An absolute path uses the full web address of a file like Relative paths make websites easier to move. Absolute paths often point to external resources. Image Formats JPEG files store photographs with small file sizes. PNG files support transparency and high image quality. GIF files support simple animations. Different image formats suit different purposes. Size and Aspect Ratio Web developers can change image width and height like width="500" Aspect ratio is the relationship between image width and height. Keeping the aspect ratio prevents image distortion. Correct sizing improves page appearance.

content.topicNotes: Impact of Microprocessor-Controlled Devices at Home Impact on lifestyle Microprocessor-controlled devices automate many household tasks. Automation reduces the time spent on daily chores. Smart home systems allow remote control of appliances. Remote control means devices can be managed using smartphones. Convenience and comfort in daily life are increased. Impact on leisure Smart televisions use microprocessors to stream online content. Games consoles use microprocessors to run complex games. Music systems use microprocessors to manage digital playlists. Leisure activities are more interactive and personalised. On-demand entertainment is easily accessible at home. Impact on fitness Fitness trackers use microprocessors to monitor activity levels. Smart watches track steps, heart rate and calories burned. Exercise data helps users set and achieve fitness goals. Feedback motivates users to stay active. Home fitness equipment uses microprocessors to control workouts. Positive and negative impacts Advantages Health and fitness monitoring encourages active lifestyles. Leisure experiences are more engaging and convenient. Disadvantages Increased screen time can reduce physical activity. Over-reliance on technology may reduce motivation.

content.topicNotes: Impact on Security and Social Interactions Impact on home security Microprocessor-controlled devices improve home security. Smart alarms use sensors and microprocessors to detect intruders. Smart door locks allow controlled access using codes or smartphones. Security cameras monitor homes in real time. Alerts can be sent automatically to homeowners. Advantages for security Automated systems respond quickly to security threats. Remote monitoring allows homeowners to check property from anywhere. Recorded footage provides evidence after incidents. Timed lighting systems can deter burglars. Overall home safety is increased. Impact on social interactions Smart devices enable communication through video calls and messaging. Family members stay connected using networked devices. Social media platforms increase online interaction. Entertainment systems support shared digital activities. Technology enables social contact without physical presence. Positive and negative impacts Advantages Improved security systems provide reassurance and faster emergency response. Communication technology helps maintain relationships over distance. Disadvantages Over-reliance on devices can reduce face-to-face interaction. Connected security devices can be hacked if poorly protected. Weak passwords or unpatched software increase cybersecurity risks. Personal data may be intercepted or misused by cybercriminals.

content.topicNotes: Expert Systems – Inference Engine What is an inference engine An inference engine is the decision-making part of an expert system. The inference engine uses rules stored in the knowledge base. Rules are usually written as IF…THEN statements. The inference engine applies logical reasoning. The inference engine produces conclusions or recommendations. How the inference engine works The user enters data via the user interface. The inference engine operates like a search engine. It executes rules from the rule base against the supplied user data. It uses these logical rules to locate matching information within the knowledge base. A step-by-step chain of reasoning is followed to determine the conclusion. Forward and backward chaining Forward chaining starts with known facts and applies rules to reach a conclusion. Backward chaining starts with a possible conclusion and checks if supporting facts exist. Both methods use logical reasoning. Chaining improves the accuracy of decisions. The chosen method depends on the system design. Importance of the inference engine The inference engine ensures consistent decision-making. Decisions are based on expert-defined rules. The system can explain how conclusions were reached. Accuracy depends on the quality of rules and data. The inference engine is essential for expert system performance.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > ICT Applications > Expert Systems

content.topicNotes: Information Reliability Evaluating Content Accuracy Users must evaluate the accuracy of digital information because anyone can publish content on the Internet. You should cross-reference facts with other trusted sources to ensure the data remains consistent. Cross-referencing: the process of checking a piece of information against several different sources. Reliable websites often cite their references and provide evidence for the claims they make. Author Credentials and Bias Students should check the credentials of the author to determine if they possess expertise in the subject. Credentials: the qualifications, experience, or education that prove a person is an expert. You must identify potential bias where an author might present a one-sided view to influence the reader. Bias: a prejudice in favour of or against one thing, person, or group in a way considered to be unfair. Material may be unreliable if the publisher intentionally distributes false details or fails to revise facts. Currency of Information You must check the publication or 'last updated' date to ensure the information is current and not obsolete. Currency: the quality of being up-to-date and relevant to the present time. Outdated information can lead to incorrect conclusions, especially in fast-moving fields like technology or science. Reliable websites regularly maintain their content to reflect the most recent developments or findings. Website Purpose and URL You should examine the top-level domain of a URL to understand the primary purpose of a website. Top-level domain: the final part of a domain name, such as .gov for government or .edu for education. Websites with .gov or .ac.uk suffixes generally provide more reliable and objective data than personal blogs. You must determine if a site intends to inform, persuade, or sell a product to judge its objectivity.

content.topicNotes: Input & Output Devices Input Devices Input devices allow users to enter data into a computer system. They send data and instructions to the CPU. Examples include keyboards, mice, microphones, numeric keypads, touchpads, digital cameras and scanners. Input devices help users control computer operations. Output Devices Output devices present information from the computer to the user. They display or produce the results of processing. Examples include monitors, printers, speakers, and projectors. Output devices make processed data understandable.

content.topicNotes: Inputs, Outputs and Problems Identifying Inputs An input is data entered into a system for processing. The analyst identifies all input sources, such as forms and sensors. They record data types and formats, such as text, numbers or dates. They check how users enter data and whether errors occur. Identifying Outputs An output is information produced by a system after processing. The analyst examines reports, receipts and on-screen displays. They check output layout, accuracy and frequency. They ask users whether the outputs meet their needs. Identifying Current Problems The analyst identifies weaknesses in the current system. Problems may include slow processing or data entry errors. They gather evidence using observation, interviews and questionnaires. Evidence is factual information used to support decisions. Research Methods for Analysis The analyst uses observation to see real inputs and outputs. They use interviews to collect detailed user opinions. They use questionnaires to gather views from many users quickly. Each method has advantages and disadvantages, so analysts often combine them.

content.topicNotes: Internal Memory: ROM & RAM What Is Internal Memory Internal memory stores data and instructions used by the CPU. It is located inside the computer system. Internal memory allows fast access to data. The two main types are ROM and RAM. Read Only Memory (ROM) ROM stands for Read Only Memory. ROM stores essential instructions needed to start the computer. Data in ROM does not change during normal use. ROM keeps its contents when the power is turned off. ROM is used for software that usually does not change. This is also called firmware. An important example are boot-up instructions, often called BIOS (Basic Input/Output System) that decide what to do when the computer starts. Random Access Memory (RAM) RAM stands for Random Access Memory. RAM stores programs and data currently in use. RAM allows fast read and write access. RAM loses its contents when the power is turned off. Comparing ROM and RAM ROM is non-volatile, which means it keeps data without power. RAM is volatile, which means it needs power to store data. ROM stores start-up instructions. RAM stores working data and running programs. Why Internal Memory Matters Internal memory affects how quickly a computer runs programs. More RAM allows more programs to run at the same time. ROM ensures the computer starts correctly every time. Both types of memory support normal computer operation.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Types & Components of Computer Systems > Main Components of Computer Systems

content.topicNotes: Internet & Emails Safe Internet Use Only visit websites recommended by teachers or trusted sources. Use search engines that filter content to ensure age-appropriate results. Avoid clicking on unknown links or pop-ups that may contain malware. Email Safety Never open or reply to emails from unknown senders. Be cautious of phishing emails that ask for personal or financial information. Always verify the sender’s email address before responding. Risks of Sharing Personal Data via Email Sending personal information like your address or phone number via email can lead to identity theft. Avoid sharing passwords or bank details over email. Use secure methods, such as encrypted email services, when necessary.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Safety & Security > eSafety

content.topicNotes: Internet Banking What is internet banking Internet banking is a system that allows customers to manage bank accounts online. Customers access services using a web browser or mobile app. Secure login details are required. Internet banking uses computer networks to process transactions. Banking services are available without visiting a bank branch. Services provided by internet banking Account balances can be viewed online. Money can be transferred between accounts. Bills can be paid electronically. Statements can be downloaded digitally. Standing orders and direct debits can be managed. Security features Usernames and passwords protect account access. Two-factor authentication adds extra security. Two-factor authentication requires a second verification step. Encryption protects data during transmission. Automatic logout reduces the risk of unauthorised access. Advantages and Disadvantages for Customers Advantages Banking services are available 24 hours a day. Transactions can be completed quickly and conveniently. Disadvantages Internet access is required. Security risks exist if users do not follow safe practices. Advantages and Disadvantages for Banks Advantages Decreased running expenses due to fewer physical premises and lower staffing requirements. Ability to serve a wider customer base without geographical limits. Disadvantages Greater exposure to online threats and cybercrime. Substantial investment needed to establish and maintain robust IT security software.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > ICT Applications > Banking Applications

content.topicNotes: Internet Protocols What is a Protocol? A protocol provides a set of digital rules that govern how data is formatted, transmitted, and received over a network. Protocol: a standard set of rules that ensures different devices can communicate with each other successfully. Without these rules, computers would send data in incompatible formats that other devices could not understand. Protocols function like a common language for hardware and software to ensure consistency across the global Internet. TCP/IP The Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) and Internet Protocol (IP) work together to manage data transmission. TCP breaks data into smaller packets and ensures they arrive correctly at the destination. IP handles the addressing of these packets to ensure they reach the correct network location. Packet: a small unit of data that travels along a network path. HTTP and HTTPS Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) allows web browsers to request and receive web pages from servers. HTTPS provides a secure version of this protocol by encrypting the data sent between the browser and the server. Encryption: the process of converting data into a scrambled code to prevent unauthorised access. Users should always look for the padlock icon in the browser address bar to confirm a site uses HTTPS. SSL and TLS Secure Sockets Layer (SSL) provides a security protocol for establishing encrypted links between a web server and a browser. SSL: a security technology that ensures all data passed between the web server and browsers remain private. Transport Layer Security (TLS) has largely replaced SSL as a more secure and updated version of the protocol. These protocols work alongside HTTPS to protect sensitive information like credit card numbers during online transactions. FTP File Transfer Protocol (FTP) provides a specific set of rules for moving files between different computers on a network. Users often employ FTP to upload website files from a local computer to a remote web server. This protocol allows for the transfer of large files that might be too big for email attachments.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Communication > The Internet

content.topicNotes: Internet Shopping What is Internet Shopping? Internet shopping allows customers to buy goods online using a website. The system stores product details in an online database. Online Payment Process The customer adds items to an online shopping basket and proceeds to checkout. The website collects delivery details and payment information through a secure web page. The system encrypts the payment data, which means it converts the data into a coded form to keep it safe. The payment gateway sends the transaction request to the customer’s bank for authorisation. The bank approves or declines the payment and sends a confirmation message back to the online shop. Advantages Customers can shop at any time of day without visiting a physical store. Customers can compare prices quickly between different websites. Retailers can reach a global market instead of only local customers. Online shops reduce costs because they do not need as many physical premises. Customers can read reviews from other buyers before making a purchase. Disadvantages Customers cannot physically examine or try products before buying them. Customers may experience delivery delays or additional shipping costs. Online shops face security risks such as hacking and fraud. Customers must provide personal and financial data, which could be stolen if security is weak. Some customers may struggle if they have limited internet access or low digital skills.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > ICT Applications > Computers in the Retail Industry

content.topicNotes: Internet, Intranet, Extranet & WWW The Internet The Internet connects millions of computers globally through a public network of networks. Public Network: a network where any individual can access the services without restricted membership. It uses the TCP/IP protocol to allow different types of hardware to communicate. Users access a vast range of services such as email, file transfer, and the World Wide Web. The World Wide Web (WWW) The World Wide Web functions as a service that operates on top of the Internet infrastructure. World Wide Web: a collection of multimedia web pages linked together by hyperlinks. It uses the HTTP protocol to transfer data between web servers and browsers. HTTP: Hypertext Transfer Protocol, the foundation of data communication for the WWW. Intranets Organisations use an Intranet to share information securely among their own employees. Intranet: a private network accessible only to authorised members of a specific organisation. It sits behind a firewall to prevent unauthorised access from the public Internet. Businesses use Intranets to host internal policies, staff directories, and training materials. Extranets An Extranet allows an organisation to provide limited access to its internal network for trusted external users. Extranet: an extension of an Intranet that grants controlled access to partners, vendors, or customers. It requires a secure login, such as a username and password, to maintain data privacy. Companies use Extranets to allow suppliers to check inventory levels or track orders.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Communication > The Internet

content.topicNotes: Intranet, Extranet and Internet Intranet An intranet is a private network used within an organisation. Access is restricted to authorised users such as employees. An intranet uses internet technologies such as web browsers. Information shared includes documents, policies and internal messages. Security controls protect data from external access. Uses of an intranet Companies use intranets to share internal documents. Staff use intranets for communication and collaboration. Training materials are stored on intranets. Intranets improve information sharing within organisations. Centralised access reduces duplication of data. Extranet An extranet is a private network that allows limited external access. External users include suppliers or business partners. An extranet is an extension of an intranet. Secure login controls who can access information. Extranets support collaboration between organisations. Internet The internet is a global public network. Anyone with an internet connection can access it. The internet connects millions of networks worldwide. Services include websites, email and cloud storage. Security risks are higher due to public access. Comparing network types An intranet is private and internal to an organisation. An extranet allows controlled access to external users. The internet is public and globally accessible. Security levels decrease from intranet to internet. Each network type suits different communication needs.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Networks and the Effects of Using Them > Network Types

content.topicNotes: Introduction to Data Models What is a Data Model? A data model is a mathematical or logical representation of a real-world situation created inside a spreadsheet. A spreadsheet model is a system that allows users to mock up scenarios and predict outcomes. Users input variables to see how changes affect the overall results. A variable is a value or piece of data that can change depending on the situation. Spreadsheet Structure Gridlines divide a spreadsheet into rows and columns. Rows run horizontally across the screen and are identified by numbers. Columns run vertically down the screen and are identified by letters. Intersections of rows and columns form individual boxes called cells. Each cell has a unique cell reference to identify its location. A cell reference is a combination of the column letter and row number, such as A1. Uses of Spreadsheet Models Businesses use spreadsheet models to create financial reports and manage bookkeeping. Organisations project future profits by testing different financial figures. Event planners forecast total costs by changing the estimated number of guests. Scientists model environmental data to track changes over time. What-If Scenarios Spreadsheet models allow users to conduct powerful 'what-if' scenarios. A 'what-if' scenario is a process of changing cell values to see how those changes affect the outcome of formulas. Users alter key variables like price or quantity to instantly see the new calculated totals. Managers use these insights to make informed decisions before risking real money.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Spreadsheets > Data Models

content.topicNotes: Database Structure What Are Databases? A database is an organised collection of data stored electronically. A file represents a single complete collection of structured data. A record represents a single complete set of data about one specific item or person. A record forms a complete row in a database table. A field represents a single category of data within a record. A field forms a single column in a database table. Flat-file Databases A flat-file database stores all data in a single table consisting of rows and columns. Users find flat-file databases easy to set up and understand for simple data storage. Flat-file structures cause significant data redundancy because users must repeat the same information across multiple rows. Data redundancy is the unnecessary duplication of data within a database. Relational Databases A relational database stores data across multiple linked tables. A primary key is a field that uniquely identifies each record in a table. A foreign key is a primary key from one table that appears in another table to link them together. Relational structures reduce data redundancy and improve data integrity. Data integrity is the accuracy and consistency of data stored in a database. Database Relationships In relational databases, primary and foreign keys link different tables together. One-to-many is the most frequent relationship type. One row in a main table matches several rows in a linked table. For example, one client can make many purchases, but each purchase links to one client. Database Comparison Relational databases prevent data inconsistency when users update records because the data resides in only one place. Data inconsistency occurs when different versions of the same data exist in a system. Relational databases require more complex design skills and higher processing power than flat-file databases. Flat-file databases operate much faster when users handle very small amounts of information. Data Types Database designers assign a specific data type to each field to ensure validation. Alphanumeric fields accept text, numbers, symbols, and spaces. Numeric fields store numbers that computers can use in mathematical calculations. Numeric subtypes include integer for whole numbers and decimal for fractional numbers. Boolean fields store only two possible values, such as Yes or No. Date fields store calendar dates and times in a standardised format.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Databases > Database Structure

content.topicNotes: Introduction to Presentations What is a Presentation? A presentation is a structured collection of slides used to deliver information to an audience. Slide: A single screen or page within a presentation. Presenters use multimedia elements to make the information engaging. Multimedia: The combination of different content forms such as text, images, audio, and video. Uses of Presentations Teachers deliver educational lessons in classrooms to explain complex topics. Managers pitch new business ideas or financial updates to corporate investors. Individuals share information or promote awareness at public community meetings. Audience and Purpose Creators must design slides to meet the specific needs of the target audience. Target audience: The specific group of people for whom the presentation is intended. Presenters use short, simple words and bright, colourful layouts for young children. Professionals use formal language, charts, and minimal decoration for business executives. Consistency and Colour Designers apply a consistent layout across all slides to make the presentation look organised. Clear colour schemes ensure that the text is easily readable against the background. Colour scheme: A planned combination of colours chosen to give a unified appearance. Consistent placement of titles and navigation buttons helps the audience follow the structure.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Presentations > Create Presentations

content.topicNotes: Keyboard and Numeric Keypad Keyboard as an input device A keyboard is an input device used to enter text, numbers and commands. Users press keys to input data into the computer. A standard keyboard includes alphabetic keys, number keys and function keys. Function keys perform specific actions depending on the software. Keyboards are commonly used with desktop and laptop computers. Uses of a keyboard Keyboards are used for typing letters, reports and emails. Programmers use keyboards to write and edit code. Data entry operators use keyboards to input large amounts of text. Keyboard shortcuts improve efficiency. Keyboards allow precise and controlled text input. Numeric keypad A numeric keypad is a set of number keys arranged like a calculator. A numeric keypad is usually located on the right side of a full-size keyboard. Standalone numeric keypads can be connected separately. Numeric keypads are used in ATMs, point-of-sale terminals and calculators. The layout improves speed and accuracy when entering numbers. Advantages and disadvantages of a keyboard Advantages of a keyboard A keyboard allows accurate entry of text and commands. A keyboard is suitable for long documents and detailed input. Disadvantages of a keyboard Typing can be slow for inexperienced users. Prolonged use may cause repetitive strain injury (RSI), although this can be reduced by using ergonomic keyboards. Advantages and disadvantages of a numeric keypad Advantages of a numeric keypad A numeric keypad speeds up entry of numerical data. The calculator-style layout reduces input errors. Disadvantages of a numeric keypad A numeric keypad is mainly suitable for numbers only. A numeric keypad adds extra space to the keyboard.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Input & Output Devices > Input Devices

content.topicNotes: Expert Systems – Knowledge and Rule Bases Knowledge base A knowledge base stores facts and expert information. Facts are pieces of information about a subject area. Knowledge is collected from human experts. The knowledge base forms the foundation of the expert system. Accurate knowledge improves the quality of decisions. Rule base A rule base stores the rules used by the system. Rules are usually written as IF…THEN statements. An IF…THEN rule links conditions to actions. The rule base works with the inference engine. Correct rules are essential for accurate conclusions. How knowledge and rules are created Knowledge engineers interview subject-matter experts to extract key information. Development frequently utilizes an existing expert system shell framework. This shell provides both the inference mechanism and the user interface out of the box. Collected expertise and logical rules are entered directly into the shell framework. The finalized system is tested and refined. Updates are needed when knowledge changes. Advantages and limitations Advantages Expert knowledge is stored permanently. Advice is consistent and available at any time. Limitations The system cannot exceed the knowledge stored. Incorrect or outdated rules lead to poor advice.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > ICT Applications > Expert Systems

content.topicNotes: LAN, WLAN and WAN Local Area Network (LAN) A local area network (LAN) connects devices within a small geographic area such as a school or office. Devices in a LAN are usually connected using Ethernet cables. A single organisation typically owns the entire network hardware and cabling. Advantages A LAN provides fast data transfer and high security. A LAN is relatively inexpensive to set up in one building. Disadvantages A LAN is limited to a small area. Cables can restrict movement and create clutter. Wireless Local Area Network (WLAN) A wireless local area network (WLAN) connects devices using radio waves instead of cables. A wireless access point (AP) allows wireless devices to connect to the network. An access point (AP) is a device that transmits and receives wireless signals. Advantages A WLAN allows mobility within the coverage area. A WLAN reduces the need for physical cabling. Disadvantages A WLAN can be less secure if not configured correctly. Signal strength can be affected by walls and interference. Wide Area Network (WAN) A wide area network (WAN) covers a large geographic area such as a country or continent. A WAN connects multiple LANs together. The internet is the largest example of a WAN. WANs use third-party telecommunication companies to connect geographically separate locations. Advantages A WAN enables communication over long distances. A WAN allows organisations to connect multiple sites. Disadvantages A WAN is more expensive to set up and maintain. Data transfer speeds are usually slower than in a LAN. Comparing LAN, WLAN and WAN A LAN uses cables within a limited area. A WLAN uses wireless access points to provide cable-free access. A WAN connects networks across large distances. Security risks generally increase as network size increases. Each network type is chosen based on coverage area and user needs.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Networks and the Effects of Using Them > Network Types

content.topicNotes: Language and Employer Guidelines Appropriate Language Users must use professional and respectful language in all work-related email communications. Senders should avoid using slang, informal abbreviations, or emoticons in a business context. Correct grammar and spelling ensure that the message is clear and maintain the professional reputation of the sender. Avoid using all capital letters in a message as this is often interpreted as shouting. Netiquette Netiquette represents the network etiquette or the set of informal rules for acceptable online behaviour. Netiquette: a combination of the words network and etiquette. Users should keep messages concise and to the point to respect the recipient's time. Professional netiquette requires the use of a descriptive subject line so the recipient knows the email content before opening it. Senders must always check the recipient list to avoid sending private information to the wrong person. Employer Guidelines Employers use an Acceptable Use Policy (AUP) to govern proper email use. Acceptable Use Policy: rules restricting how a network may be used. Employees must not use the company email system for personal gain or to send chain letters. Guidelines often prohibit the distribution of offensive, defamatory, or copyrighted material. Violations can lead to disciplinary action, such as warnings, revoked access, or employment termination. Legal and Data Security Organisations often include a legal disclaimer at the bottom of every outgoing email. Legal disclaimer: a statement intended to specify or limit the scope of rights and obligations in a legal relationship. Users must not disclose confidential company information or personal data to unauthorised recipients. Employers may monitor email accounts to ensure employees follow the established guidelines and maintain security.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Communication > Email Communication

content.topicNotes: Laptop Computer What is a laptop computer A laptop computer is a portable computer designed for use in different locations. It integrates the screen, keyboard, touchpad and system unit into one device. A touchpad is a flat surface used to control the on-screen pointer. Laptops can operate using a rechargeable battery. They are lightweight compared to desktop computers. Uses of laptop computers Students use laptops for schoolwork and research. Business users use laptops for presentations and remote working. Laptops are used for internet access and communication while travelling. They are used for multimedia tasks such as watching videos. Teachers use laptops for lesson planning and delivery. Laptops can connect to wired or wireless networks to access shared resources like shared files, printers, and the internet. Advantages of laptop computers Laptop computers are portable and easy to carry. They can be used without a mains power supply for a period of time. All components are built into one device, reducing cable use. Wireless connectivity allows internet access in many locations. They require less space than desktop computers. Disadvantages of laptop computers Laptop computers are usually more expensive than desktops with similar performance. Components are difficult or impossible to upgrade. They have less powerful cooling systems. Battery life limits usage time away from mains power. Repairs can be more costly than for desktop computers.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Types & Components of Computer Systems > Types of Computer

content.topicNotes: Learner Performance Systems What is learner performance data Learner performance data records how well students are doing academically. Data includes test scores, grades and teacher assessments. Performance data is stored electronically in school systems. Teachers and school leaders access this data securely. Learner performance systems support academic monitoring. How learner performance is recorded Teachers enter marks and grades into the system. Results from exams and coursework are recorded. Assessment criteria are linked to each subject. Progress over time can be tracked automatically. Data entry reduces paperwork for teachers. Uses of learner performance systems Teachers use performance data to identify strengths and weaknesses. Schools monitor progress across classes and year groups. Parents can view reports through secure online portals. Target setting is supported by accurate data. Intervention can be planned for struggling learners. Advantages and disadvantages Advantages Statistical data like charts, mean, and median can be analysed. Progress can be tracked accurately and efficiently. Early support can be provided when performance drops. Disadvantages Incorrect data entry can affect decisions. Learner data must be protected to maintain privacy.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > ICT Applications > School Management Systems

content.topicNotes: Limitations and Necessary Improvements Identifying limitations A limitation is a weakness or restriction in the system. Limitations may include slow performance or limited features. User feedback helps identify practical problems. Error logs reveal recurring technical faults. Example: a school system may crash when too many users log in. Common types of limitations Hardware limitations include insufficient memory or storage. Software limitations include missing features. Security limitations include weak password policies. Compatibility limitations occur with different devices or browsers. Budget constraints may restrict upgrades. Necessary improvements Parts of the system may need to be redesigned. Developers may optimise code to improve speed. Additional features can be added to meet user needs. Security updates can patch vulnerabilities. Hardware upgrades may increase system capacity. Training can improve user efficiency. Planning future updates Evaluation results should be documented clearly. Prioritise improvements based on impact and cost. Schedule updates during low-usage periods. Test improvements before release. Continuous evaluation ensures long-term effectiveness.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > The Systems Life Cycle > Evaluating the New System

content.topicNotes: Live Data What is Live Data Live data refers to authentic, operational data gathered and actively processed during the running of the existing system. Live data represents real-world transactions and actual user records rather than dummy values. Live data is used once the new system has passed initial testing stages. Live data is different from test data created for checking the system. Live data helps verify how the new system handles genuine day-to-day operations during implementation. When Live Data is Used Live data is used during changeover to a new system. It is entered once the system is considered reliable. Real customer or student records are processed. The system must handle live data accurately. Errors at this stage can affect real users. Example of Live Data A bank processes real customer transactions. A school records actual attendance data. A shop processes real product sales. A hospital records patient information. These examples involve real consequences if errors occur. Advantages and Risks An advantage is that the system is tested in real conditions. Live data shows how the system performs in practice. A risk is that system failures can cause data loss. A risk is that incorrect processing affects real users. Backup procedures are essential when using live data.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > The Systems Life Cycle > Developing & Testing the New System

content.topicNotes: Locating Stored Files Storing Files: Hardware Computers store files on secondary storage devices like Solid State Drives (SSD) or Hard Disk Drives (HDD). SSD: a storage device that uses flash memory to store data, providing very fast file access speeds. HDD: a storage device that uses rotating magnetic platters and a moving read/write head to access data. Locating files on an SSD is much faster than an HDD because it has no moving parts to reposition. Folder Structures Users organise data by placing related files into specific digital folders. Folder: a virtual container within a computer's file system used to group files together. Hierarchical structures allow users to navigate through sub-folders to find specific information. Sub-folder: a folder contained within another folder, forming a nested organisational system. File Paths A file path describes the exact location of a file within the drive and folder hierarchy. File Path: a string of characters that specifies the unique location of a file or directory. This path usually starts with the drive letter and follows through each folder name separated by backslashes. Understanding the file path helps users identify where a document is saved on the hard drive. Search Tools Operating systems provide built-in search utilities to help users locate misplaced files. Search Utility: a software tool that scans the file system to find files based on specific criteria. Users enter keywords, file names, or extensions into the search bar to filter results. These tools can also search within the content of documents to find specific text strings. File Metadata Metadata provides additional details about a file that can be used for sorting and searching. Metadata: data that provides information about other data, such as the date created or file size. Users can filter files by the date they were last modified to find recent work. Sorting by file type allows users to quickly separate images from text documents.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > File Management > Managing Files

content.topicNotes: Lookups & External Data Sources Lookups & External Data Sources Spreadsheet lookup functions search for a specific value in a dataset and retrieve corresponding data from another row or column. External data sources refer to data stored outside the current worksheet or workbook, such as a separate file or database. Workbook: A spreadsheet file that contains one or more worksheets. For example, the formula =VLOOKUP(A2, '[Stock_Data.xlsx]Sheet1'!$A$2:$C$100, 3, FALSE) links directly to an external data file to pull a price. LOOKUP, HLOOKUP, VLOOKUP & XLOOKUP LOOKUP: Searches a single sorted row/column (vector) and returns a value from the same position in another vector. VLOOKUP: Searches vertically down a table's first column, moving right to retrieve data based on a column index number. HLOOKUP: Searches horizontally across a table's top row, moving down to retrieve data based on a row index number. XLOOKUP: Searches a specific range and returns a match from a second range in any direction. Lookup Functions Usage Examples =LOOKUP(101, A2:A4, B2:B4) finds ID 101 in a sorted vector and returns "Alice" from the result vector. =VLOOKUP(102, A2:D4, 2, FALSE) searches vertically down Column A for ID 102 and returns "Bob" from the second column. =HLOOKUP("Department", A1:D4, 4, FALSE) searches horizontally across Row 1 for "Department" and returns "Marketing" from Row 4. =XLOOKUP(103, A2:A4, D2:D4) matches ID 103 in Column A and returns the salary "£38,000" directly from Column D.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Spreadsheets > Data Models

content.topicNotes: MAC Address What a MAC Address Is A MAC address uniquely identifies a device on a network. MAC stands for Media Access Control. The manufacturer assigns a MAC address to a NIC. A NIC is a Network Interface Card that connects a device to a network. How MAC Addresses Are Used A network uses MAC addresses to deliver data to the correct device. Switches read MAC addresses to forward data efficiently. A switch is a device that connects multiple devices on a LAN. LAN means Local Area Network. MAC Address Features A MAC address is usually shown as six pairs of hexadecimal numbers like this: 00:80:41:ae:fd:7e It is fixed and does not change when a device moves networks. This makes it different from an IP address. An IP address can change depending on the network.

content.topicNotes: Magnetic Tape Drives What is magnetic tape storage Magnetic tape storage uses a long strip of plastic coated with magnetic material. Data is stored as magnetised patterns representing binary values. Magnetic tape is a sequential access storage medium. Sequential access means data is read in order from the start of the tape. Magnetic tape is non-volatile storage. How a magnetic tape drive works A magnetic tape drive reads and writes data using a read/write head. The tape is wound between reels inside a cartridge. The tape moves past the read/write head during operation. The drive must wind the tape to the correct position before reading. Latency is the delay caused while the tape moves to the required location. Uses of magnetic tape drives Organisations use magnetic tape for long-term data backup. Banks archive financial records on magnetic tape. Large companies store disaster recovery backups off-site. Data centres use tape for large volumes of rarely accessed data. Tape storage is suitable for archival purposes. Advantages and disadvantages Advantages of magnetic tape Magnetic tape has very low cost per gigabyte. Magnetic tape is suitable for large-scale backups. Disadvantages of magnetic tape Sequential access causes high latency. Data retrieval is slow compared to hard drives. Magnetic tape is unsuitable for frequently accessed data.

content.topicNotes: Margins and Gutter Margins Purpose of Margins Margins are the blank spaces around the edges of a page. Margins separate content from the page boundaries. Margins improve readability and give documents a professional appearance. Printers also need margins because they cannot print to the very edge of a page. Purpose of Gutter Margins A gutter margin is extra space added to one side of a page. Users add a gutter margin when pages will be bound together. Single-sided documents position the gutter margin along the left side. Double-sided or facing-page layouts place the gutter margin along the inside edges. The gutter prevents text from being hidden by the binding. Books and reports often use gutter margins. Effects of Margin Size Wide margins reduce the amount of space available for content but improve readability and make room for notes. Narrow margins allow more text and images to fit on a page. Very narrow margins can make a document harder to read. Users should choose margins that balance space and readability. Effects of Gutter Margins Adding a gutter margin reduces the space available for content. A gutter margin improves readability after pages are bound. Documents without a gutter may lose content near the binding. Users should adjust the gutter size to suit the binding method. Choosing Layout Settings Users should select margins and gutter margins based on the document purpose. Reports that will be bound often need a gutter margin. Digital documents may not require a gutter margin. Appropriate settings improve the overall document layout.

content.topicNotes: Master Slides What is a Master Slide? The Master slide is the top slide in a hierarchy that controls the visual elements for all subsequent slides. A master slide acts as a design template that stores information about the default theme and layout of a presentation. Changes made to this slide automatically update every single slide in the file. Purpose of Master Slides Presenters use master slides to maintain a highly professional and consistent appearance throughout the presentation. This feature saves a massive amount of time when creating large slide decks. Slide deck: A collective group of slides that make up a complete presentation file. Users edit the design layout once rather than altering every slide individually. Information Held on Master Slides Master slides store static elements that must appear in the exact same position on multiple pages. These templates hold background configurations, colour schemes, and default font styles for headings. Software programs use placeholders to position text and dynamic data automatically. Placeholder: A pre-formatted container that holds content such as body text, slide numbers, and footers. Dynamic Master Placeholders Slide Number Placeholder: Automatically assigns sequential page numbers. Automated Date Placeholder: Displays a fixed date or today's date on every page. Footer Placeholder: Holds fixed text, like student details (Name, Candidate Number, Centre Number).

content.topicNotes: Satellite Media Communication Systems What are satellite media systems Satellite media communication systems use satellites to transmit audio and video signals. Signals are sent from Earth to a satellite in orbit. The satellite retransmits the signal back to receivers on Earth. A satellite dish is used to receive the signal. These systems allow communication over very long distances. How satellite communication works A ground station sends an uplink signal to the satellite. The satellite receives and amplifies the signal. The satellite sends a downlink signal back to Earth. Receivers decode the transmitted data. Communication can occur between continents. Uses of satellite media systems Satellite television broadcasts channels to homes. Satellite radio provides audio broadcasts over wide areas. News organisations use satellites for live reporting. Remote areas use satellite internet services. Global events are transmitted worldwide. Advantages and disadvantages Advantages Coverage is available over large geographic areas. Communication is possible in remote locations. Disadvantages Satellite systems are expensive to launch and maintain. Signal delay can occur due to long transmission distances.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > ICT Applications > Satellite Systems

content.topicNotes: Media Streaming What is media streaming Media streaming delivers audio or video over the internet in real time so playback begins before the whole file is downloaded. Streaming reduces the need for permanent local storage of large media files. Common services include on-demand video, live lessons and online radio. Streaming depends on a network connection and server availability. How streaming works Media is split into many small data packets that travel across the network to the receiver. A packet is a small unit of data containing a header (addresses, sequence number) and payload (media data). The receiver reassembles packets in order and places data into a buffer for smooth playback. Error checking and retransmission handle lost or corrupted packets. Buffers, codecs and bandwidth A buffer stores received data temporarily so playback continues while more packets arrive. A codec compresses and decompresses media to reduce data size for transmission. Codec stands for coder–decoder and controls quality and file size. Bandwidth is the data rate of the connection and affects streaming quality. Requirements and pros/cons Requirements: a stable internet connection, sufficient bandwidth and a compatible player or browser. Advantages: instant access, works on multiple devices, supports live broadcasts, and does not require permanent local storage. Disadvantages: poor connections cause buffering and lower quality, and high data use may incur costs. Examples: live sports streams, on-demand films, online lessons and music services.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > ICT Applications > Communication Media

content.topicNotes: Memory Cards What are memory cards A memory card is a small solid-state storage device. Memory cards store data using flash memory. Flash memory stores data electronically with no moving parts. Memory cards are non-volatile storage devices. Data is retained when power is switched off. Types of memory cards Common types include SD, microSD and CompactFlash cards. SD stands for Secure Digital. MicroSD cards are smaller versions of SD cards. Different devices require different card formats. Adapters allow smaller cards to fit larger slots. Uses of memory cards Digital cameras use memory cards to store photos and videos. Smartphones use memory cards to expand storage capacity. Tablets and handheld devices use memory cards for extra storage. Memory cards transfer files between devices. Portable devices rely on memory cards for lightweight storage. Advantages and disadvantages Advantages Memory cards are very small and portable. Solid-state design makes memory cards resistant to shock. Disadvantages Memory cards are easy to lose due to small size. Storage capacity is lower than hard disks or SSDs.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Storage Devices & Media > Solid-State Devices & Media

content.topicNotes: Direct Changeover What is direct changeover Direct changeover is the immediate replacement of an old system with a new system at a chosen time. The organisation stops the old system and starts the new system in one action. Changeover often happens overnight or at a quiet period to reduce disruption. A successful direct changeover requires careful planning and full preparedness. Advantages of direct changeover The organisation avoids the cost of running two systems concurrently. Staff move to the new system quickly, so benefits appear sooner. The approach simplifies support because only one live system exists. The change is clear-cut, reducing long-term confusion about which system to use. Disadvantages and risks If the new system fails, there is no backup and the organisation can suffer immediate disruption. Users may face service downtime until problems are fixed. Data migration errors can cause loss or corruption of live records. The organisation must prepare contingency plans and a tested rollback procedure. Rollback is returning to the previous system if the new system fails. Key precautions and steps Schedule the change at a low-usage time and inform all stakeholders in advance. Take complete backups of all live data and verify backup integrity before switching. Provide extra support staff and monitoring during and after the change. Test the rollback procedure and rehearse recovery steps with the team. Train users and prepare clear help resources to reduce initial errors.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > The Systems Life Cycle > Implementing the New System

content.topicNotes: Parallel Running What is parallel running Parallel running is when the old system and the new system operate at the same time. The same data is entered into both systems. Outputs from both systems are compared. The old system acts as a backup during the transition. Parallel running reduces risk during implementation. Advantages of parallel running The old system can be used if the new system fails. Errors in the new system can be detected by comparing outputs. Users gain confidence while learning the new system. Business operations continue with reduced disruption. Data accuracy can be verified before full changeover. Disadvantages of parallel running Running two systems increases costs. Staff must enter data twice, increasing workload. The process can be time-consuming. Inconsistent data entry may occur between systems. Additional resources are required for support. Example of parallel running A school runs its old attendance system alongside a new one. Teachers enter attendance into both systems. Reports from both systems are compared. Errors in the new system are corrected. After successful testing, the old system is switched off.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > The Systems Life Cycle > Implementing the New System

content.topicNotes: Phased Implementation What is phased implementation Phased implementation breaks down a new system into separate modules. Different modules are implemented one at a time to the entire organisation. The old system continues to operate for parts not yet replaced. Each phase is tested before moving to the next stage. This method spreads change over a period of time. How phased implementation works The organisation identifies separate system modules. One module is installed and tested first. Users are trained on the new module. Remaining modules are introduced gradually. The full system is completed after all phases are implemented. Advantages of phased implementation Risks are reduced because only part of the system changes at a time. Problems can be corrected before the next phase begins. Staff can adjust gradually to the new system. Training can be managed more effectively. Business disruption is minimised. Disadvantages of phased implementation Implementation takes longer than direct changeover. Running old and new modules together can be complex. Integration issues may arise between phases. Overall costs may increase due to extended transition. Careful coordination is required for success.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > The Systems Life Cycle > Implementing the New System

content.topicNotes: Pilot Running What is pilot running Pilot running is when an entirely new system is introduced to one department or branch of an organisation first. Only one department or branch uses the new system initially. The rest of the organisation continues using the old system. Feedback is collected from the pilot group. The system is rolled out fully if successful. Advantages of pilot running Problems can be identified on a small scale. Risks are limited to one department or location. Staff can provide feedback for improvements. Training can be tested and refined. Disruption to the whole organisation is reduced. Disadvantages of pilot running Implementation takes longer than direct changeover. Running two systems in different areas increases management complexity. Data consistency must be maintained between pilot and old systems. Some users may feel excluded from early access. Additional support may be required during the pilot phase. Example of pilot running A bank introduces a new online system in one branch. Staff in that branch use the new system for daily transactions. Issues are recorded and corrected. Customer feedback is analysed. After successful testing, the system is introduced to all branches.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > The Systems Life Cycle > Implementing the New System

content.topicNotes: Microphones and Sensors Microphone A microphone inputs sound and creates an analogue signal This electrical signal represents the original sound. An analogue signal varies continuously in voltage. An analogue-to-digital converter (ADC) changes the signal into digital data. Digital data uses binary values of 0 and 1. The computer stores or processes the digital sound. Sensors and analogue signals A sensor is an input device that detects physical changes such as temperature or light. Most sensors produce analogue signals. An analogue signal changes smoothly over a range of values. An ADC converts the analogue signal into digital form. The digital signal can then be processed by a microprocessor. Advantages and disadvantages of a microphone Advantages of a microphone A microphone allows voice input and communication. A microphone supports hands-free control and accessibility. Disadvantages of a microphone Background noise can reduce sound quality. A microphone may require additional hardware and software. Advantages and disadvantages of sensors Advantages of sensors Sensors provide continuous and automatic data collection. Sensors allow systems to respond quickly to environmental changes. Disadvantages of sensors Sensors can be expensive to install and maintain. Faulty or inaccurate sensors can cause incorrect system responses.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Input & Output Devices > Input Devices

content.topicNotes: Microprocessor-Controlled Devices at Home What are microprocessor-controlled devices A microprocessor-controlled device uses a microprocessor to control its functions. A microprocessor is a small integrated circuit that processes instructions. Microprocessor-controlled devices follow programmed instructions automatically. Many household appliances contain microprocessors. Examples include washing machines, microwaves and smart thermostats. How the devices work Sensors (Input): Gather physical measurements from the surroundings, such as tracking temperature inside an oven or water levels in a washing machine. Microprocessor (Process): Evaluates incoming readings against preset user thresholds (for example, checking if the current temperature matches a target setting). Actuators (Output): Mechanical components triggered by the microprocessor to make physical changes, like starting a heating element or driving a drum motor. Advantages at home Microprocessor-controlled devices save time by working automatically. Tasks are completed more accurately and consistently. Energy efficiency is improved through precise control. Devices can improve safety with automatic shut-off features. Smart devices can be programmed to suit user needs. Disadvantages at home Microprocessor-controlled devices are often more expensive to buy. Repairs can be costly and require specialist knowledge. Faulty software can cause devices to malfunction. Users may become over-reliant on automation. Power cuts can stop devices from working. Examples in the home Washing machines use microprocessors to control wash cycles. Microwave ovens use microprocessors to control cooking time and power. Smart heating systems adjust temperature automatically. Dishwashers use sensors and microprocessors to control water use. Smart lighting systems allow automated control of lights.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > The Effects of Using IT > Microprocessor-controlled Devices at Home

content.topicNotes: Monitors What is a monitor A monitor is an output device that displays visual information from a computer. A monitor shows text, images, video and graphical user interfaces. The display updates as the computer processes data. Monitors allow users to see the results of their actions. Monitors are essential for most computer systems. Types of monitors LCD stands for Liquid Crystal Display. Liquid crystals change alignment to control light passing through the screen. LED stands for Light Emitting Diode. LED monitors are LCD monitors that use LED backlighting. LED is preferred over standard LCD: LED monitors offer brighter images, consume less power, have a longer lifespan, and allow the screen to be much thinner. Touch screen monitors combine display and input functions. Uses of monitors Monitors are used to view documents and web pages. Designers use monitors to edit images and videos. Teachers use monitors for presentations and demonstrations. Gamers use monitors for interactive entertainment. Control rooms use monitors to display live data. Advantages and disadvantages Advantages of monitors Monitors provide immediate visual feedback. High-resolution screens improve image clarity. Large displays support detailed work. Disadvantages of monitors Prolonged use may cause eye strain. Large monitors require desk space. Power consumption increases with screen size.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Input & Output Devices > Output Devices

content.topicNotes: Motherboard and CPU Motherboard Basics The motherboard is the main circuit board inside a computer. The motherboard connects all hardware components together. The motherboard allows components to communicate using data pathways called buses. CPU / Processor The Central Processing Unit (CPU) is the main processor of the computer. The CPU processes instructions and controls all computer operations. Processing means carrying out calculations and decisions. The CPU is fitted directly onto the motherboard. How They Work Together The motherboard holds the CPU in a special socket. The motherboard supplies power and data connections to the CPU. The CPU uses the motherboard to communicate with memory, storage, and input and output devices.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Types & Components of Computer Systems > Hardware

content.topicNotes: Multimedia Presentations and ePublications What is a multimedia presentation A multimedia presentation combines text, images, audio, video and animations. Presentation software is used to create and organise slides. Slides support a spoken explanation during lessons or meetings. Projectors or large screens display the slides to an audience. Word processors and spell-checkers help ensure text is accurate. Features and ICT tools used Text, images and charts are inserted using presentation software tools. Presentation design is adapted to specific target audiences Audio and video clips can be embedded to enhance understanding. Animations and transitions emphasise key points. Files can be exported as PDF documents for sharing. Printers or photocopiers can produce handouts for the audience. ePublications An ePublication is a digital version of printed material such as an eBook or online magazine. ePublications are created using desktop publishing or word processing software. They may include hyperlinks, images and multimedia content. Files are distributed electronically via websites or email. Updates can be made quickly without reprinting. Advantages and disadvantages Advantages Multimedia improves audience engagement and understanding. ePublications reduce printing costs and allow quick updates. Disadvantages Technical problems can interrupt presentations. Access to devices and software is required to view digital content.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > ICT Applications > Communication Media

content.topicNotes: NFC What is NFC? NFC stands for Near Field Communication. Near Field Communication allows devices to exchange data over very short distances. Devices must be within 4 centimetres apart to communicate. How NFC Works An NFC-enabled device creates a small radio field. Another NFC device enters the field and establishes a connection. The devices exchange encrypted data. The system completes the process in a few seconds. Smartphone Payments Many smartphones contain built-in NFC chips. The user stores bank card details securely in a digital wallet app. The user taps the smartphone on a payment terminal. The system authorises the payment without inserting a physical card. Advantages and Security NFC works quickly and is easy to use. Transactions are executed quickly, and waiting times are reduced. The short range reduces the risk of unauthorised access. Encryption protects sensitive payment information. Users often confirm payments using fingerprint or face recognition. Disadvantages NFC only works over very short distances. Not all devices or payment terminals support NFC. Users may face security risks if they lose their smartphone. Interference from metal objects can reduce signal reliability.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > ICT Applications > Recognition Systems

content.topicNotes: Network Interface Card (NIC) Purpose of a NIC NIC stands for Network Interface Card. A NIC allows a device to connect to a network. Every device on a network needs a NIC to send and receive data. The NIC acts as the link between the computer and the network. How a NIC Works A NIC converts data from the computer into signals for the network. It also converts incoming signals back into data the computer can use. Each NIC has a unique MAC address. A MAC address is a Media Access Control address that identifies the device. Types of NIC A wired NIC connects to a network using an Ethernet cable. A wireless NIC (WNIC) connects to a network using radio waves. Many modern devices have built-in NICs. Both types perform the same basic function.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Networks and the Effects of Using Them > Common Network Devices

content.topicNotes: NIC and Storage Devices Network Interface Card A Network Interface Card (NIC) allows a computer to connect to a network. The NIC enables data to be sent and received over a wired or wireless connection. Most modern computers have a NIC built into the motherboard. Hard Disk Drive A Hard Disk Drive (HDD) is a secondary storage device. An HDD stores data, programs, and the operating system permanently. An HDD uses spinning magnetic disks to read and write data. Solid State Drive A Solid State Drive (SSD) is a type of secondary storage. An SSD stores data using flash memory instead of moving parts. An SSD is faster, quieter, and more durable than an HDD.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Types & Components of Computer Systems > Hardware

content.topicNotes: Named Cells and Ranges Defining Named Cells and Ranges Users assign descriptive text labels to individual cells or blocks of adjacent cells. Named cell refers to a single cell identified by a custom descriptive text label instead of a letter-number coordinate. Named range refers to a group of selected cells identified collectively by a single custom text identifier. This custom identifier replaces standard absolute cell references like "$A$1:$B$10" in mathematical formulas. Purpose and Benefits Custom text identifiers make complex spreadsheet formulae significantly easier to read and audit. Formula auditing describes the process of checking mathematical expressions for structural correctness and logic. Named ranges automatically act as absolute references to prevent coordinates from shifting during replication. Creators use these meaningful names to simplify data model navigation and reduce syntax entry errors.
