content.topicNotes: Newsletters and Posters Creating Newsletters A newsletter is created using word processing or desktop publishing (DTP) software. DTP applications are preferred over word processors as they provide exact positioning of page elements and text wrapping around images. Corporate house styles ensure consistent branding, such as identical fonts, colour schemes, and logos across publications. Spell-checkers help reduce spelling and grammar errors. Images and graphics can be inserted digitally. Newsletters can be saved as PDF files for electronic distribution. Designing Posters Posters are designed using desktop publishing or graphic design software. Software tools allow resizing, colour adjustment and layout design. High-resolution images improve print quality. Templates help maintain consistent corporate house styles across visual materials. Finished posters can be printed using large-format printers. Production and Distribution Newsletters can be printed using printers or photocopiers. Digital copies can be emailed or uploaded to a website. Posters can be printed in colour for display in public areas. ICT allows quick editing before final production. Electronic distribution reduces printing costs. Advantages and Disadvantages Advantages: Editing and spell-checking improve accuracy. Digital design tools enhance visual quality. Electronic distribution saves time and resources. Disadvantages: Access to suitable software and hardware is required. Printing large quantities can increase costs.

content.topicNotes: OCR What is OCR? OCR stands for Optical Character Recognition. OCR converts printed or handwritten text into editable, digital text. An optical scanner captures an image of the page. OCR software analyses the shapes of characters to identify letters and numbers. It allows users to edit scanned text using word processing software. Automated Number Plate Recognition (ANPR) Systems ANPR stands for Automatic Number Plate Recognition. A camera captures a digital image of a vehicle's plate when it passes OCR software analyses the image to extract the registration characters. The system stores the data for uses such as car park control or law enforcement. Advantages and Disadvantages of OCR Advantages: OCR saves time by automatically retyping printed documents. It reduces human data entry errors. It is very effective and accurate if the format and font of the text are always the same as in number plates. Disadvantages: It may produce errors if the text is unclear or handwritten badly. Complex fonts and poor-quality scans can reduce accuracy.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > ICT Applications > Recognition Systems

content.topicNotes: OMR What is OMR? OMR stands for Optical Mark Recognition. Optical Mark Recognition is a technology that detects marks made in specific positions on paper. It reads shaded boxes or circles on specially designed forms. OMR is often used to mark multiple-choice examination papers quickly. How OMR Works A scanner shines a light onto the paper form. The machine detects less reflected light from shaded areas. The system records darkened areas as selected answers. The identified coordinates are checked against a master response key to assign grades. The form must follow a fixed layout so the scanner can read it accurately. Barcode A barcode stores data using a series of vertical lines of different widths. A barcode reader shines a laser or light onto the code and measures the reflected light. The system converts the pattern of lines into digital data, such as a candidate number. In OMR systems, barcodes identify each answer sheet quickly and accurately. Barcodes reduce manual input errors and speed up processing of examination papers. QR Code A QR code is a Quick Response code that stores data in a square pattern of black and white modules. An optical scanner reads the QR code by detecting the contrast between dark and light areas. The system decodes the pattern into digital data, such as a candidate number or test ID. In OMR systems, QR codes help identify each answer sheet automatically before marks are processed. Advantages OMR processes large numbers of forms very quickly. It reduces human marking errors. There can be no typing errors. If the form is filled in correctly, OMR is very accurate. Disadvantages It only reads marks in specific positions. It cannot read handwriting or interpret written answers. The design of the form is limited because of the positioning and design of the boxes or circles. If something was not filled in correctly, it takes a lot of manual effort to find and correct the error.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > ICT Applications > Recognition Systems

content.topicNotes: OMR and OCR Optical Mark Recognition (OMR) Optical Mark Recognition (OMR) detects shaded marks on paper forms. OMR reads ticks or filled circles in specific positions. OMR does not recognise printed text or handwriting. Specially designed forms are required for OMR. OMR is used for multiple-choice exam answer sheets. Uses of OMR Schools use OMR to mark exam papers quickly. Companies use OMR for customer satisfaction surveys. Election ballots can be processed using OMR. OMR reduces human marking errors. OMR saves time when processing large numbers of forms. Optical Character Recognition (OCR) Optical Character Recognition (OCR) converts scanned text into editable digital text. OCR recognises printed letters and numbers. A scanner or camera captures the original document. The software analyses character shapes. The output can be edited in a word processor. Examples of OCR Passport control/immigration services use OCR to read passport details instantly Post offices use OCR to read postal codes on envelopes. Apps use OCR to scan receipts and extract totals. Advantages and Disadvantages Advantages OMR processes forms quickly and accurately. OCR allows printed text to be reused digitally. Disadvantages OMR requires carefully completed forms. If a user creases/dirties the paper, or fails to circle completely with the correct pencil type the system will misread the data OCR may produce errors if the scan quality is poor.

content.topicNotes: Observations and Interviews Observation Method An analyst watches users carry out their normal tasks in the current system and how the system operates. The analyst records data flows, processing steps and problems. The method shows what actually happens, not what users think happens. Advantages of Observations Observation provides accurate and realistic information about tasks. The analyst sees errors, bottlenecks, and inefficiencies directly. It offers an overall, unbiased picture of how the entire system functions day-to-day. Disadvantages of Observations Observing staff can take a long time to complete. Users may change their behaviour because they know someone is watching (this is called the Hawthorne effect). It may not capture tasks that occur infrequently or outside normal observation hours. Interview Method An interview involves the analyst asking users questions face to face. The analyst prepares structured or unstructured questions. Structured questions have a fixed order and format. Unstructured questions allow open discussion. Interviews collect detailed opinions and explanations from users. Advantages of Interviews Interviews allow the analyst to ask follow-up questions for clarity. They help build a good working relationship and trust with users. The analyst can adapt questions on the spot to probe deeper into complex issues. Disadvantages of Interviews Conducting individual interviews can be time-consuming and expensive. Users may give biased answers or personal opinions rather than objective facts. Interviewees may feel intimidated or tell the analyst what they think they want to hear.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > The Systems Life Cycle > Analysing the Current System

content.topicNotes: Online Gaming Safety Using Safe Usernames Players should use nicknames instead of real names for usernames when gaming online. A username is a name used to identify a player in a game. It should not include personal details such as age or location. This reduces the risk of strangers identifying or tracking the player. Protecting Personal Information Players should avoid sharing personal information in chats or profiles. Personal information includes data that identifies a person. Examples include full name, address, school, or phone number. Sharing this data can lead to identity theft or unwanted contact. Keeping Financial Details Secure Players should never share bank or payment details in games. Financial data includes card numbers, passwords, or account details. These details allow access to money or purchases. Scammers may pretend to offer rewards to steal this information. Recognising Online Risks Players should stay alert to suspicious behaviour from others, called scams.A scam is a trick designed to steal data or money. Scammers may offer fake prizes or pretend to be an official employee of the game's company and ask for login details. Players should report suspicious users to keep the gaming environment safe. Avoid unmonitored servers featuring offensive language or media. Immediately block and report players who cause distress or engage in cyberbullying.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Safety & Security > eSafety

content.topicNotes: Opening and Importing Files Opening Native Files Users open files when they want to access a document created in its original application. Native File: a file format that is unique to a specific software application, such as .docx for Microsoft Word. Double-clicking a file icon automatically launches the associated software to display the content. This process maintains all original formatting and specific features of the software. Importing External Data Importing allows users to bring data from one application into a different, currently open file. Import: the process of converting data from an external format into a format usable by the current application. A common example includes placing a .csv file into a spreadsheet to organise raw data. CSV (Comma Separated Values): a plain text file format used to store tabular data. Application Compatibility Many applications can open files created in different software if they share compatibility. Compatibility: the ability of one software program to correctly interpret and display the data from another. A user might use a word processor to open a file originally created in a different brand of office suite. Software often provides a 'Open File With' dialogue box to let users select the specific file type they wish to access.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > File Management > Managing Files

content.topicNotes: Operating Systems What Is an Operating System An operating system (OS) controls the basic functions of a computer. It acts as an interface between the user and the hardware. The computer cannot work properly without an operating system. An operating system maintains security and logs about important events. Managing Hardware The operating system controls hardware devices. It manages the CPU, memory, and input and output devices. It decides how hardware resources are shared. This ensures the computer runs efficiently. Managing Software The operating system loads and runs application software. The operating system tries to handle errors that occur in application software. Application software allows users to perform tasks. Examples include word processors and web browsers. The operating system controls how software uses hardware. User Interface The operating system provides a user interface. A user interface allows users to interact with the computer. Examples include graphical user interfaces and command line interfaces. The interface makes the system easier to use. Common Operating Systems Different devices use different operating systems. Examples include Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, and iOS. Each operating system has its own features. All operating systems perform similar core functions.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Types & Components of Computer Systems > Main Components of Computer Systems

content.topicNotes: Operating Systems What is an Operating System? An operating system is system software that manages computer hardware and software resources. The operating system provides a user interface to interact with the computer. The operating system controls tasks such as running programs and managing files. Key Functions The operating system manages memory and allocates space for programs. The operating system schedules the CPU to run multiple programs efficiently. The operating system controls input and output devices like keyboards and printers. Examples of Operating Systems Windows is a common operating system used on many personal computers. macOS is the operating system for Apple Mac computers. Linux is an open-source operating system used in servers and some computers. Android and iOS are the most popular operating systems for mobile devices.

content.topicNotes: Point of Sale (POS) What is a POS system? POS stands for Point of Sale, which is the place where a customer pays for goods. The system usually includes a barcode scanner, receipt printer and cash drawer. The system records each sale automatically in a database. Barcode scanning The cashier scans the barcode on a product. A barcode is a series of black and white lines that represent a product code. The scanner reads the code and sends it to the computer. The system looks up the price in the product database and adds it to the total. Stock control The POS system updates stock levels automatically after each sale. Stock control is the process of managing the amount of goods available. The system can alert staff when stock levels are low. Automated restocking prevents inventory from becoming completely exhausted. Managers use sales reports to decide when to reorder products.

content.topicNotes: Page Size and Orientation Page Size Page size defines the physical dimensions of a document page. Common page sizes include A4 and A3. Users choose a page size based on the document purpose. Larger page sizes can show more content. Portrait Orientation Portrait orientation is taller than it is wide. It is often used for letters and reports. Portrait suits documents with mostly text. It helps text fit neatly down the page. Landscape Orientation Landscape orientation is wider than it is tall. It is useful for wide tables and charts. Landscape gives more space across the page. Users choose it when content needs extra width. Changing Layout Users can change page size and orientation in page setup. Page setup controls how a document appears when printed. Correct settings improve presentation. Good layout makes documents easier to read. Choosing the Best Option Users should match the page settings to the content. Reports often use A4 portrait orientation. Tables and diagrams may fit better in landscape. Careful choices improve document quality.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Document Production > Organise Page Layout

content.topicNotes: Passwords What is a password A password is a secret string of characters used to verify a user’s identity. Passwords control access to computer systems and networks. Only authorised users should know the password. Passwords help protect personal and confidential data. Passwords are a common network security method. Strong passwords A strong password is difficult for others to guess. Strong passwords include a mix of letters, numbers and symbols. Upper- and lower-case letters improve security. Passwords must contain a minimum of 8 characters to help defend against automated brute-force attacks. Unique passwords should be used for different accounts. Weak passwords and risks A weak password is easy to guess or crack. Common words and names reduce password security. Hackers use brute-force attacks to guess passwords. A brute-force attack tries many combinations automatically. Weak passwords increase the risk of unauthorised access. Good password practice Passwords should be changed regularly. Passwords must not be shared with other users. Two-factor authentication adds an extra security step. Two-factor authentication requires a second verification method. Secure password management reduces security risks.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Networks and the Effects of Using Them > Network Issues: Security

content.topicNotes: Patients & Pharmacy Records Patient records Computers store patient details such as name, address, and date of birth. Doctors record medical history, test results, and diagnoses digitally. An Electronic Health Record (EHR) stores patient medical information in digital form. EHRs allow authorised staff to access up-to-date information. Pharmacy records Pharmacies use computers to store prescription records. The system records which medicines patients receive and when. This helps pharmacists check correct dosages and avoid errors. Automated stock management requests new medication orders once inventory drops past a minimum level. Improved safety Computer systems warn staff about drug allergies or interactions. A drug interaction happens when medicines react badly together. This reduces the risk of prescribing unsafe medication. Data sharing Hospitals and pharmacies share records using secure networks. Only authorised users access confidential data. This improves communication and speeds up patient treatment.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > ICT Applications > Computers in Medicine

content.topicNotes: Payment Methods Cash Payments Customers pay using coins and banknotes. The cashier enters the amount into the POS system. The POS system calculates change automatically. The system records the cash transaction in the sales database. Card Payments Customers pay using debit or credit cards. The card reader connects to an EFTPOS terminal. EFTPOS stands for Electronic Funds Transfer at Point of Sale. The bank authorises the transaction before the system completes the sale. Contactless and Mobile Customers tap a contactless card or smartphone on the reader. Contactless payment uses NFC. NFC stands for Near Field Communication. The device sends encrypted payment data to the bank. The system processes the payment in seconds. Third-Party Payment Systems Services like PayPal act as an intermediary between buyers and sellers. Users complete purchases without sharing bank details with merchants. Accounts link directly to bank cards or stored digital balances. This simplifies checkout while adding an extra layer of privacy. How Payments are Protected Encryption scrambles sensitive financial data during transmission. Two-factor authentication confirms user identity via secondary codes. Fraud detection tools monitor transactions for unusual activity. These safeguards prevent unauthorized access and financial theft.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > ICT Applications > Computers in the Retail Industry

content.topicNotes: Practical Tips for Queries Query Criteria Operators The = symbol finds records matching an exact value. The <> symbol excludes specific values from results. Symbols like > and < filter numerical or date ranges. Symbols like >= and <= include boundary values in range checks. Wildcard Operator Rules An asterisk * replaces any amount of unknown text. Example: Like "A*" finds text starting with the letter A, such as "Austin" or "Atlanta". A question mark ? replaces just one character. Example: Like "P?t" matches words like "Pet", "Pit", or "Pot". Combining Search Criteria AND searches need records to match every condition. Put criteria on the same grid row for an AND search. OR searches need records to match at least one condition. Put criteria on separate grid rows for an OR search. Calculated Fields Calculated fields carry out math operations on existing fields during a query. Format: NewName: [Field1] * [Field2]. These fields update automatically when base data changes.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Databases > Manipulating Data

content.topicNotes: Personal Data Personal Data Characteristics Personal data includes information like a name, address, and date of birth. This data can identify an individual but may not always be sensitive. A photograph in a school uniform is also considered personal data. Sensitive Data Characteristics Sensitive data is a special type of personal data that includes medical history, religious beliefs, political opinions, biometric data (e.g., fingerprints), ethnic origin, or criminal records. This type of data requires extra protection due to its personal nature. Disclosing sensitive data without consent can lead to serious consequences. Need for Confidentiality Personal and sensitive data must be kept confidential to protect individuals. Unauthorised disclosure can result in identity theft or discrimination. Organisations must implement security measures to prevent leaks. Risks of Inappropriate Disclosure If personal data is shared without permission, it can be used maliciously. Schools and hospitals must ensure data is only accessible to authorised personnel. Failure to protect data can lead to legal penalties and loss of trust.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Safety & Security > eSafety

content.topicNotes: Personal Finance Modelling What is personal finance modelling Personal finance modelling uses software to manage and predict financial situations. Models represent income, expenses and savings. Users can change values to see different outcomes. Financial models are often created using spreadsheets. Modelling helps users plan how to manage money. How finance models work Income and expenses are entered as data. Formulas calculate totals, balances and savings. A variable is a value that can be changed, such as monthly income. Changing values updates results automatically. The model shows the effect of financial decisions. Uses of personal finance modelling Individuals use models to create household budgets. Students plan spending and savings using finance models. Families predict loan repayments and mortgage costs. Users compare different financial options. Modelling supports informed decision-making. Advantages and disadvantages Advantages Financial planning becomes clearer and more organised. Different scenarios can be tested safely. Disadvantages Models are only accurate if correct data is entered. Unexpected real-life costs may not be included.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > ICT Applications > Modelling Applications

content.topicNotes: Pharming and Prevention What is Pharming? Pharming is a cyber attack that redirects users to fake websites. A cyber attack is an attempt to damage or access a computer system. Users may enter personal data without realising the site is fake. Attackers aim to steal sensitive data such as passwords. How Pharming Works Attackers reroute web traffic by placing malware onto a user's local storage drive. This may involve corrupting the Domain Name System (DNS) which translates web addresses into IP addresses. Users are redirected even if they type the correct address. Recognising Pharming Website appearance may look slightly unusual. Users should check for HTTPS in the address bar. This is often displayed by a padlock symbol next to the web address. HTTPS encrypts data between the user and the website. This converts data into a secure coded form. Users should check the complete domain name. Attackers could use similar domain names to the original, like "instapram.com" or "google.com.asuspiciousname.biz".
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Safety & Security > Security of Data

content.topicNotes: Phishing and Prevention What is Phishing? Phishing is a scam where attackers trick users into giving personal data. A scam is a dishonest scheme used to steal information or money. Attackers often pretend to be trusted organisations. They aim to collect passwords, bank details or personal data. Email Phishing Attackers send fake emails that look official. Emails may contain links to fake websites. Users may be asked to enter personal information. These messages often create urgency to pressure users. Recognising Phishing Users should check the sender's email address carefully. Suspicious links should not be clicked. Poor spelling and grammar can indicate a phishing attempt. Unexpected requests for sensitive data should be treated as suspicious. Preventing Phishing Users should avoid clicking unknown links. Security software can detect malicious content. Two-factor authentication adds an extra layer of security. Users should verify requests directly with organisations. Two-Factor Authentication Two-factor authentication requires two forms of identification. It combines something you know and something you have. For example, a password and a code sent to a phone. This makes it harder for attackers to gain access.

content.topicNotes: Placing Images in Documents Importing Graphics Users place images into a document by using the 'Insert' or 'Import' function within the software. Importing: the process of bringing an external file into the current application. Software preserves the aspect ratio of the image to ensure it does not look stretched or squashed. Aspect Ratio: the proportional relationship between the width and the height of an image. Placing an image correctly ensures that the visual data aligns with the surrounding text. Placing Images with Precision Software allows users to place an image at an exact location using coordinates or alignment tools. Alignment: the positioning of an image relative to the margins or other objects on a page. Users can select horizontal and vertical alignment options such as top, bottom, left, or right. This ensures the graphic sits perfectly flush against the page edges without needing manual measurements. Precision tools help maintain a consistent and professional look across different pages of a document. Placing a Border Users can place a border around an image to make it stand out from the page background. Border: a decorative or solid frame that surrounds the edges of a graphic or image. Software tools allow for the adjustment of line weight, colour, and style for the frame. Line Weight: the thickness or width of a line, usually measured in points (pt). A border helps separate an image from surrounding text or similarly coloured elements.

content.topicNotes: Pointing Devices What are pointing devices A pointing device is an input device used to control the on-screen pointer. The pointer is a visual indicator that shows the user’s position on the screen. Pointing devices allow users to select, move and open items. Pointing devices are commonly used with graphical user interfaces. Movement of the device controls movement of the pointer. Mouse A mouse is a handheld pointing device moved across a flat surface. Buttons allow users to select and interact with on-screen objects. A scroll wheel allows vertical or horizontal scrolling. Optical sensors detect movement. A mouse is widely used with desktop computers. Touchpad and trackpad A touchpad is a flat touch-sensitive surface used to control the pointer. A touchpad is commonly built into laptops. Finger movement controls the pointer on the screen. Gestures such as tapping and scrolling are supported. A touchpad reduces the need for an external mouse. Trackball and joystick A trackball controls the pointer using a rotating ball. The device remains stationary during use. A trackball is ideal for users with limited mobility or disability. Trackballs are useful for industrial or moving environments like a ship A joystick is moved in different directions to control movement. Joysticks are commonly used in games and simulations. These devices offer precise control in specific tasks. Advantages and disadvantages of a mouse Advantages of a mouse A mouse provides accurate and precise pointer control. A mouse is easy to learn and suitable for most tasks. Disadvantages of a mouse A mouse requires a flat surface to operate. Repetitive use can cause strain injury. Advantages and disadvantages of a touchpad Advantages of a touchpad A touchpad is compact and built into laptops. A touchpad does not require extra desk space. Disadvantages of a touchpad A touchpad can be less precise than a mouse. A small surface area can limit detailed control. Advantages and disadvantages of a trackball and joystick Advantages of a trackball and joystick A trackball requires minimal desk space. A joystick provides excellent directional control in simulations. Disadvantages of a trackball and joystick A trackball can become dirty and require cleaning. A joystick is not suitable for general office work.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Input & Output Devices > Input Devices

content.topicNotes: Presentation Layer Purpose of the Presentation Layer The presentation layer controls how a web page appears. It displays and formats elements on a web page. The presentation layer controls features such as fonts, colours, and layout. It improves the visual appearance of a website. The presentation layer improves website consistency. Consistent formatting creates a professional appearance. Users can apply the same styles across many pages. This makes website updates faster and more efficient. What CSS Is CSS stands for Cascading Style Sheets. CSS is used to create the presentation layer of a website. CSS defines how HTML content is displayed. CSS controls formatting without changing the content. Why Stylesheets Are Used A stylesheet is a file that stores formatting rules. Stylesheets apply consistent formatting across multiple web pages. Users can update one stylesheet to change the appearance of an entire website. Stylesheets reduce duplicated formatting code. Separation of Content and Design The content layer stores information and structure. The presentation layer controls appearance and design. Separating content and design makes websites easier to maintain. Web designers can change the design without altering the content.

content.topicNotes: Printers What is a printer A printer is an output device that produces a hard copy of digital data. A hard copy is a permanent physical print on paper. Printers output text, images and graphics. They are commonly connected to computers or networks. Printers are widely used in homes, schools and offices. Inkjet printers An inkjet printer sprays tiny droplets of ink onto paper. It produces high-quality colour prints. Inkjet printers are suitable for photos and graphics. They are usually inexpensive to buy. Ink cartridges can be expensive to replace. Laser printers A laser printer uses toner and heat to produce prints. Toner is a fine powder used instead of liquid ink. Laser printers are fast and efficient. They are suitable for high-volume printing. Text quality is usually very sharp. Advantages and disadvantages An advantage is that printers produce permanent records. An advantage is that printed documents are easy to share physically. A disadvantage is the cost of ink, toner and paper. A disadvantage is that printers require maintenance. Printing uses physical resources and energy. Dot-matrix printers A dot-matrix printer strikes an inked ribbon with tiny pins to impact paper. It produces hard copies using a matrix of dots. Dot-matrix printers are suitable for multi-part carbon copies and continuous stationery. They work reliably in harsh, dusty, or dirty environments. They are very loud, slow, and produce low-quality printouts.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Input & Output Devices > Output Devices

content.topicNotes: Printing Files Print Preview Users check the Print Preview to see exactly how a document will look on paper before sending it to the printer. Print Preview: a software feature that displays a digital representation of the final printed page. This process helps identify formatting errors or layout issues, which reduces the waste of paper and ink. Checking the preview ensures that no text is cut off at the margins. Printer Settings The print dialogue box allows users to configure specific settings to control the output quality and cost. Duplex Printing: a setting that enables the printer to automatically print on both sides of a sheet of paper. Users can choose 'Greyscale' to print using only black ink, which saves expensive colour cartridges. Selecting a specific 'Page Range' allows the user to print only the necessary sections of a long document. Orientation and Scaling Users adjust the page orientation to fit the content effectively on the physical sheet. Landscape: a horizontal page orientation where the width of the page is greater than the height. Portrait: a vertical page orientation where the height of the page is greater than the width. Scaling options allow the software to shrink a large spreadsheet so it fits onto a single printed page.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > File Management > Managing Files

content.topicNotes: Privacy and Confidentiality What is privacy Privacy is the right of individuals to control how their personal data is collected and used. Personal data includes names, addresses and online activity. Organisations must only collect necessary data. Users expect their data to be handled responsibly. Privacy is important when using networks and the internet. What is confidentiality Confidentiality means keeping data secret from unauthorised users. Only authorised users are allowed to access confidential data. Authorised users are people with permission to access data. Confidential data includes medical and financial records. Networks must protect confidential information. Risks to privacy and confidentiality Hackers may gain unauthorised access to network data. Malware can steal personal or confidential information. Phishing attacks trick users into revealing details. Data can be intercepted on unsecured networks. Weak passwords increase security risks. Protecting privacy and confidentiality Encryption protects data by making it unreadable to unauthorised users. Encryption changes data into a coded form. Strong passwords limit unauthorised access. User access levels regulate whether individuals have read-only privileges or full editing rights to modify files, based on their job role. Secure networks help protect sensitive information.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Networks and the Effects of Using Them > Network Issues: Security

content.topicNotes: Expert Systems – Producing Solutions for Different Scenarios Using scenarios in expert systems A scenario is a specific set of conditions or inputs. Expert systems analyse different scenarios by changing input data. Different inputs produce different outcomes. The inference engine applies relevant rules to each case. Scenarios allow the system to model real-world situations. How solutions are produced The user enters facts related to the problem. The inference engine selects matching IF…THEN rules. Logical reasoning links facts to conclusions. The system evaluates possible solutions. The most suitable recommendation is presented. Example scenarios A medical expert system suggests different diagnoses for different symptoms. A loan approval system gives different outcomes based on income levels. A car fault system produces different advice for different warning signs. A farming system suggests treatments based on crop conditions. Each scenario leads to a different rule pathway. Advantages and limitations Advantages Multiple scenarios can be tested quickly. Consistent decisions are produced for similar inputs. Limitations Unusual scenarios may not match stored rules. Incorrect input data leads to incorrect solutions.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > ICT Applications > Expert Systems

content.topicNotes: Production Line Control What is production line control Production line control uses computer systems to manage manufacturing processes. A computer controls machines and equipment automatically. Sensors monitor conditions such as position, temperature or speed. Microprocessors process sensor data and make decisions. Production lines are common in factories. How production line control works Sensors detect items moving along the production line. Analogue signals from sensors are converted to digital format using an analogue-to-digital converter (ADC) before processing. Data from sensors is sent to the control computer. The computer sends signals to actuators. Actuators perform actions such as moving, cutting or sorting. The process repeats continuously during production. Uses of production line control Food factories use production lines to package products. Car manufacturers assemble vehicles using controlled production lines. Bottling plants fill and seal containers automatically. Electronics factories use production lines for circuit assembly. Large quantities of identical products can be produced. Advantages and disadvantages Advantages Production speed and efficiency are increased. Product quality is consistent. Disadvantages Initial setup costs are high. System failures can stop the entire production line.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > ICT Applications > Computer Controlled Systems

content.topicNotes: Proofreading Checking Layout Proofreading is the process of reviewing a document for errors. Users should check the overall layout and presentation. They should identify formatting mistakes before publication. Careful proofreading improves document quality. Line Spacing and Blank Pages Users should check that line spacing is consistent.Line spacing is the vertical distance between lines of text. Blank pages or slides should be removed if unnecessary. Consistent spacing improves readability. Widows and Orphans A widow is a short line left alone at the top of a page. An orphan is a short line left alone at the bottom of a page. Users should adjust formatting to remove widows and orphans to improve readability. Checking Styles Users should ensure styles are applied consistently.A style is a predefined set of formatting settings. Incorrect fonts, colours or spacing should be corrected. Consistent styles improve readability. Tables and Lists Tables must fit within column boundaries, fully showing all cell contents. Header rows must repeat at the top when a table splits across a page break. Bulleted lists need uniform symbols and precise margin or indent alignment. Item spacing must remain consistent, leaving space after the final item.

content.topicNotes: Prosthetics What prosthetics are Prosthetics are artificial body parts that replace missing limbs. Doctors use prosthetics to improve movement and quality of life. Modern prosthetics use computers to control movement more accurately. Computer-aided design Specialists design prosthetics using Computer Aided Design (CAD). CAD means software creates precise digital models. CAD allows prosthetics to fit the patient’s body accurately. This improves comfort and effectiveness. Sensors and control Advanced prosthetics use sensors to detect muscle signals. Sensors collect data about movement intentions. Computers process this data to move the prosthetic limb. This allows more natural movement. Benefits for patients Computer-controlled prosthetics respond quickly and accurately. Patients perform everyday tasks more easily. This increases independence and confidence.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > ICT Applications > Computers in Medicine

content.topicNotes: Protecting Software Copyright Software Licencing Developers issue a formal agreement to specify how many users can install the application. Software Licence: a legal instrument governing the use or redistribution of software. Companies use multi-user licences to allow a specific number of employees to access the program legally. Users must agree to the terms of the End User Licence Agreement (EULA) before installation. Technical Protection Methods Systems require a unique product key to verify that the user purchased a legitimate copy. Product Key: a specific alphanumeric code used to register or activate a software program. Software communicates with an online server to prevent duplicate installs. Physical security devices like dongles must be plugged into a USB port for some specialist software to function. Program code is converted into executable format and encrypted to prevent unauthorized viewing or editing. Anti-Piracy Measures Programmers include code that checks for the presence of the original physical disc during startup. Developers release regular updates that verify the software's authenticity over the internet. Digital Rights Management (DRM): technologies used to control the use, modification, and distribution of copyrighted works. Software identifies and blocks 'cracked' versions to ensure only paying customers have access.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Audience > Copyright

content.topicNotes: Stylesheet Benefits Why Stylesheets Are Used A stylesheet is a set of rules used to control the appearance of a web page. Stylesheets separate content from design. Developers use stylesheets to change colours, fonts and layouts without editing every page. Consistency Across Websites Stylesheets help keep pages consistent across a website. Consistency means using the same fonts, colours and layouts on different pages. Users can navigate a website more easily when pages have a similar appearance. Types of Styles In-line styles are written inside individual HTML elements. Internal styles are stored in the <style> section within a web page. External styles are stored in a separate CSS file and can control multiple pages. Advantages of CSS CSS reduces repeated formatting across a website. Developers can update one stylesheet instead of changing every page separately. This saves time and reduces formatting errors.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Website Authoring > Stylesheets

content.topicNotes: Questionnaires and Documents Questionnaire Method A questionnaire is a set of written questions given to users. The analyst designs closed and open questions. Closed questions have fixed answers such as yes or no. Open questions allow users to answer in their own words. Advantages of Questionnaires Questionnaires can reach a large number of users quickly across different locations. They produce structured data that is relatively fast and easy to analyse. Respondents can complete them anonymously, which encourages honest feedback. Disadvantages of Questionnaires Some users may not return the questionnaire, leading to low response rates. Users may misunderstand questions, which reduces the accuracy of data. The analyst cannot easily ask immediate follow-up questions to clarify answers. Examination of Documents The analyst studies current documents used in the system. Documents include invoices, forms, reports and receipts. This method shows data fields, formats and workflows. A data field is a single item of data, such as a customer name. Advantages of Document Examination Examining documents provides factual, objective information about the current system. It helps the analyst identify precise inputs, outputs, and data structures. It allows the analyst to understand standard business rules and official requirements. Disadvantages of Document Examination Some documents may be outdated, incomplete, or no longer used in practice. The method does not show user opinions, feelings, or satisfaction with the system. It can be time-consuming to read through large volumes of paperwork.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > The Systems Life Cycle > Analysing the Current System

content.topicNotes: RAM and ROM Memory What is RAM? Random Access Memory (RAM) stores data and programs currently in use. RAM allows the computer to access data quickly while running applications. RAM is volatile, which means it loses its contents when the power is switched off. What is ROM? Read Only Memory (ROM) stores essential instructions needed to start the computer. ROM contains start-up instructions, also known as firmware. Firmware is permanent software stored on hardware. ROM is non-volatile, so it keeps data when the power is off. RAM vs ROM RAM temporarily stores data that the CPU is actively using. ROM permanently stores start-up instructions for the computer. RAM changes frequently, while ROM usually stays the same. Both RAM and ROM are essential for a computer to function properly.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Types & Components of Computer Systems > Hardware

content.topicNotes: RFID Devices What is RFID? RFID stands for Radio Frequency IDentification. A Radio Frequency Identification device uses electromagnetic radio waves to transfer data wirelessly. An RFID tag contains a microchip and an antenna. A reader sends a signal and the tag responds with stored information. Most tags are passive, so they have no battery. They use the energy from the reader's signal to send their signal back. Tracking Stock Shops attach RFID tags to products to track stock levels. The system scans multiple items at once without needing direct line-of-sight. The database updates automatically when items move or sell. Businesses reduce human error and improve inventory control. Passports and Automobiles Modern passports contain RFID chips that store personal data securely. Border control systems read the chip to verify identity quickly. Some automobiles use RFID for keyless entry systems. The car unlocks automatically when it detects the correct RFID key. Contactless Payment Contactless bank cards contain RFID technology. The card communicates with the payment reader using radio waves. The system authorises small payments without inserting the card. Encryption protects the transmitted data from unauthorised access. Advantages and Disadvantages of RFID Advantages Inventory counts can be completed rapidly because products do not require single, line-of-sight scanning. Signals can penetrate wrapping, debris, and function across noticeable physical distances. Disadvantages Manufacturing RFID tags incurs a substantially higher cost compared to printing basic barcodes. Metallic surfaces and liquids can obstruct radio signals.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > ICT Applications > Recognition Systems

content.topicNotes: Registration and Attendance Systems What is a school management system A school management system is computer software used to manage school data. The system stores information about students and staff. Data is stored securely in a central database. Teachers and administrators access the system using computers. School management systems improve organisation and efficiency. Registration systems Registration systems record student enrolment details. Details include names, addresses and emergency contacts. Student records are updated electronically. Accurate registration supports school administration. Data can be accessed quickly when needed. Attendance systems Attendance systems record whether students are present or absent. Teachers enter attendance data electronically. Data is recorded using cards or tags swiped at a terminal (RFID), or through biometric systems. RFID stands for Radio-Frequency Identification, a wireless technology that tracks data using tags and receivers. Attendance data is stored automatically. Patterns of absence can be identified easily. Advantages and disadvantages Advantages Records are accurate and easy to update. Attendance can be monitored in real time. Disadvantages System failures can prevent access to records. Personal data must be protected from unauthorised access.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > ICT Applications > School Management Systems

content.topicNotes: Remote Control, Joysticks and Driving Wheels Remote control A remote control is an input device used to control a system from a distance. A remote control sends signals using infrared or radio waves. Infrared requires a clear line of sight between devices. Remote controls are commonly used with televisions and media systems. Buttons allow users to select options and control functions. Joystick A joystick is an input device that is moved in different directions. Movement controls an on-screen object or cursor. Joysticks often include buttons for additional actions. Joysticks are commonly used in control systems and simulators. A joystick provides precise directional control. Driving wheel A driving wheel is an input device designed to simulate steering. A driving wheel is mainly used in driving and racing simulations. Turning the wheel controls steering in the software. Pedals are often included for acceleration and braking. Driving wheels increase realism and user immersion. Advantages and disadvantages a remote control Advantages of a remote control A remote control allows operation from a distance. A remote control is simple and easy to use. Disadvantages of a remote control Infrared remote controls require line of sight. Limited input options are available. Advantages and disadvantages a joystick Advantages of a joystick A joystick provides precise directional control. A joystick enhances gaming and simulation experiences. Disadvantages of a joystick A joystick is not suitable for typing or general tasks. A joystick is mainly designed for specific applications. Advantages and disadvantages a driving wheel Advantages of a driving wheel A driving wheel provides realistic steering control. A driving wheel improves immersion in racing simulations. Disadvantages of a driving wheel A driving wheel requires additional space and hardware. A driving wheel is limited to specialised software.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Input & Output Devices > Input Devices

content.topicNotes: Repetitive Strain Injury and Back Problems Repetitive strain injury (RSI) Repetitive strain injury (RSI) is damage to muscles, tendons or nerves. RSI is caused by repeated movements over long periods. Common activities include typing or using a mouse. Symptoms include pain, stiffness and tingling. RSI can worsen without proper rest or posture. Causes of RSI Continuous keyboard or mouse use can strain muscles. Poor workstation setup increases the risk of injury. Lack of breaks prevents muscles from recovering. Incorrect hand or wrist position causes stress. High repetition tasks increase strain on joints. Back problems Back problems are caused by poor sitting posture. Sitting for long periods puts pressure on the spine. An unsupportive chair increases strain on the back. Incorrect screen height can lead to slouching. Back pain can become long-term if not corrected. Prevention methods Regular breaks reduce strain on muscles and joints. An adjustable chair supports correct posture. The keyboard and mouse should be positioned correctly. Use of ergonomic keyboards and mice improves wrist alignment and reduces finger strain. Screen height should be at eye level. Stretching exercises help prevent injury.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > The Effects of Using IT > Health Problems Related to IT Equipment

content.topicNotes: Report Data in Databases What are Reports? Database reports present information from a table or query in a structured, professional layout. A query is a search or filter applied to a database to retrieve specific data. Reports organise data so that humans can easily read and understand the findings. Users design reports to summarise large amounts of data for presentation. Purpose and Importance Managers use reports to make informed business decisions based on accurate data trends. Reports distribute key data to stakeholders who do not have direct access to the database. Database software automates the reporting process to save time and reduce human error. Users add headers, footers, and page numbers to make the data look professional. Access vs Word Processors Microsoft Access links reports directly to dynamic data for real-time updates across records. Dynamic data means database information that updates automatically when changes occur. Word processors require manual data entry and suit static, text-heavy narrative documents. Choose Access to easily sort, group, and calculate large volumes of relational database data. Access Reports Structure The "Report Header" and "Report Footer" display information only once at the absolute start and end of the document. The "Page Header" and "Page Footer" display repeating details at the top and bottom of every individual page. The "Detail" section contains the actual data fields and records retrieved from the database. Records represent individual rows of structured data stored within a database table. Practical Tips for Reporting Data Sorting and Grouping Data Sorting places records in alphabetical or numerical order. Multi-level sorting sorts by a main field, then a secondary field. Grouping collects related records under one main header. Grouping lets you run summary calculations for each distinct category. Summary Calculations Aggregate functions compute summary statistics across all listed records. Examples include =SUM() for totals, =AVG() for averages, and =COUNT() for totals counts. Put controls in the Report Footer for overall totals. Put controls in a Group Footer for category totals. Report Formatting Checklist Match page setup (Portrait/Landscape) so data does not overflow pages. Make sure all labels and values display clearly without truncation or ### errors. Add student details (Name, Candidate Number, Centre Number) in headers or footers. Display a clear main title once at the top in a large font.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Databases > Presenting Data

content.topicNotes: Risks of Using the Internet Undesirable and Offensive Content Users may accidentally or intentionally access undesirable content that is offensive, illegal, or harmful. This category includes criminal material, websites that contain harmful information, and cyberbullying. Cyberbullying: the use of digital platforms to send threatening or hurtful messages to intimidate others. Schools and parents often use filtering software to prevent exposure to these specific categories of websites. Phishing and Data Risks Fraudulent emails and websites use phishing techniques to trick users into revealing sensitive personal data. Phishing: the use of fake communications to gain personal information like passwords or credit card numbers. Stolen personal data often leads to identity theft, where criminals use the information for financial fraud. Avoiding the disclosure of personal details on public platforms helps to prevent targeted scams or security risks. Malware and Viruses Downloading files or clicking suspicious links can infect a computer with malicious software. Malware: software specifically designed to disrupt, damage, or gain unauthorised access to a computer system. These programs can delete files, steal data, or allow hackers to take control of hardware. Maintaining updated anti-virus software allows systems to detect and remove these threats effectively. Safety Precautions Individuals can protect accounts by using strong, unique passwords and enabling two-factor authentication. Schools and companies often implement robust firewalls and filtering software to monitor and block harmful traffic. Firewall: a security system that monitors and controls incoming and outgoing network traffic based on safety rules. Organisations provide regular training to help people recognise phishing attempts and secure their personal data.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Communication > The Internet

content.topicNotes: Robotics in Manufacture What are computer-controlled robots A computer-controlled robot is a machine controlled by a computer program. Robots use microprocessors to follow instructions automatically. Sensors provide input about position, speed or temperature. Actuators allow robots to move or perform actions. Robots are widely used in manufacturing industries. How robots are used in manufacture Robots assemble products such as cars and electronics. Robots are trained to perform tasks using handheld control boxes or through lead-through programming techniques. Lead-through programming trains robots by physically or electronically guiding them through motions while the controller records the path. Welding robots join metal parts accurately. Painting robots apply coatings evenly. Advantages of robotics in manufacture Robots increase production speed and efficiency. Products are made with high accuracy and consistency. Dangerous tasks are carried out safely by robots. Robots can operate 24 hours a day. Manufacturing costs may be reduced in the long term. Disadvantages of robotics in manufacture Robots are expensive to buy and install. Skilled workers are needed to program and maintain robots. Job losses may occur in manual labour roles. Robots cannot easily adapt to unexpected situations. System failures can stop production.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > ICT Applications > Computer Controlled Systems

content.topicNotes: Rotating and Reflecting Images Rotating Images Users rotate an image to change its orientation by a specific number of degrees. Rotation: the process of turning an image around a central pivot point. Software allows for fixed rotations, such as 90 or 180 degrees, or free rotation to any angle. This tool helps correct photos taken at the wrong angle or fits graphics into specific layout spaces. Reflecting Images Users reflect an image to create a mirror image of the original graphic. Reflection: the process of flipping an image over a vertical or horizontal axis. Flipping an image horizontally reverses the left and right sides, which is useful for changing the direction a subject faces. Flipping an image vertically creates a top-to-bottom reversal, often used to create a water-like mirror effect. Choosing the Right Axis Axis: an imaginary line around which an object can rotate or be reflected. X-axis: flips the image vertically (top to bottom). Y-axis: flips the image horizontally (left to right). Z-axis: rotates the image flat against the screen (like a wheel spinning). X or Y rotation creates 3D-like tilt effects. Choosing the wrong axis may result in upside-down text or a perspective that looks unnatural to the viewer, thus reducing presentation quality.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Images > Images

content.topicNotes: Routers What a Router Does A router connects different networks together. It directs data between a LAN and the internet. A LAN means Local Area Network. Routers help devices on a network access online services. Many routers include a firewall for security. How Routers Send Data A router inspects data packets to forward them from one network to another It reads the destination IP address in a packet. IP stands for Internet Protocol. It chooses the best path for the packet to travel. This process helps data reach the correct device. Router vs Switch A router connects different networks. A switch connects devices within the same network. Routers use IP addresses to route data. Switches use MAC addresses to forward data.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Networks and the Effects of Using Them > Common Network Devices

content.topicNotes: SMS, Calls and Internet Access Short Message Service (SMS) Short Message Service (SMS) allows users to send text messages between mobile phones. SMS messages are limited to a fixed number of characters. Messages are sent over a mobile network. SMS works without an internet connection. SMS is commonly used for quick communication and alerts. Mobile phone calls Mobile phone calls allow real-time voice communication. Calls use mobile network signals to transmit sound. Voice data is converted into digital signals. Calls can be made almost anywhere with network coverage. Calls are used for personal and business communication. Mobile internet access Mobile internet access allows devices to connect to the internet using mobile data. Mobile data uses 3G, 4G or 5G networks. Users can browse websites and use online services. Internet access supports email and social media. Smartphones rely heavily on mobile internet connectivity. Advantages and disadvantages Advantages Communication is possible almost anywhere. Mobile devices support multiple communication methods. Disadvantages Network coverage may be limited in some areas. Mobile data usage can be expensive.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > ICT Applications > Communication Media

content.topicNotes: SSD, Pen Drive and Flash Drive What is solid-state storage Solid-state storage stores data using electronic memory chips. No moving parts are used to store or access data. Data is stored as binary values. Binary values use 0s and 1s to represent information. Solid-state storage is non-volatile. Solid-State Drive (SSD) A solid-state drive (SSD) is used as main backing storage in computers. An SSD uses flash memory instead of spinning disks. Data access speeds are very fast. SSDs are commonly used in laptops and modern desktop computers. Faster boot times improve system performance. Pen drive and flash drive A pen drive is a small portable solid-state storage device. A flash drive connects to a computer using a USB port. Pen drives are used to transfer files between computers. Storage capacity varies from small to very large sizes. Flash drives are easy to carry and reuse. Advantages and disadvantages Advantages Solid-state devices are fast and reliable. No moving parts reduce the risk of physical damage. SSDs consume less power and generate less heat, as they have no spinning parts, which extends battery life and keeps devices cooler Disadvantages Solid-state storage is more expensive per gigabyte. Limited write cycles can reduce lifespan over time.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Storage Devices & Media > Solid-State Devices & Media

content.topicNotes: Saving Files The Save Command Users use the Save command to update an existing file with the latest changes. Save: an operation that overwrites the current version of a file stored on a storage device. This process replaces the original data with the new version held in the computer's memory. It ensures that work is not lost if the application closes or the power fails. The Save As Command The Save As command allows users to create a new version of a file while keeping the original unchanged. Save As: a function that lets a user specify a new filename, file format, or storage location. This is useful for creating templates or saving documents in different formats for compatibility. File Format: a standard way that information is encoded for storage in a computer file. Version Control Version Control is the practice of tracking and managing changes to software code or documents. Saving files with unique names or timestamps helps users manage different stages of a project. Users can revert to an older version if a mistake occurs in the current working document. This prevents the accidental loss of data that might occur when overwriting a single file repeatedly.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > File Management > Managing Files

content.topicNotes: Scanners and Digital Cameras Scanner A scanner is an input device used to convert paper documents into digital format. A scanner captures images of text or pictures. A scanner outputs a digital image Scanners are commonly used to digitise documents and photos. Uses of scanners Scanners are used to archive paper documents digitally. Scanners are used to input photographs into a computer. Offices use scanners to share documents electronically. Scanned text can be edited using OCR software. OCR stands for Optical Character Recognition and converts images of text into editable text. Scanners reduce the need for physical storage. Digital camera A digital camera is an input device that captures photographs and videos digitally. Images are stored as digital files on memory cards. Digital cameras use image sensors instead of film. Photos can be transferred directly to a computer. Many smartphones include built-in digital cameras. Advantages and disadvantages of a scanner Advantages of a scanner A scanner creates accurate digital copies of documents. A scanner allows paper documents to be stored electronically. Disadvantages of a scanner Scanned images can create large file sizes. A scanner requires additional hardware and space. Advantages and disadvantages of a digital camera Advantages of a digital camera A digital camera captures real-world images quickly. Digital photos can be transferred and shared easily. Digital cameras allow for instant previewing, editing and deleting of images eliminating the cost and time of processing physical film Disadvantages of a digital camera Image quality depends on resolution and lighting. Additional software may be required for editing.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Input & Output Devices > Input Devices

content.topicNotes: Search Engines Finding Information Search engines help users find specific information from the billions of pages on the World Wide Web. They act as a massive digital directory that users can search instantly using keywords. Keywords: simple words or phrases that describe the main topics of a search. Without search engines, users would need to know the exact URL of every website they wanted to visit. Indexing The search engine organises collected data into a massive database known as an index. Index: a structured database that stores information about web pages to allow for fast retrieval. It stores keywords, metadata, and page descriptions to help categorise each site. Metadata: data that provides information about other data, such as tags or descriptions in a website's code. Search Queries and Ranking Users input a search query to find specific information within the search engine's index. Search Query: the specific words or phrases that a user enters into a search engine. Complex algorithms rank the results based on relevance and website authority. Algorithm: a process or set of rules followed in calculations or problem-solving operations. Result Retrieval The search engine displays the most relevant matches as a list on a results page. It provides a title, a brief snippet of text, and a URL for each identified web page. Users click on these links to navigate directly to the external website stored on a web server.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Communication > The Internet

content.topicNotes: Secondary Axes Data Series A data series is a set of related values plotted on a chart. Charts can display more than one data series. Each data series usually represents a different type of data. Multiple data series allow comparisons to be made. Adding a Second Data Series Users can add a second data series to an existing chart. The chart displays both sets of data together. Different colours or patterns distinguish each series. A legend helps identify the data series. What is a Secondary Axis? A secondary axis is an additional value axis on a chart. It usually appears on the right side of the chart. Users add a secondary axis when data series use different scales. This improves the readability of the chart. Why Use a Secondary Axis? A secondary axis enables clear comparison between distinct data sets. It handles vast scale differences, such as comparing revenue in millions to unit totals in hundreds. It supports mixed metrics, like plotting rainfall in millimetres alongside temperature in degrees Celsius. Dedicated scales keep smaller data values visible alongside large ones. Benefits of Multiple Axes Multiple axes help present complex data clearly. Users can compare related data on one chart. Appropriate axis scales improve interpretation. Well-designed charts communicate information more effectively.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Graphs & Charts > Graphs & Charts

content.topicNotes: Secure Socket Layer (SSL) What is SSL? Secure Socket Layer (SSL) is a security protocol. A protocol is a set of rules for communication. SSL creates a secure connection between devices and so it protects data sent over the internet. Encrypted Links SSL creates an encrypted link between a client (user device) and a server (web provider). How the connection is established: The web browser asks the web server to start a secure connection. The server replies by sending its digital SSL certificate, which includes its public key. The web browser checks the certificate against a trusted Certificate Authority (CA) to confirm it is authentic. After successful verification, both parties generate a unique session key to encrypt and decrypt all data transferred during the visit." Identifying SSL Websites using SSL show HTTPS in the address bar. A padlock symbol indicates a secure connection. Users should check for these signs before entering data. This helps confirm the website is secure. Benefits of SSL SSL protects sensitive data such as passwords. It builds trust between users and websites. It reduces the risk of data theft. It is widely used in e-commerce and banking.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Safety & Security > Security of Data

content.topicNotes: Smart Cards and Tokens Smart cards A smart card is a plastic card containing an embedded microchip. The microchip stores encrypted data securely. A card reader communicates with the chip to verify identity. Some smart cards require a PIN for authentication. Examples include bank cards and transport cards such as Oyster cards. Magnetic stripe cards are older, passive devices that store information on a magnetic stripe, rather than on a circuit. Physical security tokens A physical token is a small hardware device used for authentication. The device generates a one-time password (OTP). An OTP is a code that changes every few seconds. The user enters the OTP along with a password. Banks use key fob tokens for online banking security. Digital security tokens A digital token is software-based authentication. A mobile app generates a one-time password. The app uses the device and time to create a unique code. The code is entered during login. Examples include authentication apps such as Google Authenticator. Advantages and disadvantages Advantages of smart cards and tokens Authentication is more secure than using passwords alone. One-time passwords reduce the risk of hacking. Both physical and digital tokens provide an additional layer of security during multi-factor authentication. Disadvantages of smart cards and tokens Physical tokens can be lost or stolen. Digital tokens require a working device and battery power.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Networks and the Effects of Using Them > Network Issues: Security

content.topicNotes: Smartphones What is a smartphone A smartphone is a portable mobile computer that also functions as a telephone. It combines computing, communication and multimedia features in one device. Smartphones use a touch screen as the main input method. They run an operating system that supports apps. An app is a software application designed to perform a specific task. Uses of smartphones Smartphones are used for voice calls and text messaging. Users access the internet and social media on smartphones. They are used for navigation using GPS. GPS is a satellite-based system that provides location information. Smartphones are used for photography and video recording. Many people use smartphones for online banking and payments. Smartphones are used to remotely control devices e.g. smart home apps to adjust heating, flying drones etc. Advantages of smartphones Smartphones are highly portable and fit easily into a pocket. They provide constant internet access through mobile data or Wi-Fi. Built-in sensors support features such as cameras and fingerprint recognition. A wide range of apps makes smartphones very versatile. They combine multiple devices into one. Disadvantages of smartphones Smartphones have small screens that limit detailed work. Battery life restricts long-term use without charging. They are less powerful than laptops or desktop computers. Small keyboards can make typing difficult. Smartphones can be easily lost or stolen.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Types & Components of Computer Systems > Types of Computer

content.topicNotes: Smishing and Vishing What is Smishing? Smishing is a phishing scam using SMS text messages. Short Message Service (SMS) is a text messaging system. Attackers send messages pretending to be trusted organisations. They try to trick users into clicking links or sharing data. What is Vishing? Vishing is a phishing scam using voice calls. Attackers call users pretending to be officials or companies. They may request personal or financial information. Users may feel pressured to respond quickly. Recognising Scams Messages or calls may create urgency or fear. Unknown numbers or unusual requests should be treated with caution. Attackers may ask for sensitive data like passwords. Preventing Smishing Users should not click links in unexpected messages. Unknown messages should be deleted immediately. Security software can block suspicious messages. Users should verify messages with the organisation directly. Users should be trained to identify suspicious text communication. Education and training help individuals identify fraudulent text messages from unknown senders. Preventing Vishing Users should not share personal data over the phone. Calls from unknown numbers should be treated carefully. Users should hang up and contact the organisation directly. Caller ID can be faked, so it should not be fully trusted. Awareness training teaches users to spot fraudulent phone calls from outside sources.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Safety & Security > Security of Data

content.topicNotes: Social Media Blocking and Reporting Users should block unwanted contacts to stop communication. This prevents a person from viewing or messaging your profile. Users should report harmful behaviour to platform moderators, so the service provider is alerted to rule-breaking content. These tools help maintain a safer online environment. Meeting Online Contacts Underage users must avoid meeting online contacts without adult supervision. Online contacts may not be who they claim to be. In some cases someone builds trust to exploit a young person, this is called Grooming. Always inform a trusted adult before any meeting. Meeting strangers alone increases personal safety risks. Responsible Sharing Users should not share inappropriate images or messages, including offensive, sexual, or harmful material. Users must respect others' personal data and privacy. Users should communicate respectfully and avoid offensive language. Posts, comments, and media published online leave a lasting digital footprint that can be viewed indefinitely.

content.topicNotes: Speakers What are speakers Speakers are output devices that produce sound from a computer. Speakers convert digital audio data into sound waves. Sound waves are vibrations that can be heard by humans. Speakers allow users to hear music, speech and alerts. Speakers are commonly connected to computers, phones and tablets. How speakers work The computer sends digital audio signals to the sound system. A DAC converts digital signals into analogue signals. DAC stands for Digital Analogue Converter. An amplifier increases the strength of the analogue signal. A diaphragm and cone vibrate to create sound waves. Uses of speakers Speakers are used to listen to music and audio files. Video conferencing systems use speakers for voice output. Games use speakers to produce sound effects. Public address systems use speakers to reach large audiences. Accessibility tools use speakers for audio feedback. Advantages and disadvantages Advantages of speakers Speakers provide clear audio output for multiple users. Speakers improve the multimedia experience. Disadvantages of speakers Loud audio can disturb other people. Sound quality varies depending on speaker design. External speakers require additional space and power.

content.topicNotes: Spell Check & Grammar Check Reducing Errors Proofing is the process of checking work for errors. Users should proofread documents before publishing them. Software tools help identify mistakes automatically. Fewer errors improve the quality of a document. Spell Check Spell check identifies words that may be spelt incorrectly. It compares words against a built-in dictionary. A dictionary is a list of recognised words. Users should review suggestions before accepting changes. Grammar Check Grammar check identifies possible grammar mistakes. The tool may suggest improvements to sentence construction. Users should check that suggestions make sense. Making Appropriate Changes Users should not accept every suggestion automatically. Some correct words may be flagged as errors. Technical terms may not appear in the dictionary. Users should apply changes only when appropriate. Benefits of Software Tools Automated tools save time when checking documents. They help improve accuracy and consistency. Professional documents should contain as few errors as possible. Proofing tools support, but do not replace, human checking.

content.topicNotes: Stages of the Analysis Identify the Problem Analysts identify weaknesses in the current system and define the problems clearly and accurately. Clear problem definition prevents misunderstandings later. They consult users and managers for different viewpoints. Investigate the Current System Analysts examine how the current system operates. They identify inputs, processes and outputs. They record findings carefully.An input is data entered into a system. A process is an action performed on data. An output is information produced by the system. Gather User Requirements Analysts identify functional and non-functional requirements. Functional requirements describe what the system must do. Non-functional requirements describe performance or security needs. Analysts collect requirements from users with the use of observation, interviews or questionnaires. Requirements Specification Analysts create a requirements specification document that lists all agreed system requirements. They include details of inputs, outputs and processing. This document is approved by users and managers and guides the design stage of the Systems Life Cycle.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > The Systems Life Cycle > Analysing the Current System
