content.topicNotes: Stages of the Systems Life Cycle Analysis Analysts identify the problem and decide whether a new system is needed. They gather requirements, which are the users’ needs and expectations. They collect information using interviews, questionnaires and observation. They produce a requirements specification, which is a document listing what the system must do. Design Designers create detailed plans for the new system. They design input screens, output reports and data structures. They create algorithms, which are step-by-step instructions to solve a problem. They may draw flowcharts to show the logical steps in the program. Development and Testing Programmers write the code based on the design documents. They carry out testing to find and fix errors. They use normal, extreme and abnormal test data to check the system. Test data is sample data used to check that the system works correctly. Implementation The organisation installs the new system. Staff receive training so they can use the system properly. The company may use direct changeover, parallel running or phased implementation. Direct changeover means the old system stops and the new one starts immediately. Parallel running means both systems run at the same time for a period. Evaluation and Maintenance The organisation evaluates the system to check if it meets the original requirements. Users give feedback about performance and usability. Technicians carry out maintenance, which means updating or fixing the system. Maintenance includes correcting errors and improving features.

content.topicNotes: Subscript, Superscript and Capitalisation Subscript Subscript places characters below the normal text line. Users apply subscript in scientific notation. Chemical formulae such as H₂O use subscript numbers. Subscript helps present scientific information correctly. Superscript Superscript places characters above the normal text line. Users apply superscript in mathematical notation. Expressions such as x² use superscript numbers. Superscript helps display powers and exponents correctly. Scientific Notation Scientific notation represents scientific information using special formatting. Chemical formulae often use subscripts. Scientific documents require accurate notation. Correct formatting improves clarity and accuracy. Mathematical Notation Mathematical notation represents mathematical expressions using symbols and formatting. Superscripts show powers and indices. Correct notation prevents misunderstanding. Users should apply mathematical formatting consistently. Capitalisation and Emphasis Capitalisation uses uppercase letters to highlight important text. Users can emphasise headings and key terms with capital letters. Capitalisation should remain consistent throughout a document. Appropriate emphasis improves readability and presentation.

content.topicNotes: Switches What a Switch Is A switch connects multiple devices on a network. It operates within a LAN. LAN means Local Area Network. A switch improves network efficiency compared to a hub. How a Switch Works A switch receives data from one device. It sends data only to the intended device. This is called Unicast. It uses MAC addresses to make decisions. A MAC address is a Media Access Control address that identifies a device. Benefits of Using Switches A switch reduces data collisions on a network. It improves network speed and performance. Each device gets its own dedicated connection. This makes switches suitable for busy networks. Switch vs Hub A switch sends data only where it is needed. A hub sends data to all connected devices. Switches are more secure than hubs. Most modern networks use switches.

content.topicNotes: Tab Stops and Tabulated Text Purpose of Tab Stops A tab stop is a predefined position where text aligns. Tab stops help users organise and align data. They create neat layouts without using multiple spaces. Tabulated text is text arranged using tab stops. Types of Tab Stops A left tab aligns text from the left edge of the tab stop. A right tab aligns text to the right edge of the tab stop. A centre tab centres text on the tab stop. A decimal tab aligns numbers by their decimal points. Tab Leaders A tab leader fills the blank space before a tab stop using repeated characters. Frequently used leader characters feature dot patterns (....), dashed lines (----), or continuous underlines (____). Tab leaders guide the reader's eye across pages in tables of contents, agendas, and menus by linking entries directly to page or price figures. Aligning Data Users align data to improve readability. Right tabs align values such as prices. Decimal tabs align numbers with decimal places. Consistent alignment makes information easier to compare. Indented Paragraphs An indented paragraph starts further from the margin. Users apply indentation to separate text from surrounding content. Indents improve document structure. Tab settings can help create consistent indentation. Hanging Paragraphs A hanging paragraph has the first line aligned with the margin. All following lines are indented. Hanging paragraphs are often used in reference lists. Users can create hanging paragraphs using tab and indentation settings.

content.topicNotes: Tables in Web Pages Table Structure The <table> tag creates a table structure on a web page. A table organises data into rows and columns. Tables help users read and compare information. Web developers use tables for structured data rather than page layout. Rows and Cells The <tr> tag creates a table row. The <td> tag creates a table cell. A cell stores individual pieces of information. Rows and cells work together to organise data clearly. Captions and Borders The <caption> tag adds a title to a table. A caption explains the purpose of the table. Table borders separate cells visually. Borders make data easier to read and identify. Headers The <th> tag creates a table header. A header identifies the content of a row or column. Headers usually appear in bold and centre aligned by default. Headers improve readability and organisation. Table Sections The <thead> tag stores table headings. The <tbody> tag stores the main table data. The <tfoot> tag stores summary or footer information. These sections organise large tables and improve structure.

content.topicNotes: Tablet and Phablet Computers What are tablets and phablets A tablet computer is a portable device with a flat touch screen and no built-in physical keyboard. A phablet is a device that is larger than a smartphone but smaller than a tablet. A phablet combines features of a phone and a tablet. Both devices use touch input as the main method of control. They run mobile operating systems designed for touch interaction. Uses of tablets and phablets Tablets are used for internet browsing, email and multimedia consumption. Students use tablets for reading digital textbooks and note-taking. Phablets are commonly used for communication and media on larger screens. Businesses use tablets for presentations and data collection. Both devices are used for gaming and educational apps. Tablets are used to remotely control devices e.g. smart home apps to adjust heating, flying drones etc. Advantages of tablets and phablets Tablets and phablets are lightweight and highly portable. Touch screens make them intuitive and easy to use. Battery life is usually longer than laptops. Built-in wireless connectivity allows mobile internet access. They start up quickly compared to traditional computers. Disadvantages of tablets and phablets Touch screen keyboards are slower for typing long documents. Limited processing power compared to desktops and laptops. Storage capacity is often smaller. Fewer professional software applications are available. Repairs and upgrades are usually not possible.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Types & Components of Computer Systems > Types of Computer

content.topicNotes: Technical Documentation What is technical documentation Technical documentation is detailed information for developers and IT staff. It explains how the system is built and how it works internally. Technical documentation supports maintenance and future upgrades. It is not usually written for end users. Clear documentation reduces dependency on original developers. Contents of technical documentation System specifications describe hardware and software requirements. Program listings include source code. Data flow diagrams show data flows through the system. Data dictionaries define fields, data types and formats. Test plans and results are included for reference. Why technical documentation is important Maintenance programmers use documentation to fix bugs. Documentation helps new developers understand the system. Clear instructions reduce errors during updates. Technical records support troubleshooting. Good documentation improves system reliability over time. Risks of poor documentation Missing documentation makes maintenance difficult. Errors are harder to identify and correct. Knowledge may be lost if staff leave the organisation. Updates may introduce new bugs. System downtime may increase.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > The Systems Life Cycle > Documenting the New System

content.topicNotes: Test Data: Normal, Abnormal and Extreme Normal test data Normal data is valid input within the expected range. Normal data should be processed without errors. It checks that the system works under typical conditions. Example: entering a mark of 65 when the valid range is 0 to 100. The expected output should be calculated correctly. Abnormal test data Abnormal data is invalid input outside the allowed range. Abnormal data should be rejected by validation rules. It checks that the system handles errors correctly. Example: entering a mark of 150 when the maximum is 100. The system should display an error message. Extreme test data Extreme data tests values at the boundaries of the range. Boundary values are the minimum and maximum allowed inputs. It checks how the system handles limit conditions. Example: entering 0 and 100 when the valid range is 0 to 100. The system should accept both boundary values correctly. Why different test data is important Using normal data checks correct processing. Using abnormal data checks error handling. Using extreme data checks boundary conditions. A combination of test data improves reliability. Poor testing can leave hidden errors in the system.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > The Systems Life Cycle > Developing & Testing the New System

content.topicNotes: Test Designs What is a test design A test design is a planned method for checking a system works correctly. A test design specifies the input data to be used. A test design includes the expected output for each test. Expected output is the correct result predicted before testing. Test designs ensure systematic and organised testing. Types of test data Normal data is valid input within the expected range. Boundary data is valid input at the limits of the range. Abnormal data is invalid input outside the allowed range. Extreme data tests the system at its maximum limits. Using different data types checks reliability. Example test design table Input: mark = 75, Expected output: grade B. Input: mark = 0, Expected output: grade U. Input: mark = 101, Expected output: error message. Input: mark = -5, Expected output: error message. Comparing actual and expected output confirms correctness. Why test designs are important Test designs ensure all functions are checked. They provide evidence that the system has been tested. Errors can be identified and corrected before release. Documentation supports user acceptance testing. Structured testing improves system quality.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > The Systems Life Cycle > Developing & Testing the New System

content.topicNotes: Test Plan What is a test plan A test plan is a document that outlines how testing will be carried out. It defines the scope, objectives and schedule of testing. A test plan identifies who is responsible for each test. The test plan ensures testing is organised and complete. A clear test plan reduces the risk of missing important tests. Contents of a test plan The test plan lists the features to be tested. It includes test data and expected results. It specifies hardware and software requirements. The test plan outlines the testing environment. It records how results will be documented. Test schedule and responsibilities The test plan includes start and end dates for testing. Developers may carry out unit testing. Users may carry out acceptance testing. Deadlines ensure testing is completed before implementation. Clear roles improve accountability. Why a test plan is important A test plan ensures systematic testing of all features. It provides evidence that testing has taken place. Errors can be tracked and retested after correction. A structured approach improves reliability. Without a test plan, important faults may be overlooked.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > The Systems Life Cycle > Developing & Testing the New System

content.topicNotes: Test Strategies What is a test strategy A test strategy is an overall plan for how a system will be tested. It defines who will test the system and when testing will occur. A test strategy identifies different levels of testing. Testing ensures the system meets user and technical requirements. A clear strategy improves system reliability. Unit testing Unit testing checks individual components of a system. A component can be a single program or module. Developers usually carry out unit testing. Errors are identified early in development. Unit testing ensures each part works correctly on its own. Integration and system testing Integration testing checks that components work together. Data is passed between modules to test compatibility. System testing checks the entire system as a whole. Realistic scenarios are used during testing. Problems with communication between modules can be identified. User acceptance testing (UAT) User acceptance testing is carried out by end users. Users test the system in real-life situations. Feedback is given on usability and performance. The system is approved before implementation. UAT ensures the system meets user expectations. Other strategies and risks Alpha testing is done internally before release. Beta testing is done by selected external users. Black-box testing checks outputs without viewing code. White-box testing examines internal program logic. Poor testing strategy increases the risk of system failure.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > The Systems Life Cycle > Developing & Testing the New System

content.topicNotes: Text Alignment Left Alignment Left alignment places text evenly against the left margin. The right side of the text appears uneven. This is the default alignment in many documents. It is easy for users to read. Right Alignment Right alignment places text evenly against the right margin. The left side of the text appears uneven. It is often used for dates or headings. It can create a different visual effect in documents. Centre Alignment Centre alignment positions text equally between both margins. It is commonly used for titles and headings. This alignment draws attention to important text. Large amounts of centred text can reduce readability. Fully Justified Text Fully justified text is distributed evenly with both margins. The software adjusts spacing between words. This creates a neat and professional appearance. Uneven word spacing can sometimes make text harder to read. Choosing Alignment Different alignments suit different document purposes. Consistent alignment improves presentation. Users should choose alignment based on readability. Good formatting makes documents easier to understand.

Appropriate Web Page Content Web page content should match the purpose of the website. Users should write clear and relevant information. Content should be accurate and easy to understand. Well-organised content improves the user experience. Structured Content Web developers combine headings and paragraphs to create structure. Structured content makes information easier to read. Users can find important information more quickly. Good structure improves website accessibility and usability.

content.topicNotes: Text Enhancement Bold, Italic and Underline Bold text makes important words stand out. Italic text slants characters to add emphasis. Underline places a line beneath text. Users apply these enhancements to improve document presentation. Highlighting Text Highlighting adds a coloured background behind text. Users highlight important information to attract attention. Highlighting makes key points easier to locate. Excessive highlighting can reduce its effectiveness and readability. Text Colour Text colour changes the appearance of characters. Users select colours to improve presentation or match a design. Good colour choices maintain readability. Poor colour contrast can make text difficult to read. Bulleted Lists A bulleted list uses symbols to separate items. Bulleted lists present related information without implying order. Users can create or edit bulleted lists. Bullets make information easier to read and scan. Numbered Lists A numbered list uses numbers to organise items. Numbered lists show a sequence or priority. Users create numbered lists for instructions or procedures. Numbering helps readers follow steps in the correct order.

content.topicNotes: Text Enhancement Bold, Italic and Underline Bold text appears darker and thicker than normal text. Italic text is slanted to the side. Underlined text has a line beneath it. These enhancements highlight important information. Paragraph Spacing Paragraph spacing controls the gaps before and after paragraphs. A paragraph is a section of related text. Extra spacing improves readability. Consistent spacing creates a neat document layout. When the last line of a paragraph appears isolated at the top of a new page it is called a widow. When the first line of a paragraph appears isolated at the bottom of a page it is called an orphan. Line Spacing Line spacing controls the vertical space between lines of text. Larger spacing can make text easier to read. Small spacing allows more text to fit on a page. Users should choose spacing suitable for the document purpose. Bullet Points Bullet points organise information into lists. Bullets can use different shapes such as circles or squares. Indent controls how far bullets are from the margin. Consistent alignment improves presentation. Using Formatting Effectively Too much enhancement can make text difficult to read. Consistent formatting improves document appearance. Bullets help users identify key points quickly. Good spacing makes information easier to understand.

content.topicNotes: Behaviour Layer Purpose of the Behaviour Layer The behaviour layer controls how elements on a web page respond to user actions. It adds interactivity to a website. Interactive features can improve usability It makes web pages more dynamic and engaging. It works alongside the content and presentation layers. Developers can update behaviour without changing page content. Separating behaviour from content and presentation simplifies website maintenance. What Scripting Is A script is a set of instructions that a computer follows. Scripting allows a web page to perform actions automatically. Scripts can respond to clicks, key presses and other events. Scripting improves the user experience. JavaScript JavaScript is a scripting language commonly used in the behaviour layer. JavaScript adds interactivity to web pages. Developers use JavaScript to control page elements. JavaScript works with HTML and CSS to create complete websites. Controlling Web Page Elements JavaScript can show or hide content on a web page. JavaScript can validate data entered into forms. JavaScript can display messages and animations. JavaScript can respond when a user clicks a button.

content.topicNotes: Head Section and Metadata Page title The <title> tag defines the page title. The page title appears in the browser tab. It helps users identify the web page quickly. Each web page should have a clear, unique title. Meta tags overview Meta tags provide information about a web page. They are placed inside the <head> section. They are not displayed on the page itself. Search engines use meta tags to understand pages. Charset and author The charset defines character encoding using <meta charset="UTF-8">. UTF-8 allows most characters and symbols to display correctly. Author meta data identifies the creator of the page. This information is useful for documentation and ownership. Description and keywords A description meta tag summarises the web page content. Keywords help search engines identify page topics. Example: <meta name="description" content="ICT notes">. Keywords improve search engine visibility. Viewport settings The viewport controls how a page displays on different devices. It ensures content fits mobile and desktop screens. Example: <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">. It helps make websites responsive.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Website Authoring > Creating a Web Page

content.topicNotes: Style Consistency What is a Style? A style is a set of formatting settings. Styles control fonts, colours and spacing. Users can apply styles to headings and text. Styles help documents to be more organised and consistent. Consistent Presentation Consistency means keeping the same appearance throughout a document. Styles ensure headings and paragraphs match. This improves readability for users. Creating and Modifying Styles Users can create custom styles for documents. A custom style is a user-defined formatting set. Existing styles can be modified when needed. Changes update all text using that style automatically. Applying Styles Styles can be applied to titles, headings and body text. Applying styles saves time when formatting. Users avoid changing each section individually. This reduces formatting errors in documents. Advantages of Styles Styles improve the appearance of documents. They make updates faster and easier. Consistent formatting helps users navigate information. Styles are useful in long or complex documents.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Styles > Styles

content.topicNotes: Validation & Verification Why Data Checking Matters Data checking helps reduce errors in stored information. Accurate data improves decision-making and reliability. Validation and verification perform different checks. Organisations often use both methods together. Verification Verification checks that data has been entered correctly. It compares entered data with the original source. Verification reduces data entry errors. It does not check whether the data is sensible. Methods of Verification Visual checking compares entered data with the source document. Double data entry requires data to be entered twice. The system compares both entries for differences. Users correct any mismatched data. Setting up and re-entering a new password is an example of verification. Validation Validation checks whether data follows predefined rules. A validation rule is a condition that data must meet. Validation helps prevent invalid data entry. It does not guarantee that data is correct. Need for Both Validation and verification serve different purposes. Verification checks accuracy against the source. Validation checks whether data is sensible and acceptable. Using both methods improves overall data quality.

content.topicNotes: What are Headers and Footers? Headers & Footers Headers appear in the top margin of a document page. Margins are the blank spaces around the edges of a page. Footers appear in the bottom margin of a document page. Software duplicates the headers and footers' content automatically across multiple pages. Purpose of Headers & Footers Headers are typically used to display the document title, chapter name, or logos. Footers are used to display page numbers or the current date. Headers and footers save time and effort by applying the relevant information to all pages. Section breaks enable distinct headers, footers, restarted page counts, or custom margins within separate parts of one file. Practical exams typically ask students to place their credentials alongside an automated file name or path in the footer. Automated Fields Automated fields update their data dynamically without manual editing. Automated fields are placeholders that fetch live system information. Users insert automated fields to show the current date or total page count. Dynamic fields save time and prevent consistency errors across long reports.

content.topicNotes: The Content Layer Purpose of the Content Layer The content layer contains the information displayed on a web page. Users enter text, images and other page content in this layer. The content layer provides the meaning and purpose of a web page. It forms the foundation of website development. Creating Structure The content layer creates the structure of a web page. Structure organises content into sections and headings. A clear structure helps users find information quickly. Well-structured pages improve usability. Using HTML HTML stands for HyperText Markup Language. HTML is used to create the content layer of a web page. HTML tags define headings, paragraphs, lists and images. HTML organises content into a logical structure. Types of Content The content layer can contain text, images, tables and hyperlinks. A hyperlink is a clickable link to another location. Different content types help communicate information. Users select content that matches the page purpose. Importance of the Content Layer The content layer ensures information is available to users. It separates content from presentation and behaviour. This separation makes websites easier to create and maintain. A strong content layer improves the effectiveness of a website.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Website Authoring > Web Development Layers

content.topicNotes: Tissue Engineering What tissue engineering is Tissue engineering creates new body tissues to repair damage. Scientists combine cells, materials, and technology. Computers support accurate design and planning. Computer modelling Computers create models of tissues before they are grown. A model is a digital representation of a real object. Modelling helps scientists predict how tissues will grow. 3D printing Some tissue engineering uses 3D printing controlled by computers. 3D printing builds objects layer by layer. Computers ensure tissues form the correct shape and size. Medical benefits Tissue engineering can replace damaged skin, bone, or cartilage. Computers improve accuracy and reduce human error. This leads to better patient recovery.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > ICT Applications > Computers in Medicine

content.topicNotes: Touch Screens Touch screen A touch screen is an input device that detects touch on the display surface. Users interact by tapping, swiping or pinching the screen. A touch screen acts as both an input and output device. Touch screens are commonly used on smartphones, tablets and kiosks. Touch input allows direct interaction with on-screen items. Uses of touch screens Touch screens are used in smartphones for apps and communication. ATMs and ticket machines use touch screens for public access. Tablets use touch screens for drawing and note-taking. Retail systems use touch screens at checkouts. Touch screens reduce the need for separate keyboards and mice. Advantages and disadvantages a touch screen Advantages of a touch screen A touch screen is intuitive and easy to use. A touch screen does not require an additional pointing device. Disadvantages of a touch screen A touch screen can become dirty or damaged. A touch screen may be less precise for detailed tasks.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Input & Output Devices > Input Devices

content.topicNotes: Touch Screens and Multimedia Projectors Touch screens as output devices A touch screen is an output device that displays visual information. It shows text, images and videos generated by the computer. Touch screens also act as input devices. An input device allows users to send data to a computer. Output appears directly on the same surface that is touched. Uses of touch screens Touch screens are used on smartphones and tablets to display apps. ATMs use touch screens to show menus and options. Interactive whiteboards display content in classrooms. Touch screens are used in self-service kiosks. They allow direct and intuitive interaction. Pros and Cons of a Touch Screen Advantages Touch screens save space by combining input and output. Disadvantages Touch screens have reduced accuracy for fine detail. The screen can become easily smudged with fingerprints or dirty, which reduces visibility. Multimedia projector A multimedia projector is an output device that displays images onto a large screen. It receives signals from a computer or media player. Images are projected using light and lenses. Projectors display presentations, videos, and images. They are used where large audiences need to see output. Pros and Cons of a Projector Advantages Projectors produce large displays Disadvantages Bright light can reduce image quality Projectors require regular maintenance. Projector bulbs are expensive to replace and the unit can overheat during prolonged use.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Input & Output Devices > Output Devices

content.topicNotes: Traffic Management Modelling What is traffic management modelling Traffic management modelling uses computer software to simulate traffic flow. Models represent roads, junctions and vehicles. The aim is to improve traffic movement and safety. Computer models predict congestion and delays. Modelling helps plan transport systems effectively. How traffic models work Data such as vehicle numbers and road layouts is entered. Traffic lights and junction timings are included in the model. A variable is a value that can be changed, such as traffic volume. The computer simulates traffic over time. Results show how changes affect traffic flow. Uses of traffic management modelling Local authorities use models to design road systems. Traffic light timings are tested to reduce congestion. Roadworks impact can be predicted before work starts. Public transport routes can be planned more efficiently. Accident risk areas can be identified. Advantages and disadvantages Advantages: Traffic problems can be tested without disrupting roads. Changes can reduce congestion and pollution. Simulations can be sped up to quickly see years of simulated traffic growth. Disadvantages: Models depend on accurate traffic data. Human behaviour is difficult to predict exactly.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > ICT Applications > Modelling Applications

content.topicNotes: Two-Factor Authentication What is 2FA? Two-factor authentication (2FA) uses two methods to verify identity. It adds extra security beyond a password. Authentication is the process of confirming a user's identity. How 2FA Works Users enter a password as the first factor. A second factor is then required. There are different kinds of second factor. Most common is a code sent to a device. Access is only granted when both factors are correct. Types of Factors Something you know, for example, passwords or PINs (Personal Identification Number). Something you have, for example, a phone or a hardware token. Something you are and what makes you unique, for example, biometrics like fingerprints. Purpose of 2FA 2FA protects sensitive data and accounts. It makes it harder for attackers to gain access. Even if a password is stolen, access is still protected by the second factor. It is widely used in banking and online services.

content.topicNotes: User Documentation What is user documentation User documentation provides end users information on how to install and operate the system. It explains how to use the system step by step. User documentation is written in simple and clear language. It helps users complete tasks correctly and safely. Good documentation reduces training time. Contents of user documentation A user guide includes instructions for common tasks. Screenshots show users what to expect on screen. A troubleshooting section helps users understand error messages and solve common problems. Contact details for technical support are provided. Frequently asked questions (FAQs) may be included. Examples in daily life A school system guide shows teachers how to record attendance. Online banking help pages explain how to transfer money. Software manuals explain how to install and update programs. Video tutorials demonstrate how to use new features. Help buttons provide instant on-screen assistance. Advantages and risks Advantages Users can solve problems without technical support. Clear guidance reduces user errors. Risks Poor documentation can confuse users. Outdated instructions may lead to mistakes.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > The Systems Life Cycle > Documenting the New System

content.topicNotes: User ID and Password What is a User ID? A user ID is a unique identifier for a user. It identifies who is accessing a system. Each user has their own user ID. It is used together with a password for security. What is a Password? A password is a secret word or code. It is used to verify a user's identity. Only the authorised user should know it. It prevents unauthorised access to data. How They Work Together The user enters a user ID to identify themselves. The password confirms their identity. Authentication checks if the details are correct. Access is granted only when both match stored data. Systems may lock accounts after failed attempts. This helps against brute-force attacks. A brute-force attack is an automated hacking method where a computer repeatedly guesses every possible combination of letters, numbers, and symbols until it finds the correct password. Improving Security Strong passwords should be long and complex. Users should include uppercase and lowercase letters, numbers and symbols. Passwords should not be shared with others. Regular password changes improve security. Users should not reuse passwords across accounts.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Safety & Security > Security of Data

content.topicNotes: Expert Systems – User Interface What is the user interface The user interface is the part of the expert system that the user interacts with. The interface allows the user to enter data and receive advice. Most expert systems use a question-and-answer format. Questions are presented clearly and logically. The interface makes the system easy to use. How the interface gathers information The system asks a series of structured questions. Answers may be selected from options or typed in. The interface guides the user step by step. The system may ask follow-up questions based on previous answers. Input provided by the user is forwarded directly to the inference engine. Accurate input improves the quality of advice. Output from the expert system The system presents conclusions or recommendations. The output may include explanations for the decision. Explanations show how the inference engine reached the conclusion. The user can review or print the advice. Clear output improves user understanding. Advantages and limitations Advantages A simple interface makes expert systems accessible to non-experts. Guided questions reduce user errors. Limitations Incorrect answers produce incorrect advice. Complex cases may not be fully supported by the interface.

content.topicNotes: Users and System Requirements Identifying Users The analyst identifies all users of the current system. Different users have different access levels and tasks. An access level is the amount of data or features a user can use. The analyst considers user skills and training needs. User Requirements User requirements describe what users need the system to do. The analyst gathers requirements using interviews and questionnaires. Requirements may include speed, accuracy and security. System Requirements System requirements describe the technical features of the new system. They include hardware, software and storage needs. Hardware means the physical parts of a computer system. Software means the programs that run on the hardware. They also specify non-functional requirements (NFRs), which define overall quality standards rather than specific features. Non-functional requirements cover system response times, hardware/software compatibility, security protocols, and reliability targets. Requirements Specification The analyst produces a requirements specification document that lists all agreed user and system requirements. It acts as a reference during design and development. The organisation uses it to evaluate the finished system.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > The Systems Life Cycle > Analysing the Current System

content.topicNotes: Validation Checks Purpose of Validation Validation is the process of checking data against pre-defined rules before processing. Validation checks ensure entered data is sensible. It helps reduce data entry errors and therefore improves data quality and reliability. Range and Character Checks A range check ensures data falls between set limits.For example, a test score must be between 0 and 100. A character check ensures only allowed characters are entered. For example, a name should not contain numbers. Length and Type Checks A length check ensures data contains the correct number of characters.A password may require at least eight characters. A type check ensures the correct data type is entered.For example, an age field should contain numbers. Format and Presence Checks A format check ensures data follows a required pattern.An email address must follow a valid email format. A presence check ensures a field is not left blank. Required fields must contain data before submission. Importance of Validation Validation helps prevent incorrect data from being stored. It reduces the need to correct errors later. Validation does not guarantee data is accurate. It only checks whether data meets defined rules.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Proofing > Software Tools

content.topicNotes: Video, Audio and Web Conferences What are online conferences Online conferences allow people to communicate over a network in real time. Communication can include audio, video and shared content. Participants use computers or mobile devices. An internet connection is required. Online conferences support remote communication. Audio conferencing Audio conferencing allows users to communicate using sound only. Microphones capture speech and speakers output sound. Audio conferencing uses less bandwidth than video. Bandwidth is the amount of data that can be transmitted. Audio conferences are useful when video is not needed. Video conferencing Video conferencing allows users to see and hear each other. Web cameras capture live video. Video conferencing supports face-to-face communication remotely. More bandwidth is required than audio-only communication. Video conferencing is used for meetings and lessons. Web conferencing Web conferencing includes audio, video and screen sharing. Screen sharing allows users to view another person’s screen. Presentations and documents can be shared live. Web conferencing supports collaboration. Many businesses use web conferencing for remote work. Hardware and Software Requirements Input devices A webcam is required to capture live video. A microphone is needed to capture voice input. Output devices A monitor or screen displays video feeds and shared content. Speakers or headphones output incoming sound. Network hardware A router or Network Interface Card (NIC) connects the device to high-speed internet. Software Dedicated conferencing applications or a web browser are used to connect participants. Advantages and disadvantages Advantages Travel costs and time are reduced. Remote collaboration is made easier. Disadvantages A reliable internet connection is required. Technical problems can disrupt communication.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Networks and the Effects of Using Them > Network Communications

content.topicNotes: Avoiding Malware from Downloads Risk of Downloaded Files Downloaded files may contain malware which is harmful software designed to damage systems. Files from unknown sources are higher risk. Opening infected files can spread viruses. Trusted Sources Users should download files from trusted websites. A trusted source is a reliable and verified provider. Official websites reduce the risk of malware. Third-party sites may contain modified harmful files. Antivirus Protection Antivirus software scans files before opening and detects and removes malicious software. Real-time protection checks files automatically. Regular updates improve detection of new threats. Safe Behaviour Users should avoid clicking unknown download links. Email attachments from unknown senders should not be opened. Software should be kept up to date. This regularly fixes security weaknesses in systems.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Safety & Security > Security of Data

content.topicNotes: Visual Verification What is Visual Verification? Visual verification is the process of checking data by sight. Users compare entered data with the original source. This helps identify data entry errors. It improves the accuracy of completed work. Transposed Numbers A transposed number error occurs when digits are swapped. For example, 54 may be entered as 45. Users should compare numbers carefully. Visual verification helps detect these mistakes. Automated validation, like check digits, detects swapped numbers in long IDs and barcodes. Spelling Errors Users should check words against the original source. Incorrect spelling can change the meaning of information. Visual verification helps identify spelling mistakes. Corrections improve the quality of documents. Spacing and Case Character spacing is the space between letters or words. Inconsistent spacing can make text more difficult to read. Case refers to uppercase and lowercase letters. Users should correct inconsistent case throughout a document. Benefits of Visual Verification Visual verification helps improve data accuracy. It identifies errors that automated tools may miss. Consistent and accurate data is easier to understand. Careful checking produces professional work.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Proofing > Proofing Techniques

content.topicNotes: VoIP and Video Calling Voice over Internet Protocol (VoIP) Voice over Internet Protocol (VoIP) allows voice calls using the internet. Voice data is converted into digital packets. Data packets are transmitted over an internet connection. VoIP does not use traditional phone networks. Examples include internet-based calling services. Uses of VoIP Businesses use VoIP for low-cost international calls. Users make voice calls using smartphones or computers. VoIP supports group calls and conferencing. Calls can be made wherever internet access is available. VoIP reduces reliance on mobile network minutes. Video calling Video calling allows users to see and hear each other in real time. Web cameras capture live video. Microphones capture voice input. Video calling requires more bandwidth than voice-only calls. Internet access is essential for video calling. Advantages and disadvantages Advantages VoIP and video calling are often cheaper than traditional calls. Visual communication improves understanding. Disadvantages Call quality depends on internet speed. Poor connections can cause latency (a time delay between when data is sent and when it is received) or dropped calls.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > ICT Applications > Communication Media

content.topicNotes: Voice-Activated and Gesture-Based Interfaces Voice Activated Assistants Voice-activated assistants respond to spoken commands. They use speech recognition to understand a user's voice. They can search for information and answer questions. They can control smart devices and perform everyday tasks. Examples include Siri, Google Assistant and Amazon Alexa. Gesture-based interface A gesture-based interface allows users to control a system using physical movements. Gestures are body or hand movements detected by sensors or cameras. Touch screens detect finger gestures such as swiping or pinching. Gesture-based interfaces allow natural and intuitive interaction. Smartphones and gaming systems often use gesture control. Advantages of gesture-based interfaces Gesture-based interfaces are intuitive and easy to learn. Users can interact without physical controllers. They are useful where keyboards or mice are impractical. They improve accessibility for some users. Visual feedback helps users understand actions.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Types & Components of Computer Systems > User Interfaces

content.topicNotes: Weather Forecasting Modelling What is weather forecasting modelling Weather forecasting modelling uses computers to predict future weather conditions. Models represent the atmosphere and weather systems. Large amounts of data are processed by computers. Forecasts predict temperature, rainfall and wind. Modelling helps people prepare for weather events. How weather models work Data is collected from satellites, weather stations and sensors. Variables include temperature, air pressure and humidity. A variable is a value that can change. The data is processed through mathematical equations. Supercomputers process the massive volume of live data and simulate how weather systems change over time. Uses of weather forecasting Weather forecasts help people plan daily activities. Farmers use forecasts to plan planting and harvesting. Airlines use weather models to plan safe flight routes. Emergency services prepare for extreme weather. Accurate forecasts reduce risk to life and property. Advantages and disadvantages Advantages Large areas can be analysed quickly. Early warnings can be given for severe weather. Disadvantages Forecasts are not always completely accurate. Sudden weather changes are difficult to predict.

content.topicNotes: Websites What is a website A website is a collection of related web pages, which are accessed using a web browser. Websites are stored on web servers accessed through the internet. Websites are a common digital communication medium. Uses of websites Businesses use websites to promote products and services. Schools use websites to share information with students and parents. Governments use websites to provide public information. Websites support online shopping and bookings. Individuals use websites to share content and ideas. Features of websites Websites can include text, images, audio and video. Hyperlinks allow users to navigate between pages. Interactive elements include forms and buttons. Content can be updated quickly and easily. Websites can target a global audience. Advantages and disadvantages Advantages Websites can reach a large audience worldwide. Information can be updated instantly. Disadvantages Internet access is required. Poor design can make information difficult to find.

content.topicNotes: Why Compress Files? Saving Storage Space Compression reduces the overall size of a file so it occupies less physical space on a storage medium. Storage Medium: a secondary storage device such as a Hard Disk Drive (HDD) or Solid State Drive (SSD) used to keep data permanently. This allows users to store more files, such as high-resolution images or videos, on a single device. Smaller file sizes help manage data more efficiently when storage capacity is limited. Faster File Transmission Smaller files travel more quickly across a network or the internet. Transmission: the process of sending data from one computer system to another over a communication channel. Reducing file size shortens the upload and download times for users. This is essential for streaming services or when sending large datasets over low-bandwidth connections. Bandwidth: the maximum rate of data transfer across a network path. Email Attachment Limits Most email service providers set a maximum limit on the size of file attachments. Compression enables users to send large documents or folders that would otherwise exceed these limits. Attachment: a file that is sent along with an email message. Users often bundle multiple files into a single compressed folder, such as a .zip file, to make sharing simpler and more reliable. Cost Efficiency Reducing file sizes can lower the costs associated with data storage and transfers. Cloud storage providers often charge users based on the amount of space they occupy. Cloud Storage: a service where data is remotely maintained, managed, and backed up over the internet. Organisations save money by compressing archived data that they do not need to access frequently.

content.topicNotes: Why Test Before Implementing Purpose of testing Testing checks that a new system works as intended. Developers compare actual results with expected results. Errors found during testing are called bugs. Testing ensures the system meets user requirements. Early testing reduces the risk of failure after launch. Types of errors Syntax errors occur when code breaks language rules. Logic errors occur when the program produces incorrect results. Runtime errors occur while the program is running. Testing identifies these errors before users see them. Fixing errors early is less expensive than fixing them later. Daily-life example A school registration system must calculate attendance correctly. Test data is entered to check calculations and validation. Expected results are compared with actual output. Incorrect totals show that logic needs correction. Testing prevents incorrect reports being sent to parents. Advantages of testing Testing improves system reliability and stability. Users gain confidence in a well-tested system. Data accuracy is improved before implementation. Security weaknesses can be identified. Downtime and disruption are reduced after release. Risks of not testing Unidentified bugs may cause system crashes. Incorrect calculations may affect business decisions. Security flaws may allow hacking or data breaches. Poor user experience can damage reputation. Fixing faults after implementation is more costly.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > The Systems Life Cycle > Developing & Testing the New System

content.topicNotes: Wi-Fi What Wi-Fi Is Wi-Fi stands for Wireless Fidelity Wi-Fi is a wireless technology that connects devices to a network. It uses radio waves instead of cables. A Wi-Fi router provides the wireless signal. How Wi-Fi Works Devices connect to a wireless access point to join a Wi-Fi network. The access point sends and receives data using radio signals with several different frequencies. The most common frequencies are 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz, where a connection with 5 GHz is faster but has less range. Wi-Fi networks use SSIDs to identify the network name. SSID stands for Service Set Identifier. Advantages of Wi-Fi Wi-Fi provides high data transmission speeds, making it ideal for streaming high-definition video and sharing large files. Wi-Fi allows devices to move around without cables. It supports many devices in homes and schools. It makes it easy to connect laptops and phones. It is suitable for general internet use. Limitations of Wi-Fi Wi-Fi signals can be weaker through walls and floors. The connection can slow down with many users. Interference from other devices can reduce speed. Wi-Fi is less secure if it uses weak passwords.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Networks and the Effects of Using Them > Bluetooth & Wi-Fi

content.topicNotes: Word Processing, Spreadsheet & DBMS Word Processing Software Word processing software allows users to create, edit, and format text documents. Users can change fonts, add images, and check spelling and grammar. Word processing software is commonly used for letters, reports, and essays. Spreadsheet Software Spreadsheet software organises data into rows and columns. Single data entries in these rows and columns are called cells. Users can perform calculations using formulas and functions. Spreadsheet software is often used for budgets, timetables, and data analysis. Database Management Systems A database management system (DBMS) is application software. It is used to create, store and manage databases. It organises data so it can be accessed efficiently. It allows users to search, sort and update records. Examples include Microsoft Access and MySQL.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Types & Components of Computer Systems > Applications Software

content.topicNotes: Wrapping Text Around Images Text Wrap Basics Users apply text wrapping to control how document text flows around an inserted graphic. Text Wrapping: a feature that allows text to surround an image rather than treating the image as a single large character. Designers use this to integrate images naturally within paragraphs of a report or newsletter. This technique ensures that there is no large, awkward white space around the image area. Common Wrapping Styles - Part 1 In line with text: treats the image like a piece of text within the sentence or paragraph. Square: forces the text to flow around the rectangular border of the image frame. Tight: allows the text to follow the actual contours or outline of the image. Contours: the outer edges or shape of an object. Through: enables text to flow into any open white space or gaps within the image itself. Common Wrapping Styles - Part 2 Top and Bottom: places text only above and below the graphic, leaving the sides empty. Behind text: positions the image on a layer underneath the words so they overlap the graphic. Behind text is useful to set a background image in a document. In front of text: places the image on the top layer so it covers any text behind it.
content.description: ICT: Cambridge International GCSE > Images > Images

content.topicNotes: Zero Login and Biometric Methods Zero login Zero login is a security method that does not require a password. The system recognises the user automatically. Authentication blends physical traits with behaviour patterns. Recognition may use a trusted device or location. Zero login reduces the need to remember passwords. This method improves convenience for users. Biometric authentication Biometric authentication uses unique physical characteristics. Physical characteristics include fingerprints, facial features or iris patterns. Biometric data is stored securely on the system. The system compares live input with stored data. Only matching data allows access. Uses of biometric methods Smartphones use fingerprints or face recognition to unlock devices. Airports use biometrics for identity verification. Secure buildings use biometric access control. Schools may use biometrics for attendance systems. Biometrics reduce the risk of password sharing. Advantages and disadvantages Advantages Biometric methods are difficult to copy or guess. Zero login improves speed and ease of access. Disadvantages Biometric systems can be expensive to install. Biometric data cannot be changed if compromised.
